u9d3496952b3d2c0dbde6.text: The ⟦0⟧ file stores custom CPU models, which can be used by VMs to get access to advanced CPU features (for example custom CPU flags).

u27dfa0c47b6180937f38.text: CPU models each have their own section in the file, beginning with the header:

ue76bf269e96b31b67670.text: Note that <name> does not include the ⟦0⟧custom-⟦1⟧ prefix, which is required in VM configs to denote custom CPU models.

u016a81ba5ad26a2335e7.text: For example, if the <name> is ⟦0⟧foobar⟦1⟧, the CPU for a VM would need to be configured as ⟦2⟧custom-foobar⟦3⟧.

ubaf3d33dc2e59f5d2d2d.text: Each section can specify several options. They are indented by either one TAB character or multiple spaces. Every option and its value is separated by one space, for example:

u279943af416be00f47b6.text: See below for all available options.

u623cf59744dad3f6098a.text: Blank lines and those starting with a ⟦0⟧ are ignored.

u75a4fddb0b15007542ad.text: List of additional CPU flags separated by ⟦0⟧;⟦1⟧. Use ⟦2⟧+FLAG⟦3⟧ to enable, ⟦4⟧-FLAG⟦5⟧ to disable a flag. There is a special ⟦6⟧nested-virt⟦7⟧ shorthand which controls nested virtualization for the current CPU (⟦8⟧svm⟦9⟧ for AMD and ⟦10⟧vmx⟦11⟧ for Intel). Custom CPU models can specify any flag supported by QEMU/KVM, VM-specific flags must be from the following set for security reasons: aes, amd-no-ssb, amd-ssbd, hv-evmcs, hv-tlbflush, ibpb, md-clear, nested-virt, pcid, pdpe1gb, spec-ctrl, ssbd, virt-ssbd

uce1435e6979cb2830b6b.text: Describes the policy for handling HA services on poweroff or reboot of a node. Freeze will always freeze services which are still located on the node on shutdown, those services won’t be recovered by the HA manager. Failover will not mark the services as frozen and thus the services will get recovered to other nodes, if the shutdown node does not come up again quickly (< 1min). ⟦0⟧conditional⟦1⟧ chooses automatically depending on the type of shutdown, i.e., on a reboot the service will be frozen but on a poweroff the service will stay as is, and thus get recovered after about 2 minutes. Migrate will try to move all running services to another node when a reboot or shutdown was triggered. The poweroff process will only continue once no running services are located on the node anymore. If the node comes up again, the service will be moved back to the previously powered-off node, at least if no other migration, reloaction or recovery took place.

ucad3e36eacae8e5ad5e8.text: Our modern society depends heavily on information provided by computers over the network. Mobile devices amplified that dependency, because people can access the network any time from anywhere. If you provide such services, it is very important that they are available most of the time.

u5287ffb3d0d344cbce9c.text: We can mathematically define the availability as the ratio of (A), the total time a service is capable of being used during a given interval to (B), the length of the interval. It is normally expressed as a percentage of uptime in a given year.

ubbbe0fdb36fd241c15d7.text: There are several ways to increase availability. The most elegant solution is to rewrite your software, so that you can run it on several hosts at the same time. The software itself needs to have a way to detect errors and do failover. If you only want to serve read-only web pages, then this is relatively simple. However, this is generally complex and sometimes impossible, because you cannot modify the software yourself. The following solutions works without modifying the software:

u672af3a15adc1dd18efa.text: Computer components with the same functionality can have varying reliability numbers, depending on the component quality. Most vendors sell components with higher reliability as “server” components - usually at higher price.

u6bd249328318d6abe14e.text: Eliminate single point of failure (redundant components)

uaaeb90f574b30a9c521d.text: use redundant power supplies in your servers

u8c10381bbf860f305596.text: use distributed, redundant storage for VM data

ucb8941876dc84233b31c.text: availability of spare parts (other nodes in a Proxmox VE cluster)

uae26da0ca84735fb996e.text: Virtualization environments like Proxmox VE make it much easier to reach high availability because they remove the “hardware” dependency. They also support the setup and use of redundant storage and network devices, so if one host fails, you can simply start those services on another host within your cluster.

u04a6edbc0ca47544fc79.text: Better still, Proxmox VE provides a software stack called ⟦0⟧, which can do that automatically for you. It is able to automatically detect errors and do automatic failover.

ua7edbae7454b29cab75f.text: Proxmox VE ⟦0⟧ works like an “automated” administrator. First, you configure what resources (VMs, containers, …) it should manage. Then, ⟦1⟧ observes the correct functionality, and handles service failover to another node in case of errors. ⟦2⟧ can also handle normal user requests which may start, stop, relocate and migrate a service.

u804fac08eeabca12ae1a.text: But high availability comes at a price. High quality components are more expensive, and making them redundant doubles the costs at least. Additional spare parts increase costs further. So you should carefully calculate the benefits, and compare with those additional costs.

u9083291b8fc67f51722c.text: Increasing availability from 99% to 99.9% is relatively simple. But increasing availability from 99.9999% to 99.99999% is very hard and costly. ⟦0⟧ has typical error detection and failover times of about 2 minutes, so you can get no more than 99.999% availability.

u4e425311b2106946188e.text: You must meet the following requirements before you start with HA:

u4c1fd40a44d8f6f61ba5.text: at least three cluster nodes (to get reliable quorum)

u59d7b56befb865211f9b.text: shared storage for VMs and containers

ud6dc94c75be539c5ce6b.text: Optionally, a hardware watchdog can be used - if not available we fall back to the linux kernel software watchdog (⟦0⟧).

u57f53d645c1397bdc147.text: The HA Manager’s primary management unit is called an HA resource (or “HA service”). Currently, an HA resource can be either a Virtual Machine (VM) or a Linux Container (CT).

u3b16f89d999f5087c994.text: Each HA resource is uniquely identified by a service ID (⟦0⟧), which consists of the resource type and a type-specific ID, which is the VMID for VMs and containers. For example, for the VM with VMID ⟦1⟧, the service ID is ⟦2⟧.

u94082fdb7770064db0c2.text: An HA resource can only run on nodes where all of its dependencies are available. By default, the HA Manager treats every cluster node as eligible. To keep this default, a VM or container should:

ua3735c4e1cdf9190d182.text: use options that are compatible with all cluster nodes

u598e2be14412eebe4944.text: use only shared storage that is accessible from all cluster nodes

u63ea479ba89573ada8b2.text: use only network interfaces that exist on all cluster nodes

u477d045c4253c87cfd7b.text: use only device passthroughs that are present on all cluster nodes

u68d2db62149172dc7aca.text: If any of these dependencies is only available on a subset of nodes, restrict the HA resource to that subset with a strict ⟦0⟧node affinity rule⟦1⟧. The HA Manager then limits placement, recovery, and migration to the rule’s nodes.

u6cec79d29dfa0cd6c19d.text: But all HA related tasks can be done in the GUI, so there is no need to use the command line at all.

ud63e9a49de4a9b7e7ec3.text: This section provides a detailed description of the Proxmox VE HA manager internals. It describes all involved daemons and how they work together. To provide HA, two daemons run on each node:

uefde43e7ec953c7e5834.text: The local resource manager (LRM), which controls the services running on the local node. It reads the requested states for its services from the current manager status file and executes the respective commands.

u93eb2b4fc7da1069e3fc.text: The cluster resource manager (CRM), which makes the cluster-wide decisions. It sends commands to the LRM, processes the results, and moves resources to other nodes if something fails. The CRM also handles node fencing.

uf34c2eff54153ab28ae9.text: ⟦0⟧Locks in the LRM & CRM⟦1⟧Locks are provided by our distributed configuration file system (pmxcfs). They are used to guarantee that each LRM is active once and working. As an LRM only executes actions when it holds its lock, we can mark a failed node as fenced if we can acquire its lock. This then lets us recover any failed HA services securely without any interference from the now unknown failed node. This all gets supervised by the CRM which currently holds the manager master lock.

ud817cd0529a2d11fe158.text: The CRM uses a service state enumeration to record the current service state. This state is displayed on the GUI and can be queried using the ⟦0⟧ command-line tool:

u98e29ec63813d9761db7.text: Here is the list of possible states:

uf2a1a510ab0c5aff1073.text: Service is stopped (confirmed by LRM). If the LRM detects a stopped service is still running, it will stop it again.

uc720507dbee98968566c.text: Service should be stopped. The CRM waits for confirmation from the LRM.

u929585c1ee91cb8799b7.text: Pending stop request. But the CRM did not get the request so far.

u2d00728475d0ce3792ea.text: Service is active an LRM should start it ASAP if not already running. If the Service fails and is detected to be not running the LRM restarts it (see ⟦0⟧Start Failure Policy⟦1⟧).

ub693ed28519cc0611d4b.text: Pending start request. But the CRM has not got any confirmation from the LRM that the service is running.

u058b5709a0a4762633c9.text: Wait for node fencing as the service node is not inside the quorate cluster partition (see ⟦0⟧Fencing⟦1⟧). As soon as node gets fenced successfully the service will be placed into the recovery state.

u2753ab708d99db7ae1fb.text: Wait for recovery of the service. The HA manager tries to find a new node where the service can run on. This search depends on the list of online and quorate nodes as well as the affinity rules the service is part of, if any. As soon as a new available node is found, the service will be moved there and initially placed into stopped state. If it’s configured to run the new node will do so.

ud731124f7a87c10a864d.text: Do not touch the service state. We use this state while we reboot a node, or when we restart the LRM daemon (see ⟦0⟧Package Updates⟦1⟧).

ud7f70b419f0e930eaef5.text: Act as if the service were not managed by HA at all. Useful, when full control over the service is desired temporarily, without removing it from the HA configuration.

u3ae1c2660bcdb07b6b00.text: Service is disabled because of LRM errors. Needs manual intervention (see ⟦0⟧Error Recovery⟦1⟧).

u5318ad918d112709a84e.text: Service is newly added, and the CRM has not seen it so far.

u6660941a7c3f6a5ef126.text: Service is stopped and marked as ⟦0⟧

ub779e5fb534cf7a1927e.text: The local resource manager (⟦0⟧) is started as a daemon on boot and waits until the HA cluster is quorate and thus cluster-wide locks are working.

udebfe2b694cb8cb3f424.text: It can be in three states:

ud5d0044cb7b466b71277.text: The LRM waits for our exclusive lock. This is also used as idle state if no service is configured.

ua4725a735ea0c6266a34.text: The LRM holds its exclusive lock and has services configured.

u9434ec877bf084aae2a2.text: The LRM lost its lock, this means a failure happened and quorum was lost.

u6ba04e805e335151b69a.text: After the LRM gets in the active state it reads the manager status file in ⟦0⟧ and determines the commands it has to execute for the services it owns. For each command a worker gets started, these workers are running in parallel and are limited to at most 4 by default. This default setting may be changed through the datacenter configuration key ⟦1⟧. When finished the worker process gets collected and its result saved for the CRM.

ue75f3d38d1352f6223ab.text: ⟦0⟧Maximum Concurrent Worker Adjustment Tips⟦1⟧The default value of at most 4 concurrent workers may be unsuited for a specific setup. For example, 4 live migrations may occur at the same time, which can lead to network congestions with slower networks and/or big (memory wise) services. Also, ensure that in the worst case, congestion is at a minimum, even if this means lowering the ⟦2⟧ value. On the contrary, if you have a particularly powerful, high-end setup you may also want to increase it.

ud00c3e9928c7728da329.text: Each command requested by the CRM is uniquely identifiable by a UID. When the worker finishes, its result will be processed and written in the LRM status file ⟦0⟧. There the CRM may collect it and let its state machine - respective to the commands output - act on it.

u234c73237927d936a59f.text: The actions on each service between CRM and LRM are normally always synced. This means that the CRM requests a state uniquely marked by a UID, the LRM then executes this action ⟦0⟧one time⟦1⟧ and writes back the result, which is also identifiable by the same UID. This is needed so that the LRM does not execute an outdated command. The only exceptions to this behaviour are the ⟦2⟧ and ⟦3⟧ commands; these two do not depend on the result produced and are executed always in the case of the stopped state and once in the case of the error state.

u946a6c6399d575f9aae4.text: ⟦0⟧Read the Logs⟦1⟧The HA Stack logs every action it makes. This helps to understand what and also why something happens in the cluster. Here its important to see what both daemons, the LRM and the CRM, did. You may use ⟦2⟧ on the node(s) where the service is and the same command for the pve-ha-crm on the node which is the current master.

ud0a1a8bec6c8ebe1968a.text: The cluster resource manager (⟦0⟧) starts on each node and waits there for the manager lock, which can only be held by one node at a time. The node which successfully acquires the manager lock gets promoted to the CRM master.

ucd967199653c5690c03a.text: The CRM waits for our exclusive lock. This is also used as idle state if no service is configured

uc8a9c63c6e4fbd4c1c9b.text: The CRM holds its exclusive lock and has services configured

u5077ef3ad6073644dd8d.text: The CRM lost its lock, this means a failure happened and quorum was lost.

ua58e4f056cc3672aacf2.text: Its main task is to manage the services which are configured to be highly available and try to always enforce the requested state. For example, a service with the requested state ⟦0⟧started⟦1⟧ will be started if its not already running. If it crashes it will be automatically started again. Thus the CRM dictates the actions the LRM needs to execute.

u3153ab1e12f48429f3c5.text: When a node leaves the cluster quorum, its state changes to unknown. If the current CRM can then secure the failed node’s lock, the services will be ⟦0⟧stolen⟦1⟧ and restarted on another node.

u11ec698f0d4e8ccbdabe.text: When a cluster member determines that it is no longer in the cluster quorum, the LRM waits for a new quorum to form. Until there is a cluster quorum, the node cannot reset the watchdog. If there are active services on the node, or if the LRM or CRM process is not scheduled or is killed, this will trigger a reboot after the watchdog has timed out (this happens after 60 seconds).

u741a3422a3b6109aa963.text: Note that if a node has an active CRM but the LRM is idle, a quorum loss will not trigger a self-fence reset. The reason for this is that all state files and configurations that the CRM accesses are backed up by the ⟦0⟧clustered configuration file system⟦1⟧, which becomes read-only upon quorum loss. This means that the CRM only needs to protect itself against its process being scheduled for too long, in which case another CRM could take over unaware of the situation, causing corruption of the HA state. The open watchdog ensures that this cannot happen.

u398a60bfc93abf9ff6b3.text: If no service is configured for more than 15 minutes, the CRM automatically returns to the idle state and closes the watchdog completely.

ua9a6a7a8cab77ad5e3e4.text: By using the HA simulator you can test and learn all functionalities of the Proxmox VE HA solutions.

ue41ec4903c7be04f78f6.text: By default, the simulator allows you to watch and test the behaviour of a real-world 3 node cluster with 6 VMs. You can also add or remove additional VMs or Container.

uaf3686d18ab71c01e210.text: You do not have to setup or configure a real cluster, the HA simulator runs out of the box.

u3aec93debbfb4a83b4c4.text: You can even install the package on any Debian-based system without any other Proxmox VE packages. For that you will need to download the package and copy it to the system you want to run it on for installation. When you install the package with apt from the local file system it will also resolve the required dependencies for you.

u0159c3036aa8f3c4331c.text: To start the simulator on a remote machine you must have an X11 redirection to your current system.

uf574392688ce6bf475ea.text: First you need to create a working directory where the simulator saves its current state and writes its default config:

u0f894e15bf235484cbfc.text: Then, simply pass the created directory as a parameter to ⟦0⟧pve-ha-simulator⟦1⟧:

udb858c9c3b88288e1db4.text: The HA stack is well integrated into the Proxmox VE API. So, for example, HA can be configured via the ⟦0⟧ command-line interface, or the Proxmox VE web interface - both interfaces provide an easy way to manage HA. Automation tools can use the API directly.

u7200bc5e6c0fca1853ba.text: All HA configuration files are within ⟦0⟧, so they get automatically distributed to the cluster nodes, and all nodes share the same HA configuration.

u81df0bcd69a35af3b04f.text: The resource configuration file ⟦0⟧ stores the list of resources managed by ⟦1⟧. A resource configuration inside that list looks like this:

u146887216785b0f6ecab.text: It starts with a resource type followed by a resource specific name, separated with colon. Together this forms the HA resource ID, which is used by all ⟦0⟧ commands to uniquely identify a resource (example: ⟦1⟧ or ⟦2⟧). The next lines contain additional properties:

u1e74316f85b0097cbd1d.text: Requested resource state. The CRM reads this state and acts accordingly. Please note that ⟦0⟧ is just an alias for ⟦1⟧.

ubcd50ccab2d5e1559911.text: The CRM tries to start the resource. Service state is set to ⟦0⟧ after successful start. On node failures, or when start fails, it tries to recover the resource. If everything fails, service state it set to ⟦1⟧.

u28654134101ace431560.text: The CRM tries to keep the resource in ⟦0⟧ state, but it still tries to relocate the resources on node failures.

u80f16b9c9f5da87f3224.text: The CRM tries to put the resource in ⟦0⟧ state, but does not try to relocate the resources on node failures. The main purpose of this state is error recovery, because it is the only way to move a resource out of the ⟦1⟧ state.

ua469819f511308c9fa69.text: The resource gets removed from the manager status and so the CRM and the LRM do not touch the resource anymore. All {pve} API calls affecting this resource will be executed, directly bypassing the HA stack. CRM commands will be thrown away while the resource is in this state. The resource will not get relocated on node failures.

ufcf401536e53b84ad821.text: HA Groups are deprecated and migrated to HA Node Affinity rules since Proxmox VE 9.0.

uac84ceb9f391a83a40a7.text: The HA group configuration file ⟦0⟧ is used to define groups of cluster nodes. A resource can be restricted to run only on the members of such group. A group configuration look like this:

u4dc6763c2ef1266a82ff.text: List of cluster node members, where a priority can be given to each node. A resource will run on the available nodes with the highest priority. If there are more nodes in the highest priority class, the resources will get distributed to those nodes. The priorities have a relative meaning only. The higher the number, the higher the priority.

u3357227becf7d5e73643.text: Resources bound to restricted groups may only run on nodes defined by the group. The resource will be placed in the stopped state if no group node member is online. Resources on unrestricted groups may run on any cluster node if all group members are offline, but they will migrate back as soon as a group member comes online. One can implement a ⟦0⟧preferred node⟦1⟧ behavior using an unrestricted group with only one member.

If ⟦1⟧ is not available, you want to run them equally split on ⟦2⟧ and ⟦3⟧. If those nodes also fail, the services should run on ⟦4⟧. To achieve this you could set the node list to:

u5cc490cdb701cfe2348e.text: The ⟦0⟧ options is mostly useful to avoid unwanted resource movements during administration tasks. For example, if you need to migrate a service to a node which doesn’t have the highest priority in the group, you need to tell the HA manager not to instantly move this service back by setting the ⟦1⟧ option.

u2e750b057d95d18c5d07.text: Another scenario is when a service was fenced and it got recovered to another node. The admin tries to repair the fenced node and brings it up online again to investigate the cause of failure and check if it runs stably again. Setting the ⟦0⟧ flag prevents the recovered services from moving straight back to the fenced node.

u6707312b74e79e4e01ff.text: HA rules are used to put certain constraints on HA-managed resources, which are defined in the HA rules configuration file ⟦0⟧.

u570e8f7d7b52d083c12a.text: Places affinity from one or more HA resources to one or more nodes.

u5ee057bd2ad2b41bc2ee.text: The affinity ⟦0⟧ specifies that HA resources should or must be kept on one of the specified nodes, while the affinity ⟦1⟧ specifies that the HA resources should or must avoid the specified nodes.

u994cff480ee7120f8c33.text: The strictness attribute ⟦0⟧ specifies whether it is a soft constraint ("should") or whether it is a hard constraint ("must").

u4a29d8e71b06648cc209.text: Places affinity between two or more HA resources.

u3cf7c4358cc14c2b67a7.text: The affinity ⟦0⟧ specifies that HA resources must be kept on the same node, while the affinity ⟦1⟧ specifies that HA resources must be kept on separate nodes.

ue0b5ba6f367bb7e609a1.text: By default, an HA resource is able to run on any cluster node, but a common requirement is that an HA resource should run on a specific node. That can be implemented by defining an HA node affinity rule to make the HA resource ⟦0⟧ prefer the node ⟦1⟧:

u0179e906b93671e2b362.text: By default, node affinity rules are not strict, i.e., if there is none of the specified nodes available, the HA resource can also be moved to other nodes. If, on the other hand, an HA resource must be restricted to the specified nodes, then the node affinity rule must be set to be strict.

ub5a32fad9680bc6a180f.text: In the previous example, the node affinity rule can be modified to restrict the resource ⟦0⟧ to be only on ⟦1⟧:

u041a30800dbf51863c0c.text: Furthermore, node affinity rules use positive affinity by default, meaning that the preferred cluster nodes must be explicitly specified. However, in larger clusters, it is often more practical to define node affinity using an opt-out approach to avoid long and verbose lists of cluster nodes. For example, the following command defines an HA node affinity rule that makes the HA resources ⟦0⟧ and ⟦1⟧ avoid the node ⟦2⟧:

uc9e49c1d5c865b0d7638.text: Moreover, specific use cases might require defining a more detailed failover behavior. For example, the resources ⟦0⟧ and ⟦1⟧ should run on ⟦2⟧. If ⟦3⟧ becomes unavailable, the resources should be distributed on ⟦4⟧ and ⟦5⟧. If ⟦6⟧ and ⟦7⟧ are also unavailable, the resources should run on ⟦8⟧.

ubc6b868e5e76ebbf96ce.text: To implement this behavior in a node affinity rule, nodes can be paired with priorities to order the preference for nodes. If two or more nodes have the same priority, the resources can run on any of them. For the above example, ⟦0⟧ gets the highest priority, ⟦1⟧ and ⟦2⟧ get the same priority, and at last ⟦3⟧ gets the lowest priority, which can be omitted to default to ⟦4⟧:

u9c625db5f33d81b357c0.text: A non-strict node affinity rule makes resources prefer to be on the defined nodes. If none of the defined nodes are available, the resource may run on any other node.

ub83add3fc151c286544e.text: A strict node affinity rule makes resources be restricted to the defined nodes. If none of the defined nodes are available, the resource will be stopped.

u7a69bad6e3161c8f712f.text: Another common requirement is that two or more HA resources should run on either the same node, or should be distributed on separate nodes. These are also commonly called "Affinity/Anti-Affinity constraints".

u23f3b2946548ad1e7cf3.text: For example, suppose there is a lot of communication traffic between the HA resources ⟦0⟧ and ⟦1⟧, for example, a web server communicating with a database server. If those HA resources are on separate nodes, this could potentially result in a higher latency and unnecessary network load. Resource affinity rules with the affinity ⟦2⟧ implement the constraint to keep the HA resources on the same node:

ufba27d5130cb3d394f65.text: If there are two or more positive resource affinity rules, which have common HA resources, then these are treated as a single positive resource affinity rule. For example, if the HA resources ⟦0⟧ and ⟦1⟧ and the HA resources ⟦2⟧ and ⟦3⟧ are each in a positive resource affinity rule, then it is the same as if ⟦4⟧, ⟦5⟧ and ⟦6⟧ would have been in a single positive resource affinity rule.

u3126e27eca37d0916ac0.text: If the HA resources of a positive resource affinity rule are currently running on different nodes, the CRS will move the HA resources to the node, where most of them are running already. If there is a tie in the HA resource count, the node whose name appears first in alphabetical order is selected.

u8cfed58928b061ef99e4.text: However, suppose there are computationally expensive, and/or distributed programs running on the HA resources ⟦0⟧ and ⟦1⟧, for example, sharded database instances. In that case, running them on the same node could potentially result in pressure on the hardware resources of the node and will slow down the operations of these HA resources. Resource affinity rules with the affinity ⟦2⟧ implement the constraint to spread the HA resources on separate nodes:

uf4e554557d4f494b5e69.text: Other than node affinity rules, resource affinity rules are strict by default, i.e., if the constraints imposed by the resource affinity rules cannot be met for an HA resource, the HA Manager will put the HA resource in recovery state in case of a failover or in error state elsewhere.

u61138c3a0d1b6a8adf0f.text: The above commands created the following rules in the rules configuration file:

ufff2681e465cc223243e.text: Interactions between Positive and Negative Resource Affinity Rules

u6e65d0257ecede92cc22.text: If there are HA resources in a positive resource affinity rule, which are also part of a negative resource affinity rule, then all the other HA resources in the positive resource affinity rule are in negative affinity with the HA resources of these negative resource affinity rules as well.

ud20b7914309f244effe9.text: For example, if the HA resources ⟦0⟧, ⟦1⟧, and ⟦2⟧ are in a positive resource affinity rule, and ⟦3⟧ is in a negative resource affinity rule with the HA resource ⟦4⟧, then ⟦5⟧ and ⟦6⟧ are each in negative resource affinity with ⟦7⟧ as well.

ue9987e84c28fbe414c79.text: Note that if there are two or more HA resources in both a positive and negative resource affinity rule, then those will be disabled as they cause a conflict: Two or more HA resources cannot be kept on the same node and separated on different nodes at the same time. For more information on these cases, see the section about ⟦0⟧rule conflicts and errors⟦1⟧ below.

u5e12ce0ef10b46259b07.text: Interactions between Node and Positive Resource Affinity Rules

u1f8bbc32c72feb967f25.text: If there are HA resources in a node affinity rule, which are also part of a positive resource affinity rule, then all the other HA resources in the positive resource affinity rule inherit the node affinity rule as well.

u3daf3e037dac7487cb54.text: For example, if the HA resources ⟦0⟧, ⟦1⟧, and ⟦2⟧ are in a positive resource affinity rule, and ⟦3⟧ is in a node affinity rule, which restricts ⟦4⟧ to be only on ⟦5⟧, then ⟦6⟧ and ⟦7⟧ are restricted to be only on ⟦8⟧ as well.

ud63ce9ab380a6c4b142e.text: Please note that if there are two or more HA resources in a positive resource affinity rule and in different node affinity rules, then those rules will cause an error and will be disabled as this is currently not supported. For more information on these cases, see the section about ⟦0⟧rule conflicts and errors⟦1⟧ below.

uaa9a66cfe10f4fd5b053.text: HA rules can impose rather complex constraints on the HA resources. To ensure that a new or modified HA rule does not introduce uncertainty into the HA stack’s CRS scheduler, HA rules are tested for feasibility before these are applied. For any rules that fail these tests, these rules are disabled until the conflicts and errors have been resolved.

u5d035a67b888671190e2.text: Currently, HA rules are checked for the following feasibility tests:

ueec5cab99c8f5ceabde7.text: An HA resource can only be part of a single HA node affinity rule.

u68bc21c063f18439f4f1.text: Negative HA node affinity rules cannot specify node priorities.

udee5522376ac7235e938.text: Negative HA node affinity rules cannot specify all cluster nodes.

uc772fcbe38f25107a678.text: An HA resource affinity rule must have at least two HA resources.

uc8eadec52e854a8f3ca1.text: A negative HA resource affinity rule cannot specify more HA resources than there are nodes in the cluster. Otherwise, the HA resources do not have enough nodes to be separated.

u8e9bb53a2211520ca27f.text: A positive HA resource affinity rule cannot specify the same two or more HA resources as a negative HA resources affinity rule. That is, two or more HA resources cannot be kept together and separate at the same time.

ub53e951e49232a3772b8.text: An HA resource can only be part of an HA node affinity rule and an HA resource affinity rule at the same time, if the HA node affinity rule has a single priority class.

u475b24ff15c992df65ae.text: The HA resources of a positive HA resource affinity rule can only be part of a single HA node affinity rule at most.

u1206f92091e0b2e5aa70.text: The HA resources of a negative HA resource affinity rule cannot be restricted to less nodes than HA resources by their node affinity rules. Otherwise, the HA resources do not have enough nodes to be separated.

u715fcbac92bcfc2c0501.text: On node failures, fencing ensures that the erroneous node is guaranteed to be offline. This is required to make sure that no resource runs twice when it gets recovered on another node. This is a really important task, because without this, it would not be possible to recover a resource on another node.

u489928773a96f3e77f12.text: If a node did not get fenced, it would be in an unknown state where it may have still access to shared resources. This is really dangerous! Imagine that every network but the storage one broke. Now, while not reachable from the public network, the VM still runs and writes to the shared storage.

u9bb47bd58ebd41ee1d15.text: If we then simply start up this VM on another node, we would get a dangerous race condition, because we write from both nodes. Such conditions can destroy all VM data and the whole VM could be rendered unusable. The recovery could also fail if the storage protects against multiple mounts.

u929804e259a2207cf6d2.text: There are different methods to fence a node, for example, fence devices which cut off the power from the node or disable their communication completely. Those are often quite expensive and bring additional critical components into a system, because if they fail you cannot recover any service.

u36219c322c0f329642af.text: We thus wanted to integrate a simpler fencing method, which does not require additional external hardware. This can be done using watchdog timers.

ucff23017237b9badd40e.text: isolate nodes by disabling complete network traffic on the switch

u8dad38ae0eca4016af36.text: Watchdog timers have been widely used in critical and dependable systems since the beginning of microcontrollers. They are often simple, independent integrated circuits which are used to detect and recover from computer malfunctions.

ubaa9833542e94059df38.text: During normal operation, ⟦0⟧ regularly resets the watchdog timer to prevent it from elapsing. If, due to a hardware fault or program error, the computer fails to reset the watchdog, the timer will elapse and trigger a reset of the whole server (reboot).

u7c9d9d5be2ff7e023cfb.text: Recent server motherboards often include such hardware watchdogs, but these need to be configured. If no watchdog is available or configured, we fall back to the Linux Kernel ⟦0⟧softdog⟦1⟧. While still reliable, it is not independent of the servers hardware, and thus has a lower reliability than a hardware watchdog.

u186a6f888ea763287bff.text: By default, all hardware watchdog modules are blocked for security reasons. They are like a loaded gun if not correctly initialized. To enable a hardware watchdog, you need to specify the module to load in ⟦0⟧⟦1⟧⟦2⟧, for example:

u5b6f5311cbae7bc7700a.text: This configuration is read by the ⟦0⟧watchdog-mux⟦1⟧ service, which loads the specified module at startup.

u3bd5c4a71611e3ff709f.text: After a node failed and its fencing was successful, the CRM tries to move services from the failed node to nodes which are still online.

ua409de7de164d7b7e3af.text: The selection of the recovery nodes is influenced by the list of currently active nodes, their respective loads depending on the used scheduler, and the affinity rules the service is part of, if any.

uf4f68bf1ea67a54d31e3.text: First, the CRM builds a set of nodes available to the service. If the service is part of a node affinity rule, the set is reduced to the highest priority nodes in the node affinity rule. If the service is part of a resource affinity rule, the set is further reduced to fulfill their constraints, which is either keeping the service on the same node as some other services or keeping the service on a different node than some other services. Finally, the CRM selects the node with the lowest load according to the used scheduler to minimize the possibility of an overloaded node.

u361a9bd8e65f17be72e3.text: On node failure, the CRM distributes services to the remaining nodes. This increases the service count on those nodes, and can lead to high load, especially on small clusters. Please design your cluster so that it can handle such worst case scenarios.

u5d4a02a1ce396b5411bd.text: The ⟦0⟧ output includes a fencing entry that shows the CRM watchdog state. Each LRM entry additionally shows its own watchdog state.

u7a7a56fc781090a0ef04.text: The CRM is actively managing services and has its watchdog open. Each node’s LRM also holds a watchdog while it has its agent lock. On quorum loss or daemon failure, the respective watchdog triggers a node reset to ensure safe failover.

u1a97986aa64669be61a5.text: The HA stack is ready but no CRM is actively running as master, for example when no HA resources are configured yet or the cluster just started. The CRM watchdog is not open. Fencing automatically transitions to ⟦0⟧ once a CRM takes over as master.

ue871188d7b66b4f3a543.text: A ⟦0⟧ command was issued. The CRM is freezing or suspending services from tracking and waiting for all LRMs to release their watchdogs. The CRM watchdog is still active during this phase. Each LRM entry’s watchdog status changes to ⟦1⟧ as it acknowledges the disarm.

u61f7558009d5e698696b.text: All watchdogs have been released cluster-wide. No automatic fencing, failover, or recovery takes place. See ⟦0⟧Disarming HA for Cluster Maintenance⟦1⟧.

u77ff26da0d73d5ee5b19.text: The ⟦0⟧ service keeps the underlying ⟦1⟧ device open for its entire lifetime, even when no HA client is connected. This prevents other processes from claiming the device and ensures the HA stack can always re-acquire it. Not all hardware watchdog drivers support magic close, so closing the device could trigger an unintended reset.

u10d41c276c9dedc76c49.text: The start failure policy comes into effect if a service failed to start on a node one or more times. It can be used to configure how often a restart should be triggered on the same node and how often a service should be relocated, so that it has an attempt to be started on another node. The aim of this policy is to circumvent temporary unavailability of shared resources on a specific node. For example, if a shared storage isn’t available on a quorate node anymore, for instance due to network problems, but is still available on other nodes, the relocate policy allows the service to start nonetheless.

u398984f52c27f5b9842a.text: There are two service start recover policy settings which can be configured specific for each resource.

uabe267754ef45bb93b50.text: Maximum number of attempts to restart a failed service on the actual node. The default is set to one.

u8d82e734b5c9b6e3b1fd.text: Maximum number of attempts to relocate the service to a different node. A relocate only happens after the ⟦0⟧ value is exceeded on the actual node. The default is set to one.

ufee095b255ccf1721e34.text: The relocate count state will only reset to zero when the service had at least one successful start. That means if a service is re-started without fixing the error only the restart policy gets repeated.

ub13a3fb6ab7dba31a67f.text: If, after all attempts, the service state could not be recovered, it gets placed in an error state. In this state, the service won’t get touched by the HA stack anymore. The only way out is disabling a service:

u71b01d7914e19e15fd06.text: This can also be done in the web interface.

u1c96ba9a1abc9ce79531.text: To recover from the error state you should do the following:

udd1fe43a185e348733f5.text: bring the resource back into a safe and consistent state (e.g.: kill its process if the service could not be stopped)

u6a9e3bc10004ead889e7.text: disable the resource to remove the error flag

u1eb0088035a24f2a32ef.text: fix the error which led to this failures

ud8d1e204c0f9adc20018.text: ⟦0⟧after⟦1⟧ you fixed all errors you may request that the service starts again

u6327d326b1209cc0d508.text: When updating the ha-manager, you should do one node after the other, never all at once for various reasons. First, while we test our software thoroughly, a bug affecting your specific setup cannot totally be ruled out. Updating one node after the other and checking the functionality of each node after finishing the update helps to recover from eventual problems, while updating all at once could result in a broken cluster and is generally not good practice.

u4b610fdd2b559bad0a7c.text: Also, the Proxmox VE HA stack uses a request acknowledge protocol to perform actions between the cluster and the local resource manager. For restarting, the LRM makes a request to the CRM to freeze all its services. This prevents them from getting touched by the Cluster during the short time the LRM is restarting. After that, the LRM may safely close the watchdog during a restart. Such a restart happens normally during a package update and, as already stated, an active master CRM is needed to acknowledge the requests from the LRM. If this is not the case the update process can take too long which, in the worst case, may result in a reset triggered by the watchdog.

u46fa6275833cd64e86f5.text: Sometimes it is necessary to perform maintenance on a node, such as replacing hardware or simply installing a new kernel image. This also applies while the HA stack is in use.

u6ff9a3225913ee250ed3.text: The HA stack can support you mainly in two types of maintenance:

u4fac0e771027f0ab12ae.text: for general shutdowns or reboots, the behavior can be configured, see ⟦0⟧Shutdown Policy⟦1⟧.

ucdd5903c11e6a05780a2.text: for maintenance that does not require a shutdown or reboot, or that should not be switched off automatically after only one reboot, you can enable the manual maintenance mode.

ue14dc524e38322ff31fd.text: You can use the manual maintenance mode to mark the node as unavailable for HA operation, prompting all services managed by HA to migrate to other nodes.

ub1a2fe7072cf8ad00552.text: The target nodes for these migrations are selected from the other currently available nodes, and determined by the HA rules configuration and the configured cluster resource scheduler (CRS) mode. During each migration, the original node will be recorded in the HA managers' state, so that the service can be moved back again automatically once the maintenance mode is disabled and the node is back online.

u133d4bde44600e24106f.text: Currently you can enabled or disable the maintenance mode using the ha-manager CLI tool.

uf2960f0bf5d4ee2af5b0.text: Enabling maintenance mode for a node

ud0a736ed7b5666f5f6dd.text: This will queue a CRM command, when the manager processes this command it will record the request for maintenance-mode in the manager status. This allows you to submit the command on any node, not just on the one you want to place in, or out of the maintenance mode.

ufd004e8c8b17483314cf.text: Once the LRM on the respective node picks the command up it will mark itself as unavailable, but still process all migration commands. This means that the LRM self-fencing watchdog will stay active until all active services got moved, and all running workers finished.

uf50b2f1e107b3ee2348f.text: Note that the LRM status will read ⟦0⟧ mode as soon as the LRM picked the requested state up, not only when all services got moved away, this user experience is planned to be improved in the future. For now, you can check for any active HA service left on the node, or watching out for a log line like: ⟦1⟧ to know when the node finished its transition into the maintenance mode.

u4cd57397a8a25ac53bcd.text: The manual maintenance mode is not automatically deleted on node reboot, but only if it is either manually deactivated using the ⟦0⟧ CLI or if the manager-status is manually cleared.

u246336a3791cf18ecaf6.text: Disabling maintenance mode for a node

uf41c0351f5105cd51611.text: The process of disabling the manual maintenance mode is similar to enabling it. Using the ⟦0⟧ CLI command shown above will queue a CRM command that, once processed, marks the respective LRM node as available again.

u643ce80db89ed1855717.text: If you deactivate the maintenance mode, all services that were on the node when the maintenance mode was activated will be moved back.

u93a4bd3a99fc95b72f69.text: Below you will find a description of the different HA policies for a node shutdown. Currently ⟦0⟧Conditional⟦1⟧ is the default due to backward compatibility. Some users may find that ⟦2⟧Migrate⟦3⟧ behaves more as expected.

ucc61aa510f4ce09b0266.text: The shutdown policy can be configured in the Web UI (⟦0⟧ → ⟦1⟧ → ⟦2⟧), or directly in ⟦3⟧:

u14ee19c2b8ec46360029.text: Once the Local Resource manager (LRM) gets a shutdown request and this policy is enabled, it will mark itself as unavailable for the current HA manager. This triggers a migration of all HA Services currently located on this node. The LRM will try to delay the shutdown process, until all running services get moved away. But, this expects that the running services ⟦0⟧can⟦1⟧ be migrated to another node. In other words, the service must not be locally bound, for example by using hardware passthrough. For example, strict node affinity rules tell the HA Manager that the service cannot run outside of the chosen set of nodes. If all of these nodes are unavailable, the shutdown will hang until you manually intervene. Once the shut down node comes back online again, the previously displaced services will be moved back, if they were not already manually migrated in-between.

u951f7a016cd1abeec5cb.text: The watchdog is still active during the migration process on shutdown. If the node loses quorum it will be fenced and the services will be recovered.

u03c22796eb6d08272354.text: If you start a (previously stopped) service on a node which is currently being maintained, the node needs to be fenced to ensure that the service can be moved and started on another available node.

uf5b00a455b03811d6714.text: This mode ensures that all services get stopped, but that they will also be recovered, if the current node is not online soon. It can be useful when doing maintenance on a cluster scale, where live-migrating VMs may not be possible if too many nodes are powered off at a time, but you still want to ensure HA services get recovered and started again as soon as possible.

u5cdd8f84fbd173365124.text: This mode ensures that all services get stopped and frozen, so that they won’t get recovered until the current node is online again.

u6c5daefa527cc8768da8.text: The ⟦0⟧Conditional⟦1⟧ shutdown policy automatically detects if a shutdown or a reboot is requested, and changes behaviour accordingly.

u31b334b662e7fcc0e9f3.text: A shutdown (⟦0⟧poweroff⟦1⟧) is usually done if it is planned for the node to stay down for some time. The LRM stops all managed services in this case. This means that other nodes will take over those services afterwards.

ucfaa7c66ac68734f2340.text: Recent hardware has large amounts of memory (RAM). So we stop all resources, then restart them to avoid online migration of all that RAM. If you want to use online migration, you need to invoke that manually before you shutdown the node.

u45e4960f0175971b94f7.text: Node reboots are initiated with the ⟦0⟧reboot⟦1⟧ command. This is usually done after installing a new kernel. Please note that this is different from “shutdown”, because the node immediately starts again.

uf3704c18bff1fed3db14.text: The LRM tells the CRM that it wants to restart, and waits until the CRM puts all resources into the ⟦0⟧ state (same mechanism is used for ⟦1⟧Package Updates⟦2⟧). This prevents those resources from being moved to other nodes. Instead, the CRM starts the resources after the reboot on the same node.

u7df1bfcd5a871a7952cf.text: Last but not least, you can also manually move resources to other nodes, before you shutdown or restart a node. The advantage is that you have full control, and you can decide if you want to use online migration or not.

u390ee5ec7ffd0d3f919c.text: Please do not ⟦0⟧kill⟦1⟧ services like ⟦2⟧, ⟦3⟧ or ⟦4⟧. They manage and use the watchdog, so this can result in an immediate node reboot or even reset.

uef6fe764e1fcb0e6a4b3.text: Certain cluster maintenance tasks, such as reconfiguring the network or the cluster communication stack (corosync), can cause temporary quorum loss or network partitions. Normally, HA would interpret this as a node failure and trigger self-fencing, disrupting services unnecessarily.

u2cc4541236a0331fdb59.text: The disarm mechanism releases all CRM and LRM watchdogs cluster-wide, allowing you to perform such maintenance safely without the risk of nodes being fenced.

uc3d3945856870f874739.text: While disarmed, HA does not protect your services. Failures during this period are not automatically recovered. Keep the disarm window as short as possible.

u658eda9cee4bf1342655.text: When disarming HA, you must choose a resource mode that controls how HA managed resources are handled while disarmed. The current state of resources is not affected.

u2518163f09634077c09e.text: New commands and state changes are not applied. Services stay in their current state, but the HA stack does not react to failures or process new requests. This is the safest choice when you expect all nodes to remain running.

u10ea24581fd33b18c6c4.text: Resources are suspended from HA tracking and can be managed as if they were not HA managed. This allows you to manually start, stop, or migrate services while HA is disarmed. Use this when you need to manually relocate services during maintenance. When re-arming, the CRM rechecks service locations against the configuration to pick up any manual migrations.

uf5c9caee4737c0424a61.text: To disarm HA with the desired resource mode:

u01407e22b6d3299d0341.text: To re-arm HA after maintenance is complete:

uccc647bae76db547eb18.text: You can monitor the current state with:

u5f1bc86de8fffe47b0f6.text: The fencing status line shows the current state of the fencing mechanism (see ⟦0⟧Fencing Status⟦1⟧), including the CRM and LRM watchdog states.

u8b502cb67e7cb836539b.text: After you request disarm, the following sequence happens:

u25a7d82d193e733d291d.text: The CRM freezes all services or suspends them from tracking, depending on the chosen resource mode.

u4a664b151f42e6bf9081.text: Each LRM finishes its active workers, then releases its agent lock and watchdog.

uc00a9c68eb156ce8dfc7.text: Once all online LRMs are idle, the CRM releases its own watchdog too.

u93d14b858e1261163091.text: The CRM keeps the manager lock throughout this process, so it can accept and process the ⟦0⟧ command to reverse it.

ub86fca713de4fc5c5ae9.text: If any services are currently being fenced, recovered, or migrated, the disarm is deferred until these operations complete. This ensures that services in the middle of a transition do not end up in an inconsistent state.

uc5859b8c8138a434510f.text: If a node is offline when HA is disarmed, its LRM cannot process the disarm request. The CRM proceeds to the disarmed state once all ⟦0⟧online⟦1⟧ LRMs have completed their part. The offline node does not block this.

ubb731fda34e13736ace9.text: When the offline node comes back online while HA is still disarmed, its LRM picks up the disarm state and releases its watchdog without attempting any service recovery.

u62dc7b93d7eaf89447bc.text: When you re-arm HA, any services that were on the offline node are handled according to normal HA recovery rules: they are fenced and recovered if the node is still unreachable, or restarted on the node if it has come back online.

ua59c48657c8927ca73c5.text: If a node is already in maintenance mode when disarm is requested, the maintenance migration continues until all services have been moved away. Once no active services and workers remain, the LRM releases its lock and watchdog as part of the disarm process.

uad9e12336530367db861.text: When HA is re-armed, the maintenance mode state is preserved. The node remains in maintenance and services are not moved back until maintenance mode is explicitly disabled.

u9c0702409acd4997c575.text: While the HA stack is disarmed, no automatic recovery, failover, or fencing takes place. A node failure during this window is not detected or handled by HA. Keep the disarm window as short as possible and ensure that the cluster is in a healthy state before re-arming.

u16cc1a76e6e7e011af76.text: The Cluster Resource Scheduler (CRS) is responsible for selecting new node placements for HA resources and keeping HA resources on their allowed nodes.

uff52f8aeb9fa6a42d55b.text: In every HA Manager round, the scheduler goes through every HA resource and checks whether the HA resource needs any new node placement. This new node placement can be caused by different actions, such as recovering HA resources from a fenced node or a new HA affinity rule. See the section ⟦0⟧CRS Scheduling Points⟦1⟧ for a more thorough description of which actions the CRS takes for specific changes in the cluster.

uad08568a280a927b4712.text: The CRS scheduling mode controls how the CRS will calculate the usage information for the cluster. This usage information is used as a basis for the scheduling decisions. The CRS mode can be changed in the web interface (⟦0⟧ → ⟦1⟧ → ⟦2⟧). The default mode is ⟦3⟧. The change will take effect starting with the next HA Manager round, which should take no longer than 10 seconds.

u4d18d4cf560fe956e38c.text: The number of active guests on each node is used to choose the best-fitting node for an HA resource.

uc81f935d985dcc128e58.text: Static usage information from active guests on each node is used to choose the best-fitting node for an HA resource. This includes the configured CPU and memory quotas for the active guests.

uf51f373df112eba60b24.text: Dynamic usage information from active guests on each node is used to choose the best-fitting node for an HA resource. This includes the average CPU and memory usage as well as the configured CPU and memory quotas for the active guests.

uc0acc718619c2a1596b1.text: In every HA Manager round, the CRS checks whether any HA resources need a new node placement, which can be caused by any of the following scheduling points:

ud4813669fdfae186d9e3.text: When a node with active HA resources fails, all its HA resources need to be recovered to other nodes. The CRS algorithm will be used here to balance that recovery over the remaining nodes.

u4ac9f7a5c164dc0ce906.text: If a rule imposes different constraints on the HA resources, the HA stack will use the CRS algorithm to find a new target node for the HA resources affected by these rules depending on the type of the new rules:

uc6b4880128c01c7fb920.text: Node affinity rules: If a node affinity rule is created or HA resources/nodes are added to an existing node affinity rule, the HA stack will use the CRS algorithm to ensure that these HA resources are assigned according to their node and priority constraints.

u3a237448af00ea94e8be.text: Positive resource affinity rules: If a positive resource affinity rule is created or HA resources are added to an existing positive resource affinity rule, the HA stack will use the CRS algorithm to ensure that these HA resources are moved to a common node.

u38c808d19eab0a74d38a.text: Negative resource affinity rules: If a negative resource affinity rule is created or HA resources are added to an existing negative resource affinity rule, the HA stack will use the CRS algorithm to ensure that these HA resources are moved to separate nodes.

u2a7e9b3f50b440f57aaa.text: When starting an HA resource with rebalance on start enabled, the CRS will select the node best suited for the HA resource. If the selected node is not the current node, the HA resource will be migrated to the selected node.

u2e9b3f31ee0157eb52a6.text: For the ⟦0⟧basic scheduler mode⟦1⟧, the node with the fewest active guests is considered the best-suited node.

uf6e282d15f20bef529bd.text: For the ⟦0⟧static-load⟦1⟧ and ⟦2⟧dynamic-load⟦3⟧ scheduler modes, each node in turn is considered as if the HA resource was already running on it, using CPU and memory usage from the associated guest configuration. Then for each such alternative, CPU and memory usage of all nodes are considered, with memory being weighted much more, because it’s a truly limited resource. For both, CPU and memory, highest usage among nodes (weighted more, as ideally no node should be overcommitted) and average usage of all nodes (to still be able to distinguish in case there already is a more highly committed node) are considered.

ufb21fdfcac90105ff7d4.text: This setting can be enabled with the CRS option ⟦0⟧ in the web interface under ⟦1⟧ → ⟦2⟧ → ⟦3⟧.

u341b884bc404b53512bb.text: For the static-load and dynamic-load scheduler modes, this functionality is still in technology preview. The more HA resources the more possible combinations there are, so it’s currently not recommended to use it if you have thousands of HA resources.

u22cb17ab60dde06c5b1b.text: The utilization of individual cluster nodes can vary greatly depending on where guests are currently running and how much load these exert at any moment. This can cause the node utilizations to become imbalanced over time, where HA resources on one node become bottlenecked due to resource contention, while another node is barely utilized.

u11a9e01d3fa8c9b53bf3.text: The HA Manager’s automatic load balancer can lower the overall cluster imbalance by automatically issuing rebalancing migrations. Currently, these migrations are issued only for HA resources and executed sequentially. Furthermore, these migrations always obey the current HA affinity rules.

u502b2b7a4ac4662857a1.text: Disabling ⟦0⟧ for an HA resource prevents the resource from being part of automatically issued rebalancing migrations.

u925cbc02e6a04283abba.text: Any HA resource with a positive affinity for an HA resource with ⟦0⟧ disabled won’t be part of rebalancing migrations either.

u7d8354dc66ea51999118.text: The automatic load balancing system can be enabled and configured in the web interface under ⟦0⟧ → ⟦1⟧ → ⟦2⟧. This allows fine-tuning the various parameters as described in the next paragraph for different cluster setups and requirements. The load balancer requires either the ⟦3⟧static-load⟦4⟧ or ⟦5⟧dynamic-load⟦6⟧ scheduler mode to be in use.

u64d7913b6900eab6a3d5.text: In every HA Manager round, each of which lasts around 10 seconds, the automatic load balancer checks whether the cluster imbalance exceeds the ⟦0⟧imbalance threshold⟦1⟧. If the cluster imbalance stays above the threshold for at least as many consecutive HA Manager rounds as the ⟦2⟧hold duration⟦3⟧, then the load balancer will select the rebalancing migration for an HA resource, which lowers the overall cluster imbalance the most. The method used to select the best rebalancing migration can be set with the ⟦4⟧rebalancing method⟦5⟧ option. Finally, if the selected migration reduces the current cluster imbalance by at least the percentage given by the ⟦6⟧imbalance improvement⟦7⟧ option, the load balancer issues the selected migration.

udf57919c79634d99ecd7.text: The cluster imbalance is derived from the standard deviation and mean of the individual node loads and is normalized to a 0-100% range. Both the ⟦0⟧imbalance threshold⟦1⟧ and the ⟦2⟧imbalance improvement⟦3⟧ are configured in percent. The ⟦4⟧imbalance threshold⟦5⟧ defaults to 30% and controls the sensitivity of the load balancer; with a value of ⟦6⟧ it will try to select a rebalancing migration every time the ⟦7⟧hold duration⟦8⟧ is exceeded. The ⟦9⟧imbalance improvement⟦10⟧ defaults to 10% and filters what constitutes an acceptable rebalancing migration; with a value of ⟦11⟧ it will always commit to a migration even if the expected imbalance does not change at all. The value can never be negative, so the balancer will never commit to a migration with an expected imbalance worse than the current one.

u3dd11d27b7eb24e13ba3.text: It is planned that load balancing will also include non-HA resources in the future.

ue80783cb6bb897570bb4.text: Containers are a lightweight alternative to fully virtualized machines (VMs). They use the kernel of the host system that they run on, instead of emulating a full operating system (OS). This means that containers can access resources on the host system directly.

u1461ab372df843729866.text: The runtime costs for containers is low, usually negligible. However, there are some drawbacks that need be considered:

u298b6e07c2e086b040b1.text: Only Linux distributions can be run in Proxmox Containers. It is not possible to run other operating systems like, for example, FreeBSD or Microsoft Windows inside a container.

uae2aa977bccca34ae3c3.text: For security reasons, access to host resources needs to be restricted. Therefore, containers run in their own separate namespaces. Additionally some syscalls (user space requests to the Linux kernel) are not allowed within containers.

ucebac7a1d1c9b91aa381.text: Proxmox VE uses ⟦0⟧Linux Containers (LXC)⟦1⟧ as its underlying container technology. The “Proxmox Container Toolkit” (⟦2⟧) simplifies the usage and management of LXC, by providing an interface that abstracts complex tasks.

u8124d73f1eba45e22a8b.text: Containers are tightly integrated with Proxmox VE. This means that they are aware of the cluster setup, and they can use the same network and storage resources as virtual machines. You can also use the Proxmox VE firewall, or manage containers using the HA framework.

u0e41601573bb42466ef0.text: Our primary goal has traditionally been to offer an environment that provides the benefits of using a VM, but without the additional overhead. This means that Proxmox Containers have been primarily categorized as “System Containers”.

ue9aaa1de1f234b8019e9.text: With the introduction of OCI (⟦0⟧O⟦1⟧pen ⟦2⟧C⟦3⟧ontainer ⟦4⟧I⟦5⟧nitiative) image support, Proxmox VE now also integrates “Application Containers” as a technology preview. When creating a container from an OCI image, the image is automatically converted to the LXC stack that Proxmox VE uses.

u77c80d925ff478901888.text: This approach allows users to benefit from a wide ecosystem of pre-packaged applications while retaining the robust management features of Proxmox VE.

uee5bf377906bc52fa8e9.text: While running lightweight “Application Containers” directly offers significant advantages over a full VM, for use cases demanding maximum isolation and the ability to live-migrate, nesting containers inside a Proxmox QEMU VM remains a recommended practice.

u269f718cba4b43268e9d.text: General settings of a container include

uf52b5c0eb2dd7a42fa65.text: the ⟦0⟧Node⟦1⟧ : the physical server on which the container will run

ue49d779823bd5df2ee0c.text: the ⟦0⟧CT ID⟦1⟧: a unique number in this Proxmox VE installation used to identify your container

u03d5c1d6dfebc3c92713.text: ⟦0⟧Resource Pool⟦1⟧: a logical group of containers and VMs

u0483766d6c6ebcfb3d50.text: ⟦0⟧Password⟦1⟧: the root password of the container

uf5414d7ddeed69f3c3f5.text: ⟦0⟧SSH Public Key⟦1⟧: a public key for connecting to the root account over SSH

u7a5d2e4d9a05546c3bdc.text: ⟦0⟧Unprivileged container⟦1⟧: this option allows to choose at creation time if you want to create a privileged or unprivileged container.

u20c179c23e796a2d6e4f.text: ⟦0⟧Nesting⟦1⟧: expose procfs and sysfs to allow nested containers. Note that systemd also uses this to isolate services.

u3c4d334f80a68b82452a.text: Unprivileged containers use a new kernel feature called user namespaces. The root UID 0 inside the container is mapped to an unprivileged user outside the container. This means that most security issues (container escape, resource abuse, etc.) in these containers will affect a random unprivileged user, and would be a generic kernel security bug rather than an LXC issue. The LXC team thinks unprivileged containers are safe by design.

u2961da01b902e63bb0d2.text: This is the default option when creating a new container.

u6081baddac33911f5acf.text: If the container uses systemd as an init system, please be aware the systemd version running inside the container should be equal to or greater than 220.

uf43f9c348892f5e2f3f9.text: Security in containers is achieved by using mandatory access control ⟦0⟧AppArmor⟦1⟧ restrictions, ⟦2⟧seccomp⟦3⟧ filters and Linux kernel namespaces. The LXC team considers this kind of container as unsafe, and they will not consider new container escape exploits to be security issues worthy of a CVE and quick fix. That’s why privileged containers should only be used in trusted environments.

A special task inside ⟦7⟧ tries to distribute running containers among available CPUs periodically. To view the assigned CPUs run the following command:

ue6f9f549df52fe41df6e.text: Containers use the host kernel directly. All tasks inside a container are handled by the host CPU scheduler. Proxmox VE uses the Linux ⟦0⟧CFS⟦1⟧ (⟦2⟧C⟦3⟧ompletely ⟦4⟧F⟦5⟧air ⟦6⟧S⟦7⟧cheduler) scheduler by default, which has additional bandwidth control options.

Number is relative to the weights of all the other running containers. The default is ⟦0⟧ (or ⟦1⟧ if the host uses legacy cgroup v1). You can use this setting to prioritize some containers.

ufc33c6346ed772d53f5f.text: The root mount point is configured with the ⟦0⟧ property. You can configure up to 256 additional mount points. The corresponding options are called ⟦1⟧ to ⟦2⟧. They can contain the following settings:

u06f1a095d7fc9c4ce3df.text: Currently there are three types of mount points: storage backed mount points, bind mounts, and device mounts.

uf4cc89d69a27cc7e6916.text: Storage backed mount points are managed by the Proxmox VE storage subsystem and come in three different flavors:

u77c3fd8dc7e497125579.text: Image based: these are raw images containing a single ext4 formatted file system.

u0172e5d23424b6be9435.text: ZFS subvolumes: these are technically bind mounts, but with managed storage, and thus allow resizing and snapshotting.

u60a805d8f71b82b1996a.text: Directories: passing ⟦0⟧ triggers a special case where instead of a raw image a directory is created.

uea6d9997408245df7f98.text: The special option syntax ⟦0⟧ for storage backed mount point volumes will automatically allocate a volume of the specified size on the specified storage. For example, calling

u540305b268349ebdb566.text: will allocate a 10GB volume on the storage ⟦0⟧ and replace the volume ID place holder ⟦1⟧ with the allocated volume ID, and setup the moutpoint in the container at ⟦2⟧

u13e1715874aed88518f1.text: Bind mounts allow you to access arbitrary directories from your Proxmox VE host inside a container. Some potential use cases are:

ub4b64a1d050fdfbd3646.text: Accessing your home directory in the guest

u6918396fd023d847bfcd.text: Accessing an USB device directory in the guest

u3d549a1c094924888234.text: Accessing an NFS mount from the host in the guest

u2c5555838779a434efd9.text: Bind mounts are considered to not be managed by the storage subsystem, so you cannot make snapshots or deal with quotas from inside the container. With unprivileged containers you might run into permission problems caused by the user mapping and cannot use ACLs.

ue39196fa0ba5c538122a.text: The contents of bind mount points are not backed up when using ⟦0⟧.

uc4b9d6cc41aaa36e7808.text: For security reasons, bind mounts should only be established using source directories especially reserved for this purpose, e.g., a directory hierarchy under ⟦0⟧. Never bind mount system directories like ⟦1⟧, ⟦2⟧ or ⟦3⟧ into a container - this poses a great security risk.

u3c60da7b165aad6d81fc.text: The bind mount source path must not contain any symlinks.

u801afd79ebc5e18a7c24.text: Device mount points allow to mount block devices of the host directly into the container. Similar to bind mounts, device mounts are not managed by Proxmox VE’s storage subsystem, but the ⟦0⟧ and ⟦1⟧ options will be honored.

u9a00c3fd48ff35c60c4e.text: Device mount points should only be used under special circumstances. In most cases a storage backed mount point offers the same performance and a lot more features.

uc133cba62ae919314615.text: The contents of device mount points are not backed up when using ⟦0⟧.

u650363eae5c9ae044c2e.text: If you want to fine tune the boot order of your containers, you can use the following parameters:

ua5c011719d3c520d1dd7.text: ⟦0⟧Start/Shutdown order⟦1⟧: Defines the start order priority. For example, set it to 1 if you want the CT to be the first to be started. (We use the reverse startup order for shutdown, so a container with a start order of 1 would be the last to be shut down)

u5aeb10106d1a0a8bcbb2.text: Containers use the kernel of the host system. This exposes an attack surface for malicious users. In general, full virtual machines provide better isolation. This should be considered if containers are provided to unknown or untrusted people.

u3bad8b1b548647dfc5d3.text: To reduce the attack surface, LXC uses many security features like AppArmor, CGroups and kernel namespaces.

ub8bbadc63d5bfcd5db9d.text: AppArmor profiles are used to restrict access to possibly dangerous actions. Some system calls, i.e. ⟦0⟧, are prohibited from execution.

u48d95c34e14154a749ed.text: ⟦0⟧cgroup⟦1⟧ is a kernel mechanism used to hierarchically organize processes and distribute system resources.

u817a4438e12c42d31c90.text: The main resources controlled via ⟦0⟧cgroups⟦1⟧ are CPU time, memory and swap limits, and access to device nodes. ⟦2⟧cgroups⟦3⟧ are also used to "freeze" a container before taking snapshots.

The memory and swap settings for containers can map directly to these values, whereas previously only the memory limit and the limit of the ⟦4⟧sum⟦5⟧ of memory and swap could be limited.

u6dbb13606d6301707856.text: The Proxmox VE LXC container storage model is more flexible than traditional container storage models. A container can have multiple mount points. This makes it possible to use the best suited storage for each application.

u14ea93606c0837a929a6.text: For example the root file system of the container can be on slow and cheap storage while the database can be on fast and distributed storage via a second mount point. See section ⟦0⟧ Mount Points⟦1⟧ for further details.

ud6eca80515fff5751e29.text: Any storage type supported by the Proxmox VE storage library can be used. This means that containers can be stored on local (for example ⟦0⟧, ⟦1⟧ or directory), shared external (like ⟦2⟧, ⟦3⟧) or even distributed storage systems like Ceph. Advanced storage features like snapshots or clones can be used if the underlying storage supports them. The ⟦4⟧ backup tool can use snapshots to provide consistent container backups.

u031cc10f2249b8fdbe8f.text: Furthermore, local devices or local directories can be mounted directly using ⟦0⟧bind mounts⟦1⟧. This gives access to local resources inside a container with practically zero overhead. Bind mounts can be used as an easy way to share data between containers.

u7fc2a33c995bfbe359e7.text: Because of existing issues in the Linux kernel’s freezer subsystem the usage of FUSE mounts inside a container is strongly advised against, as containers need to be frozen for suspend or snapshot mode backups.

ud064925f2409c022ed52.text: The Proxmox Cluster file system (“pmxcfs”) is a database-driven file system for storing configuration files, replicated in real time to all cluster nodes using ⟦0⟧. We use this to store all Proxmox VE related configuration files.

uae2c4afd37f181228307.text: Although the file system stores all data inside a persistent database on disk, a copy of the data resides in RAM. This imposes restrictions on the maximum size, which is currently 128 MiB. This is still enough to store the configuration of several thousand virtual machines.

u14934637fe8b1b7216e3.text: This system provides the following advantages:

uc8c8d7c5fc9a5deb3f2d.text: Seamless replication of all configuration to all nodes in real time

u5cb20e9460b0044239b5.text: Provides strong consistency checks to avoid duplicate VM IDs

u39da4d0641435fcd22f9.text: Automatic updates of the corosync cluster configuration to all nodes

u550069446b23a8a3319c.text: The recommended way is to reinstall the node after you remove it from your cluster. This ensures that all secret cluster/ssh keys and any shared configuration data is destroyed.

ub144f72c59430787e84b.text: In some cases, you might prefer to put a node back to local mode without reinstalling, which is described in ⟦0⟧Separate A Node Without Reinstalling⟦1⟧

ueda603899ed57c659994.text: For the guest configuration files in ⟦0⟧ (VMs) and ⟦1⟧ (containers), Proxmox VE sees the containing node ⟦2⟧ as the owner of the respective guest. This concept enables the usage of local locks instead of expensive cluster-wide locks for preventing concurrent guest configuration changes.

uba9646f4e4366dc0486c.text: As a consequence, if the owning node of a guest fails (for example, due to a power outage, fencing event, etc.), a regular migration is not possible (even if all the disks are located on shared storage), because such a local lock on the (offline) owning node is unobtainable. This is not a problem for HA-managed guests, as Proxmox VE’s High Availability stack includes the necessary (cluster-wide) locking and watchdog functionality to ensure correct and automatic recovery of guests from fenced nodes.

uf413748ef41570eb8e7a.text: If a non-HA-managed guest has only shared disks (and no other local resources which are only available on the failed node), a manual recovery is possible by simply moving the guest configuration file from the failed node’s directory in ⟦0⟧ to an online node’s directory (which changes the logical owner or location of the guest).
