ub5c64139b3445214a19e.text: Before manually recovering a guest like this, make absolutely sure that the failed source node is really powered off/fenced. Otherwise Proxmox VE’s locking principles are violated by the ⟦0⟧ command, which can have unexpected consequences.

u40d7c5d2dab45063cce6.text: Guests with local disks (or other local resources which are only available on the offline node) are not recoverable like this. Either wait for the failed node to rejoin the cluster or restore such guests from backups.

ud3e5d6e2a74a7f02c233.text: Proxmox VE is a platform for running virtual machines and containers. It is based on Debian GNU/Linux and completely open source. For maximum flexibility, Proxmox VE provides two virtualization technologies—Kernel-based Virtual Machine (KVM) and Linux Containers (LXC).

u8f0ba196cd6dfd020aee.text: A core design goal is to make administration as easy as possible. You can use Proxmox VE on a single node, or assemble a cluster of many nodes. All management tasks can be done through the web-based management interface, and even a novice user can set up and install Proxmox VE within minutes.

ue8f911bffb13e722e735.text: While many people start with a single node, Proxmox VE can scale out to a large set of clustered nodes. The cluster stack is fully integrated and ships with the default installation.

u44782a1cc29a70a0ce76.text: Every node in a Proxmox VE cluster can perform all management tasks. There is no single-point-of-failure central management server—any node can manage the entire cluster. This multi-master architecture keeps the cluster manageable even if individual nodes are temporarily unavailable.

u22133c0e67d73b86f6d2.text: Proxmox VE uses the Proxmox Cluster File System (pmxcfs), a database-driven file system for storing configuration files. It can store the configuration of thousands of virtual machines. Corosync replicates these files in real time to all cluster nodes. The file system stores all data inside a persistent database on disk, while a copy resides in RAM, providing a maximum storage size of 128 MiB—more than enough for thousands of VMs.

ud7fed848bbf36c484c19.text: Proxmox VE is the only virtualization platform using this cluster file system.

u9a11ced0ac2ad15b8ac2.text: Proxmox VE is simple to use. The included web-based interface, built on the ExtJS JavaScript framework, provides a clean overview of all KVM guests and Linux containers, and full control over all cluster resources. You can manage VMs, containers, storage, and networking from the GUI, including history and syslog viewing for each node, running backup or restore jobs, live migration, and HA-triggered activities. There is no need to install a separate management tool or additional management node.

ufd4e6b37bbfcbcd58f47.text: For advanced users who prefer the comfort of a Unix shell or Windows PowerShell, Proxmox VE provides a command-line interface to manage all components of the virtual environment. This command-line interface has intelligent tab completion and full documentation in the form of man pages.

ub28473158f65fd407de2.text: Proxmox VE uses a RESTful API with JSON as the primary data format. The entire API is formally defined using JSON Schema, enabling fast and easy integration for third-party management tools such as custom hosting environments.

ubd3c76af52704728deca.text: You can define granular access for all objects (such as VMs, storage, and nodes) by using role-based user and permission management. Each permission specifies a subject (a user or group) and a role (set of privileges) on a specific path, following the access control list model.

u663bc4733c4cabad7bb8.text: Proxmox VE supports multiple authentication sources, including Microsoft Active Directory, LDAP, Linux PAM standard authentication, and the built-in Proxmox VE authentication server.

u85dc517d56931e3331bb.text: The Proxmox VE storage model is very flexible. Virtual machine images can be stored on one or several local storages, or on shared storage such as NFS or SAN. You may configure as many storage definitions as you like, using all storage technologies available for Debian GNU/Linux.

u6e0da888989c4cf03e01.text: One major benefit of storing VMs on shared storage is the ability to live-migrate running machines without any downtime, as all nodes in the cluster have direct access to VM disk images.

u735542f629be272a4200.text: The following network storage types are supported:

u20c2470d8295dd7a4c7a.text: LVM group (network backing with iSCSI targets)

u24dc950ee3b3281b34c4.text: The following local storage types are supported:

u9c76703d06a3e802b41c.text: LVM group (local backing devices such as block devices, Fibre Channel devices, and DRBD)

ue45358d042403f0a5dfd.text: The integrated backup tool (⟦0⟧) creates consistent snapshots of running containers and KVM guests. It creates an archive of the VM or container data, including the configuration files.

ud2698ae0f37869add7bc.text: Additionally, the ⟦0⟧Proxmox Backup Server integration⟦1⟧ provides advanced features, including the ability to combine full backups and data deduplication, perform client-side encryption, back up to tape or S3 object storage, and sync with other offsite Proxmox Backup Server installations.

ube863859de43a10a8d9e.text: KVM live backup works for all storage types including VM images on NFS, CIFS, iSCSI LUN, and Ceph RBD. The backup format is optimized for storing VM backups efficiently—using sparse files, out-of-order data, and minimized I/O.

ud3e60c886c643494df58.text: A multi-node Proxmox VE HA cluster enables highly available virtual machines and containers. The integrated ⟦0⟧High Availability (HA) manager⟦1⟧ automatically detects node failures using watchdog-based fencing and restarts affected services on healthy nodes. No external tools like Pacemaker are needed—the HA stack ships with Proxmox VE and is configured entirely through the web interface or command line.

u3fe636f994f5ba78573c.text: Proxmox VE uses a bridged networking model. All VMs can share one bridge as if virtual network cables from each guest were all plugged into the same switch. For connecting VMs to the outside world, bridges are attached to physical network cards and assigned a TCP/IP configuration.

u556f359c1057ca749298.text: For further flexibility, Virtual LANs (VLANs, IEEE 802.1q) and network bonding/aggregation are available, allowing you to build complex, flexible virtual networks for the Proxmox VE hosts and leverage the full power of the Linux network stack.

u5af0d2f0153b7d3829a3.text: For larger or multi-tenant environments, the ⟦0⟧Software Defined Network (SDN)⟦1⟧ stack provides zone-based network isolation and supports protocols such as VXLAN and EVPN. SDN is fully integrated into the web interface and installed by default.

u1ae1e2e85198eaab610f.text: The integrated firewall allows you to filter network packets on any VM or container interface. Common sets of firewall rules can be grouped into “security groups”.

u70cdf1b07c2149d92b86.text: Proxmox VE is a virtualization platform that tightly integrates compute, storage and networking resources, manages highly available clusters, backup/restore as well as disaster recovery. All components are software-defined and compatible with one another.

udeaa8a2b31722d355c84.text: Therefore it is possible to administrate them like a single system via the centralized web management interface. These capabilities make Proxmox VE an ideal choice to deploy and manage an open source ⟦0⟧hyper-converged infrastructure⟦1⟧.

u1cca1bfd22bed706dddb.text: 1.7.1. Benefits of a Hyper-Converged Infrastructure (HCI) with Proxmox VE

ue05803f39528059c9700.text: A hyper-converged infrastructure (HCI) is especially useful for deployments in which a high infrastructure demand meets a low administration budget, for distributed setups such as remote and branch office environments or for virtual private and public clouds.

u5236fee483e610f526b8.text: Scalability: seamless expansion of compute, network and storage devices (i.e. scale up servers and storage quickly and independently from each other).

uda512cf0d9d0753532a7.text: Low cost: Proxmox VE is open source and integrates all components you need such as compute, storage, networking, backup, and management center. It can replace an expensive compute/storage infrastructure.

u6509307e4f7eb4270bb2.text: Data protection and efficiency: services such as backup and disaster recovery are integrated.

u69a0263400ec545d149f.text: Simplicity: easy configuration and centralized administration.

u9a268c11fd71ad6b7071.text: Proxmox VE has tightly integrated support for deploying a hyper-converged storage infrastructure. You can, for example, deploy and manage the following two storage technologies by using the web interface only:

uce6808ca823fffabd840.text: ⟦0⟧Ceph⟦1⟧: a self-healing and self-managing shared, reliable and highly scalable storage system. Check out ⟦2⟧how to manage Ceph services on Proxmox VE nodes⟦3⟧

ua5c8d5f4499b34ccc869.text: ⟦0⟧ZFS⟦1⟧: a combined file system and logical volume manager with extensive protection against data corruption, various RAID modes, fast and cheap snapshots - among other features. Find out ⟦2⟧how to leverage the power of ZFS on Proxmox VE nodes⟦3⟧.

u30dccb625022325cd0b8.text: Besides above, Proxmox VE has support to integrate a wide range of additional storage technologies. You can find out about them in the ⟦0⟧Storage Manager chapter⟦1⟧.

ue5436ee277d529cf69ee.text: Proxmox VE uses a Linux kernel and is based on the Debian GNU/Linux distribution. The source code of Proxmox VE is released under the ⟦0⟧GNU Affero General Public License, version 3⟦1⟧. This means that you are free to inspect the source code at any time or contribute to the project yourself.

ud893f3bb7aeddf022687.text: Proxmox is committed to using open source software whenever possible. Open source software guarantees full access to all functionality—as well as high security and reliability. Everybody should have the right to access the source code of software to run it, build on it, or submit changes back to the project. Everybody is encouraged to contribute while Proxmox ensures the product always meets professional quality criteria.

u9874f1d9fee1ff191626.text: Open source software also helps to keep costs low and makes core infrastructure independent from a single vendor.

u7705b1d242a207043ea5.text: The project started in 2007, followed by a first stable version in 2008. At the time, it used OpenVZ for containers and KVM for virtual machines. The clustering features were limited, and the user interface was simple (a server-generated web page).

u65b18d17d1f8b527dc4a.text: The project quickly developed new features using the ⟦0⟧Corosync⟦1⟧ cluster stack, and the introduction of the Proxmox Cluster File System (pmxcfs) was a big step forward, because it completely hides the cluster complexity from the user. Managing a cluster of 16 nodes is as simple as managing a single node.

u11f032b872db90cb4d3a.text: The introduction of the REST API, with a complete declarative specification written in JSON Schema, enabled other people to integrate Proxmox VE into their infrastructure and made it easy to provide additional services.

u95f49b051efd3ae19fb6.text: The REST API also made it possible to replace the original user interface with a modern client-side single-page application using JavaScript. The old Java-based VNC console code was replaced with ⟦0⟧noVNC⟦1⟧, so only a web browser is needed to manage VMs.

u3f4b0029832cebbf9f08.text: The support for various storage types is another big achievement. Notably, Proxmox VE was the first distribution to ship ⟦0⟧ZFS on Linux⟦1⟧ by default in 2014. Another milestone was the ability to run and manage ⟦2⟧Ceph⟦3⟧ storage on the hypervisor nodes. Such setups are extremely cost effective.

u375cab617a428f1cac5c.text: When the project started, Proxmox was among the first companies providing commercial support for KVM. The KVM project itself continuously evolved and is now a widely used hypervisor. New features arrive with each release. The KVM live backup feature, developed by Proxmox, makes it possible to create snapshot backups on any storage type.

udb2e8ff43d56ddd683db.text: The most notable change with version 4.0 was the move from OpenVZ to ⟦0⟧LXC⟦1⟧. Containers are now deeply integrated, and they can use the same storage and network features as virtual machines. At the same time, the easy-to-use ⟦2⟧High Availability (HA) manager⟦3⟧ was introduced, simplifying the configuration and management of highly available setups.

ua6f05dadc9697a028372.text: During the development of Proxmox VE 5, asynchronous ⟦0⟧storage replication⟦1⟧ as well as automated ⟦2⟧certificate management⟦3⟧ using ACME/Let’s Encrypt were introduced, among many other features.

ud308c6c6972161de2a9f.text: The ⟦0⟧Software Defined Network (SDN)⟦1⟧ stack was developed in cooperation with the community. It was integrated into the web interface as an experimental feature in version 6.2, simplifying the management of sophisticated network configurations. Since version 8.1, the SDN integration is fully supported and installed by default.

u69cdb4d3dbe649cc5982.text: 2020 marked the release of a new project, the ⟦0⟧Proxmox Backup Server⟦1⟧, written in the Rust programming language. Proxmox Backup Server is deeply integrated with Proxmox VE and significantly improves backup capabilities by implementing incremental backups, deduplication, and much more.

uc531731609495642e84a.text: Another new tool, the ⟦0⟧Proxmox Offline Mirror⟦1⟧, was released in 2022, enabling subscriptions for systems which have no connection to the public internet.

u00b13483a5fd3335233f.text: The highly requested dark theme for the web interface was introduced in 2023. Later that year, version 8.0 integrated access to the Ceph enterprise repository. Access to the most stable Ceph repository is included with any Proxmox VE subscription.

uf45187804c8c15b88044.text: Automated and unattended installation for the official ⟦0⟧ISO installer⟦1⟧ was introduced in version 8.2, significantly simplifying large deployments of Proxmox VE.

u27046103030c50ae05c0.text: With the ⟦0⟧import wizard⟦1⟧, equally introduced in version 8.2, users can easily and efficiently migrate guests directly from other hypervisors like VMware ESXi ⟦2⟧⟦3⟧[Migrate to Proxmox VE ⟦4⟧⟦5⟧⟦6⟧]⟦7⟧⟦8⟧. Additionally, archives in Open Virtualization Format (OVF/OVA) can now be directly imported from file-based storages in the web interface.

u9c51be415c3fa20261f7.text: Proxmox VE is based on Debian GNU/Linux. The install disk images (ISO files) provided by Proxmox include a complete Debian system as well as all necessary Proxmox VE packages.

u0fe6408a25abe28003c1.text: The installer guides you through the setup, allowing you to partition the local disk(s), apply basic system configurations (for example, timezone, language, network), and install all required packages. This process should not take more than a few minutes. Installing with the provided ISO is the recommended method for new and existing users.

u9dd709e2881382005737.text: Alternatively, Proxmox VE can be installed on top of an existing Debian system. This option is only recommended for advanced users because detailed knowledge about Proxmox VE is required.

ub5c839d1fc130fb186d7.text: We recommend using high quality server hardware, when running Proxmox VE in production. To further decrease the impact of a failed host, you can run Proxmox VE in a cluster with highly available (HA) virtual machines and containers.

u01393de59be2dc8f9ef8.text: Proxmox VE can use local storage (DAS), SAN, NAS, and distributed storage like Ceph RBD. For details see ⟦0⟧chapter storage⟦1⟧.

uad000bbbbe5d89e47445.text: These minimum requirements are for evaluation purposes only and should not be used in production.

ufeb8d417304f1cbb0d8d.text: CPU: 64-bit x86 (Intel 64 or AMD64). Alternatively, 64-bit ARM (arm64, aarch64) with an ARMv8-A or newer CPU, see ⟦0⟧64-bit ARM (arm64) Support⟦1⟧.

u930351e35d56066a04ce.text: For x86 hosts, an Intel VT or AMD-V capable CPU and motherboard for KVM full virtualization support. On the supported arm64 platforms, KVM hardware-assisted virtualization needs no equivalent CPU flag.

u27eda969835b005d6ef6.text: RAM: 1 GB RAM, plus additional RAM needed for guests

ucc68d52ff55300197110.text: Intel 64 or AMD64 with an Intel VT or AMD-V CPU flag. Alternatively, a 64-bit ARM host with an ARMv9-A or newer CPU, see ⟦0⟧64-bit ARM (arm64) Support⟦1⟧.

udf0c44348472b10b31f8.text: Memory: Minimum 2 GB for the OS and Proxmox VE services, plus designated memory for guests. For Ceph and ZFS, additional memory is required; approximately 1GB of memory for every TB of used storage.

u4199dbb5a1e00a74b550.text: Fast and redundant storage, best results are achieved with SSDs.

u38fe28c2f03607d80959.text: OS storage: Use a hardware RAID with battery protected write cache (“BBU”) or non-RAID with ZFS (optional SSD for ZIL).

uda5a970b16f8a1fa3d32.text: For local storage, use either a hardware RAID with battery backed write cache (BBU) or non-RAID for ZFS and Ceph. Neither ZFS nor Ceph are compatible with a hardware RAID controller.

uf68353eff164db5c48ab.text: Shared and distributed storage is possible.

ub9eda5c2e6c7d8a91aa3.text: SSDs with Power-Loss-Protection (PLP) are recommended for good performance. Using consumer SSDs is discouraged.

uf157bbfc106abbefbeca.text: Redundant (Multi-)Gbit NICs, with additional NICs depending on the preferred storage technology and cluster setup.

uc85c1bdb71fac643e2fa.text: For PCI(e) passthrough, the CPU and motherboard need to support an input/output memory management unit (IOMMU): Intel VT-d or AMD-Vi on x86, or a System Memory Management Unit (SMMU) on arm64.

u204eab64ecb2275c26a5.text: IOMMU usually also needs to be enabled in the BIOS/UEFI. See the ⟦0⟧PCI(e) Passthrough⟦1⟧ chapter for details.

ude105f8e10d1bff5d35d.text: Proxmox VE supports native 64-bit ARM (arm64, aarch64) on the NVIDIA Grace Hopper and NVIDIA Vera platforms. On other UEFI-based ARMv9-A or newer hardware, support is best-effort. Device-tree-only single-board computers, such as the Raspberry Pi, are not supported.

ua26f95f81554a2f05e1e.text: An arm64 host must boot through UEFI and describe its hardware through ACPI (Advanced Configuration and Power Interface). Proxmox VE does not support device-tree-only or legacy BIOS boot on arm64.

ud307a604a83222b33ed7.text: Several x86-specific features are not available on arm64:

ud29d2b21a9484b2fe781.text: Virtual machines cannot use SeaBIOS. On arm64, guests always boot through UEFI, provided by the ARM build of OVMF, also known as AAVMF.

u3552765821feca280668.text: AMD SEV (Secure Encrypted Virtualization) memory encryption and Intel’s GVT-g mediated vGPUs are x86-only.

u3b4ad56bb3b5c030c8c1.text: There is no operating-system-level CPU microcode package, unlike ⟦0⟧ and ⟦1⟧ on x86.

u21867faeeac4c55a63f2.text: A cluster can contain both x86 and arm64 nodes, but guests cannot move between nodes of different architectures while running:

ue7ada51b34cac1a527d4.text: Live migration is only possible between nodes of the same architecture, because a running guest’s CPU state cannot be transferred across architectures.

u32cd6eaf8a4576f4d115.text: A guest, whether a virtual machine or a container, only runs on a node whose architecture matches the guest. Offline migration, backup and restore, or shared storage can move a guest’s data to a node of a different architecture, but the guest still needs to be reinstalled or reconfigured for that architecture before it starts.

uf15d82cd1634346e0e69.text: This is just a very quick and general benchmark. More detailed tests are recommended, especially regarding the I/O performance of your system.

u84e30086b5429f2c7a79.text: Installing on top of an existing Debian installation looks easy, but it presumes that the base system has been installed correctly and that you know how you want to configure and use the local storage. You also need to configure the network manually.

ufb2172e1041dbb31a227.text: In general, this is not trivial, especially when LVM or ZFS is used.

u45fa641fc544614acf13.text: The following sections will focus on common virtualization tasks and explain the Proxmox VE specifics regarding the administration and management of the host machine.

u2d01804f1c8b98cea215.text: Proxmox VE is based on ⟦0⟧Debian GNU/Linux⟦1⟧ with additional repositories to provide the Proxmox VE related packages. This means that the full range of Debian packages is available including security updates and bug fixes. Proxmox VE provides its own Linux kernel based on the Ubuntu kernel. It has all the necessary virtualization and container features enabled and includes ⟦2⟧ZFS⟦3⟧ and several extra hardware drivers.

u6d2acd563400ae96de09.text: Firmware updates from this chapter should be applied when running Proxmox VE on a bare-metal server. Whether configuring firmware updates is appropriate within guests, e.g. when using device pass-through, depends strongly on your setup and is therefore out of scope.

u7a1315f96152e147f4a0.text: In addition to regular software updates, firmware updates are also important for reliable and secure operation.

u50a2d5d6d3f0854fe694.text: When obtaining and applying firmware updates, a combination of available options is recommended to get them as early as possible or at all.

u6b5fd2e1e39962a2a0d9.text: The term firmware is usually divided linguistically into microcode (for CPUs) and firmware (for other devices).

ucb93dd4d6c0aaad2a487.text: This section is suitable for all devices. Updated microcode, which is usually included in a BIOS/UEFI update, is stored on the motherboard, whereas other firmware is stored on the respective device. This persistent method is especially important for the CPU, as it enables the earliest possible regular loading of the updated microcode at boot time.

u021fc88a48c5676ac653.text: With some updates, such as for BIOS/UEFI or storage controller, the device configuration could be reset. Please follow the vendor’s instructions carefully and back up the current configuration.

uc7c14fa8e93b4479077f.text: Please check with your vendor which update methods are available.

u1a3885b9d1b919f76846.text: Convenient update methods for servers can include Dell’s Lifecycle Manager or Service Packs from HPE.

u5c4c3dbb7395d26cfc20.text: Sometimes there are Linux utilities available as well. Examples are ⟦0⟧⟦1⟧mlxup⟦2⟧⟦3⟧ for NVIDIA ConnectX or ⟦4⟧⟦5⟧bnxtnvm⟦6⟧/⟦7⟧niccli⟦8⟧⟦9⟧ for Broadcom network cards.

uc6bee607b0a2d642f6d9.text: CPU microcode updates as described in this section are specific to x86 hosts. There is no equivalent operating-system-level microcode package for arm64.

u65c3d32837263e3c5385.text: Microcode updates are intended to fix found security vulnerabilities and other serious CPU bugs. While the CPU performance can be affected, a patched microcode is usually still more performant than an unpatched microcode where the kernel itself has to do mitigations. Depending on the CPU type, it is possible that performance results of the flawed factory state can no longer be achieved without knowingly running the CPU in an unsafe state.

u74fd1f69a881569bfbf6.text: To get an overview of present CPU vulnerabilities and their mitigations, run ⟦0⟧. Current real-world known vulnerabilities can only show up if the Proxmox VE host is ⟦1⟧up to date⟦2⟧, its version not ⟦3⟧end of life⟦4⟧, and has at least been rebooted since the last kernel update.

u6689f4b85a083befd588.text: Besides the recommended microcode update via ⟦0⟧persistent⟦1⟧ BIOS/UEFI updates, there is also an independent method via ⟦2⟧Early OS Microcode Updates⟦3⟧. It is convenient to use and also quite helpful when the motherboard vendor no longer provides BIOS/UEFI updates. Regardless of the method in use, a reboot is always needed to apply a microcode update.

u6085ad71a20f14e92b23.text: Depending on your current network organization and your resources you can choose either a bridged, routed, or masquerading networking setup.

u3f95054052f82c5afb1d.text: The ⟦0⟧Bridged⟦1⟧ model makes the most sense in this case, and this is also the default mode on new Proxmox VE installations. Each of your Guest system will have a virtual interface attached to the Proxmox VE bridge. This is similar in effect to having the Guest network card directly connected to a new switch on your LAN, the Proxmox VE host playing the role of the switch.

udb9a5957d8bbbd834f3d.text: In that case the only way to get outgoing network accesses for your guest systems is to use ⟦0⟧Masquerading⟦1⟧. For incoming network access to your guests, you will need to configure ⟦2⟧Port Forwarding⟦3⟧.

u617b0cb0a617ab833b30.text: For further flexibility, you can configure VLANs (IEEE 802.1q) and network bonding, also known as "link aggregation". That way it is possible to build complex and flexible virtual networks.

u43941d678db72ee93b5a.text: Bridges are like physical network switches implemented in software. All virtual guests can share a single bridge, or you can create multiple bridges to separate network domains. Each host can have up to 4094 bridges.

u5be5cb839c656fd3d7b2.text: Virtual machines behave as if they were directly connected to the physical network. The network, in turn, sees each virtual machine as having its own MAC, even though there is only one network cable connecting all of these VMs to the network.

u24ba908593b8fe108261.text: Most hosting providers do not support the above setup. For security reasons, they disable networking as soon as they detect multiple MAC addresses on a single interface.

ucbc99a4cf73511d8da70.text: Some providers allow you to register additional MACs through their management interface. This avoids the problem, but can be clumsy to configure because you need to register a MAC for each of your VMs.

ub66fc15ac03bd9beb35c.text: You can avoid the problem by “routing” all traffic via a single interface. This makes sure that all network packets use the same MAC address.

u4168329cf2b9df7fd68c.text: A common scenario is that you have a public IP (assume ⟦0⟧ for this example), and an additional IP block for your VMs (⟦1⟧). We recommend the following setup for such situations:

u4baff4948c2c71740eee.text: Masquerading allows guests having only a private IP address to access the network by using the host IP address for outgoing traffic. ud6aaf1aafff6a4b90770.text: Bonding (also called NIC teaming or Link Aggregation) is a technique for binding multiple NIC’s to a single network device. It is possible to achieve different goals, like make the network fault-tolerant, increase the performance or both together.

ue60dad998040c42388ae.text: High-speed hardware like Fibre Channel and the associated switching hardware can be quite expensive. By doing link aggregation, two NICs can appear as one logical interface, resulting in double speed. This is a native Linux kernel feature that is supported by most switches. If your nodes have multiple Ethernet ports, you can distribute your points of failure by running network cables to different switches and the bonded connection will failover to one cable or the other in case of network trouble.

u68afc0ee617413843e76.text: Aggregated links can improve live-migration delays and improve the speed of replication of data between Proxmox VE Cluster nodes.

u33105e6f2e0ae4c1e30a.text: ⟦0⟧Round-robin (balance-rr):⟦1⟧ Transmit network packets in sequential order from the first available network interface (NIC) slave through the last. This mode provides load balancing and fault tolerance.

u792d6c5568be4c03bfdf.text: ⟦0⟧Active-backup (active-backup):⟦1⟧ Only one NIC slave in the bond is active. A different slave becomes active if, and only if, the active slave fails. The single logical bonded interface’s MAC address is externally visible on only one NIC (port) to avoid distortion in the network switch. This mode provides fault tolerance.

u5586f0764e4aa223f46e.text: ⟦0⟧XOR (balance-xor):⟦1⟧ Transmit network packets based on [(source MAC address XOR’d with destination MAC address) modulo NIC slave count]. This selects the same NIC slave for each destination MAC address. This mode provides load balancing and fault tolerance.

u069519050d96cfc5b070.text: ⟦0⟧Broadcast (broadcast):⟦1⟧ Transmit network packets on all slave network interfaces. This mode provides fault tolerance.

u1a1bb1ebd69ea4c4216d.text: ⟦0⟧IEEE 802.3ad Dynamic link aggregation (802.3ad)(LACP):⟦1⟧ Creates aggregation groups that share the same speed and duplex settings. Utilizes all slave network interfaces in the active aggregator group according to the 802.3ad specification.

uad43e1715cecbf6390c0.text: ⟦0⟧Adaptive transmit load balancing (balance-tlb):⟦1⟧ Linux bonding driver mode that does not require any special network-switch support. The outgoing network packet traffic is distributed according to the current load (computed relative to the speed) on each network interface slave. Incoming traffic is received by one currently designated slave network interface. If this receiving slave fails, another slave takes over the MAC address of the failed receiving slave.

ud42485a6b0c943757f89.text: ⟦0⟧Adaptive load balancing (balance-alb):⟦1⟧ Includes balance-tlb plus receive load balancing (rlb) for IPV4 traffic, and does not require any special network switch support. The receive load balancing is achieved by ARP negotiation. The bonding driver intercepts the ARP Replies sent by the local system on their way out and overwrites the source hardware address with the unique hardware address of one of the NIC slaves in the single logical bonded interface such that different network-peers use different MAC addresses for their network packet traffic.

u24387e1d97f9fb872b5d.text: If your switch supports the LACP (IEEE 802.3ad) protocol, then we recommend using the corresponding bonding mode (802.3ad). Otherwise you should generally use the active-backup mode.

ucf05c09cd9be8f241c49.text: The bond modes ⟦0⟧balance-alb⟦1⟧ and ⟦2⟧balance-tlb⟦3⟧ are not suitable when the local addresses are not known to the host. These bond modes should not be used when a Linux bridge with guests is used in combination with the bond.

u83ccafb7a0090d83cd0f.text: For the cluster network (Corosync) we recommend configuring it with multiple networks. Corosync does not need a bond for network redundancy as it can switch between networks by itself, if one becomes unusable. Some bond modes are known to be problematic for Corosync, see ⟦0⟧Corosync over Bonds⟦1⟧.

u533c19d238a121833d21.text: A virtual LAN (VLAN) is a broadcast domain that is partitioned and isolated in the network at layer two. So it is possible to have multiple networks (4096) in a physical network, each independent of the other ones.

ub9325c818c653a0af6c9.text: Each VLAN network is identified by a number often called ⟦0⟧tag⟦1⟧. Network packages are then ⟦2⟧tagged⟦3⟧ to identify which virtual network they belong to.

uf27b4c5c924d5072dc54.text: Proxmox VE supports this setup out of the box. You can specify the VLAN tag when you create a VM. The VLAN tag is part of the guest network configuration. The networking layer supports different modes to implement VLANs, depending on the bridge configuration:

udc2d83e4086acfc286e6.text: ⟦0⟧VLAN awareness on the Linux bridge:⟦1⟧ In this case, each guest’s virtual network card is assigned to a VLAN tag, which is transparently supported by the Linux bridge. Trunk mode is also possible, but that makes configuration in the guest necessary.

u0cf455e428e629b3b4d4.text: ⟦0⟧"traditional" VLAN on the Linux bridge:⟦1⟧ In contrast to the VLAN awareness method, this method is not transparent and creates a VLAN device with associated bridge for each VLAN. That is, creating a guest on VLAN 5 for example, would create two interfaces eno1.5 and vmbr0v5, which would remain until a reboot occurs.

u8c64277fd0cf14eb02c6.text: ⟦0⟧Open vSwitch VLAN:⟦1⟧ This mode uses the OVS VLAN feature.

u3587ed1f398caae7eebb.text: ⟦0⟧Guest configured VLAN:⟦1⟧ VLANs are assigned inside the guest. In this case, the setup is completely done inside the guest and can not be influenced from the outside. The benefit is that you can use more than one VLAN on a single virtual NIC.

u47c076d5b50c1a492b88.text: To allow host communication with an isolated network. It is possible to apply VLAN tags to any network device (NIC, Bond, Bridge). In general, you should configure the VLAN on the interface with the least abstraction layers between itself and the physical NIC.

u253748d058d1edb4a7b2.text: ZFS is a combined file system and logical volume manager designed by Sun Microsystems. Starting with Proxmox VE 3.4, the native Linux kernel port of the ZFS file system is introduced as optional file system and also as an additional selection for the root file system. There is no need for manually compile ZFS modules - all packages are included.

ud2d5d06ee4f88b8af7ff.text: By using ZFS, its possible to achieve maximum enterprise features with low budget hardware, but also high performance systems by leveraging SSD caching or even SSD only setups. ZFS can replace cost intense hardware raid cards by moderate CPU and memory load combined with easy management.

u75a9519b42e0ed06ddd1.text: ZFS depends heavily on memory, so you need at least 8GB to start. In practice, use as much as you can get for your hardware/budget. To prevent data corruption, we recommend the use of high quality ECC RAM.

u79624b187011df3e0382.text: If you use a dedicated cache and/or log disk, you should use an enterprise class SSD. This can increase the overall performance significantly.

u90c5a2d9bcf028236782.text: Do not use ZFS on top of a hardware RAID controller which has its own cache management. ZFS needs to communicate directly with the disks. An HBA adapter or something like an LSI controller flashed in “IT” mode is more appropriate.

u422f09f7ef5e94573cb0.text: There are a few factors to take into consideration when choosing the layout of a ZFS pool. The basic building block of a ZFS pool is the virtual device, or ⟦0⟧. All vdevs in a pool are used equally and the data is striped among them (RAID0). Check the ⟦1⟧ manpage for more details on vdevs.

ua37862a7efd58e0e8034.text: Each ⟦0⟧ type has different performance behaviors. The two parameters of interest are the IOPS (Input/Output Operations per Second) and the bandwidth with which data can be written or read.

u2a93e03a44b789bf7da1.text: A ⟦0⟧mirror⟦1⟧ vdev (RAID1) will approximately behave like a single disk in regard to both parameters when writing data. When reading data the performance will scale linearly with the number of disks in the mirror.

u070213d2b8cce38bcbf9.text: A common situation is to have 4 disks. When setting it up as 2 mirror vdevs (RAID10) the pool will have the write characteristics as two single disks in regard to IOPS and bandwidth. For read operations it will resemble 4 single disks.

ubcc4aa30fe7897456087.text: A ⟦0⟧RAIDZ⟦1⟧ of any redundancy level will approximately behave like a single disk in regard to IOPS with a lot of bandwidth. How much bandwidth depends on the size of the RAIDZ vdev and the redundancy level.

u68354618c5463ee7109d.text: A ⟦0⟧dRAID⟦1⟧ pool should match the performance of an equivalent ⟦2⟧RAIDZ⟦3⟧ pool.

ua106b3ab99c12ece3198.text: For running VMs, IOPS is the more important metric in most situations.

uedf7b8f6a4b76665bd17.text: While a pool made of ⟦0⟧mirror⟦1⟧ vdevs will have the best performance characteristics, the usable space will be 50% of the disks available. Less if a mirror vdev consists of more than 2 disks, for example in a 3-way mirror. At least one healthy disk per mirror is needed for the pool to stay functional.

ua9e5af1cae88dc5292c3.text: The usable space of a ⟦0⟧RAIDZ⟦1⟧ type vdev of N disks is roughly N-P, with P being the RAIDZ-level. The RAIDZ-level indicates how many arbitrary disks can fail without losing data. A special case is a 4 disk pool with RAIDZ2. In this situation it is usually better to use 2 mirror vdevs for the better performance as the usable space will be the same.

ud0696af679be7912bbf9.text: Another important factor when using any RAIDZ level is how ZVOL datasets, which are used for VM disks, behave. For each data block the pool needs parity data which is at least the size of the minimum block size defined by the ⟦0⟧ value of the pool. With an ashift of 12 the block size of the pool is 4k. The default block size for a ZVOL is 8k. Therefore, in a RAIDZ2 each 8k block written will cause two additional 4k parity blocks to be written, 8k + 4k + 4k = 16k. This is of course a simplified approach and the real situation will be slightly different with metadata, compression and such not being accounted for in this example.

u222e33909e222b3f266d.text: This behavior can be observed when checking the following properties of the ZVOL:

u3e0d60fa92018659e64c.text: ⟦0⟧ (if the pool is not thin provisioned)

u109517b26aa8c7398485.text: ⟦0⟧ (if the pool is thin provisioned and without snapshots present)

u0f8136424fbcaa7df563.text: ⟦0⟧ is the size of the disk as it is presented to the VM, while ⟦1⟧ shows the reserved space on the pool which includes the expected space needed for the parity data. If the pool is thin provisioned, the ⟦2⟧ will be set to 0. Another way to observe the behavior is to compare the used disk space within the VM and the ⟦3⟧ property. Be aware that snapshots will skew the value.

u423d72d08c9d25350b00.text: Mirror vdevs (RAID1, RAID10) have favorable behavior for VM workloads. Use them, unless your environment has specific needs and characteristics where RAIDZ performance characteristics are acceptable.

u2985c3ba0c46a1ba445f.text: In a ZFS dRAID (declustered RAID) the hot spare drive(s) participate in the RAID. Their spare capacity is reserved and used for rebuilding when one drive fails. This provides, depending on the configuration, faster rebuilding compared to a RAIDZ in case of drive failure. More information can be found in the official OpenZFS documentation. ⟦0⟧⟦1⟧[OpenZFS dRAID ⟦2⟧⟦3⟧⟦4⟧]⟦5⟧⟦6⟧

u0540b10e44bbb6573d8e.text: The number of ⟦0⟧ tells the system how many disks it should keep ready in case of a disk failure. The default value is 0 ⟦1⟧. Without spares, rebuilding won’t get any speed benefits.

This challenge is fulfilled by creating a certain DNS record in the domain’s zone.

u18d8caf6c27343d2527e.text: Proxmox VE supports both of those challenge types out of the box, you can configure plugins either over the web interface under ⟦0⟧, or using the ⟦1⟧ command.

uf79c155410c2da761c45.text: Kernel Samepage Merging (KSM) is an optional memory deduplication feature offered by the Linux kernel, which is enabled by default in Proxmox VE. KSM works by scanning a range of physical memory pages for identical content, and identifying the virtual pages that are mapped to them. If identical pages are found, the corresponding virtual pages are re-mapped so that they all point to the same physical page, and the old pages are freed. The virtual pages are marked as "copy-on-write", so that any writes to them will be written to a new area of memory, leaving the shared physical page intact.

uc64a37f5afd488b7df05.text: KSM can optimize memory usage in virtualization environments, as multiple VMs running similar operating systems or workloads could potentially share a lot of common memory pages.

u8d97bb9866eba65dbd44.text: However, while KSM can reduce memory usage, it also comes with some security risks, as it can expose VMs to side-channel attacks. Research has shown that it is possible to infer information about a running VM via a second VM on the same host, by exploiting certain characteristics of KSM.

ueb4de57591be1a59e88a.text: Thus, if you are using Proxmox VE to provide hosting services, you should consider disabling KSM, in order to provide your users with additional security. Furthermore, you should check your country’s regulations, as disabling KSM may be a legal requirement.

u21767ada280bf4034c38.text: KSM can be disabled on a node or on a per-VM basis.

uc68d2cf7702a39d654e1.text: The Proxmox VE cluster manager ⟦0⟧ is a tool to create a group of physical servers. Such a group is called a ⟦1⟧cluster⟦2⟧. We use the ⟦3⟧Corosync Cluster Engine⟦4⟧ for reliable group communication. There’s no explicit limit for the number of nodes in a cluster. In practice, the actual possible node count may be limited by the host and network performance. Currently (2021), there are reports of clusters (using high-end enterprise hardware) with over 50 nodes in production.

u4a916ad0a248c0d16227.text: ⟦0⟧ can be used to create a new cluster, join nodes to a cluster, leave the cluster, get status information, and do various other cluster-related tasks. The ⟦1⟧P⟦2⟧rox⟦3⟧m⟦4⟧o⟦5⟧x⟦6⟧ ⟦7⟧C⟦8⟧luster ⟦9⟧F⟦10⟧ile ⟦11⟧S⟦12⟧ystem (“pmxcfs”) is used to transparently distribute the cluster configuration to all cluster nodes.

u7799c471d1e98f3edaa8.text: Grouping nodes into a cluster has the following advantages:

ud3e118e0d12e1951198e.text: Multi-master clusters: each node can do all management tasks

u158d2c56cb2732eb4fdb.text: Use of ⟦0⟧, a database-driven file system, for storing configuration files, replicated in real-time on all nodes using ⟦1⟧

ua4d388e4ce0afeea8c11.text: Easy migration of virtual machines and containers between physical hosts

uf2e03ccf920b7f2f07a6.text: Cluster-wide services like firewall and HA

u00885c9eed9bf089a94e.text: All nodes must be able to connect to each other via UDP ports 5405-5412 for corosync to work.

ud94f11681a7b72353ea9.text: Date and time must be synchronized.

u0a731e9da8ebeb985a7e.text: An SSH tunnel on TCP port 22 between nodes is required.

ufad6e36e234d20cf509d.text: If you are interested in High Availability, you need to have at least three nodes for reliable quorum. All nodes should have the same version.

ud92145e4bc363e7107b9.text: For smaller 2-node clusters, the ⟦0⟧QDevice⟦1⟧ can be used to provide a 3rd vote.

u9eed2cbdfc894872e6f9.text: We recommend a dedicated physical NIC for the cluster traffic.

ue81513bdcb7b075c4dc0.text: The Proxmox VE cluster communication uses the Corosync protocol. It needs consistent low latency but not a lot of bandwidth. A dedicated 1 Gbit NIC is enough in most situations. It helps to avoid situations where other services can use up all the available bandwidth. Which in turn would increase the latency for the Corosync packets.

ua7aace0215c6546c011f.text: Additional links for cluster traffic offers redundancy in case the dedicated network is down.

ue3817917c29986064421.text: To ensure reliable Corosync redundancy, it is essential to have at least another link on a different physical network. This enables Corosync to keep the cluster communication alive should the dedicated network be down.

u6da6487533536d85db0c.text: A single link backed by a bond can be problematic in certain failure scenarios, see ⟦0⟧Corosync Over Bonds⟦1⟧.

uf805eff61196c426330d.text: The root password of a cluster node is required for adding nodes.

u1b7fd386db1aea315ad0.text: Online migration of virtual machines is only supported when nodes have CPUs from the same vendor. It might work otherwise, but this is never guaranteed.

u219b51e9181d99b49a3a.text: First, install Proxmox VE on all nodes. Make sure that each node is installed with the final hostname and IP configuration. Changing the hostname and IP is not possible after cluster creation.

ubaeccfcc92de17f9fe72.text: While it’s common to reference all node names and their IPs in ⟦0⟧ (or make their names resolvable through other means), this is not necessary for a cluster to work. It may be useful however, as you can then connect from one node to another via SSH, using the easier to remember node name (see also ⟦1⟧Link Address Types⟦2⟧). Note that we always recommend referencing nodes by their IP addresses in the cluster configuration.

u1ffefaf60d0b278ca93c.text: You can either create a cluster on the console (login via ⟦0⟧), or through the API using the Proxmox VE web interface (⟦1⟧Datacenter → Cluster⟦2⟧).

u9f820221dd1bcc143ab5.text: Use a unique name for your cluster. This name cannot be changed later. The cluster name follows the same rules as node names.

u6baa96f89254cfd6c525.text: Under ⟦0⟧Datacenter → Cluster⟦1⟧, click on ⟦2⟧Create Cluster⟦3⟧. Enter the cluster name and select a network connection from the drop-down list to serve as the main cluster network (Link 0). It defaults to the IP resolved via the node’s hostname.

ua8b3823301c6648ec7fe.text: As of Proxmox VE 6.2, up to 8 fallback links can be added to a cluster. To add a redundant link, click the ⟦0⟧Add⟦1⟧ button and select a link number and IP address from the respective fields. Prior to Proxmox VE 6.2, to add a second link as fallback, you can select the ⟦2⟧Advanced⟦3⟧ checkbox and choose an additional network interface (Link 1, see also ⟦4⟧Corosync Redundancy⟦5⟧).

While the cluster network itself produces small amounts of data, it is very sensitive to latency. Check out full ⟦0⟧cluster network requirements⟦1⟧.

u46f29f1c7ae3254de39f.text: 5.3.3. Multiple Clusters in the Same Network

uc4defd93d56bdaf707e1.text: It is possible to create multiple clusters in the same physical or logical network. In this case, each cluster must have a unique name to avoid possible clashes in the cluster communication stack. Furthermore, this helps avoid human confusion by making clusters clearly distinguishable.

ud4bd63850ac86c2f9a40.text: While the bandwidth requirement of a corosync cluster is relatively low, the latency of packets and the packets per second (PPS) rate is the limiting factor. Different clusters in the same network can compete with each other for these resources, so it may still make sense to use separate physical network infrastructure for bigger clusters.

u95f749f0e213e14a6563.text: All existing configuration in ⟦0⟧ is overwritten when joining a cluster. In particular, a joining node cannot hold any guests, since guest IDs could otherwise conflict, and the node will inherit the cluster’s storage configuration. To join a node with existing guest, as a workaround, you can create a backup of each guest (using ⟦1⟧) and restore it under a different ID after joining. If the node’s storage layout differs, you will need to re-add the node’s storages, and adapt each storage’s node restriction to reflect on which nodes the storage is actually available.

u5c0756518bfea9821e65.text: 5.4.1. Join Node to Cluster via GUI

u97c9c3521b9059518a47.text: Log in to the web interface on an existing cluster node. Under ⟦0⟧Datacenter → Cluster⟦1⟧, click the ⟦2⟧Join Information⟦3⟧ button at the top. Then, click on the button ⟦4⟧Copy Information⟦5⟧. Alternatively, copy the string from the ⟦6⟧Information⟦7⟧ field manually.

u2b7409f92451a06c1284.text: Next, log in to the web interface on the node you want to add. Under ⟦0⟧Datacenter → Cluster⟦1⟧, click on ⟦2⟧Join Cluster⟦3⟧. Fill in the ⟦4⟧Information⟦5⟧ field with the ⟦6⟧Join Information⟦7⟧ text you copied earlier. Most settings required for joining the cluster will be filled out automatically. For security reasons, the cluster password has to be entered manually.

u70adf39e838d134ea8ea.text: To enter all required data manually, you can disable the ⟦0⟧Assisted Join⟦1⟧ checkbox.

ucfe7bde2555673d9ba4e.text: After clicking the ⟦0⟧Join⟦1⟧ button, the cluster join process will start immediately. After the node has joined the cluster, its current node certificate will be replaced by one signed from the cluster certificate authority (CA). This means that the current session will stop working after a few seconds. You then might need to force-reload the web interface and log in again with the cluster credentials.

u12f47532b66a071e3a5c.text: Now your node should be visible under ⟦0⟧Datacenter → Cluster⟦1⟧.

u386bb59e9e941de5d4d5.text: The following steps explain how to remove a node from a cluster that was also part of a ⟦0⟧Ceph⟦1⟧ cluster. If Ceph was not installed on your node, you can simply ignore the steps that mention it.

ue7c304cc52335ebde39e.text: If your configuration contains a QDevice, you will need to remove it before removing the cluster node, as outlined in the FAQ ⟦0⟧here⟦1⟧.

ua2048d22dbc56e675a24.text: Move all virtual machines and containers away from the node.

udd0d71f4ddeeb6fd17c9.text: Back up all local data on the node to be deleted.

u88161dc5dbc57cbd6730.text: Make sure the node to be deleted is not part of any replication job anymore.

ue90e14792cf46b511281.text: If you fail to remove replication jobs from a node before removing the node itself, the replication job will become irremovable. Note that replication automatically switches direction when a replicated VM is migrated. Therefore, migrating a replicated VM from a node that is going to be deleted will set up replication jobs to that node automatically.

u3bbb84c94fa7fdf3b667.text: Ensure that the remaining Ceph cluster has sufficient storage space and that the OSDs are running (i.e. ⟦0⟧ and ⟦1⟧). The destruction of any OSD, especially the last one on a node, will trigger a data rebalance in Ceph.

u62d3236c75f4878ca034.text: Make sure that there are still enough nodes with OSDs available to satisfy the ⟦0⟧ parameters configured for the Ceph pools. If there are fewer than ⟦1⟧ (default: 3) nodes available, data redundancy will be degraded. If there are fewer than ⟦2⟧ (default: 2) nodes available, the I/O of the pools will be blocked until there are enough replicas available. Affected guests may crash if their I/O is blocked.

uecb9858f4e807a7e9372.text: Ensure that sufficient ⟦0⟧monitors⟦1⟧, ⟦2⟧managers⟦3⟧ and, if using CephFS, ⟦4⟧metadata servers⟦5⟧ remain available in the Ceph cluster.

u311df9a5fd23bec05ecf.text: Before a node can be removed from a cluster, you must ensure that it is no longer part of a Ceph cluster and that no Ceph resources or services are residing on it.

ufee57f92e4f4a791ad66.text: In the following example, the cluster node ⟦0⟧ will be removed from both the Ceph-, and Proxmox VE corosync-cluster.

ub8a3437ed44b87b3af9c.text: Start by removing the node from the Ceph cluster, this consists of multiple steps:

u307b4161c83d43c92d85.text: Start by ⟦0⟧destroying⟦1⟧ the remaining Ceph OSDs on the node to be deleted, one after another.

uccd90110b3e0a3b1b145.text: Wait until the ⟦0⟧CEPH status⟦1⟧ reaches ⟦2⟧ again.

u91a13458a673a0a0efd2.text: If any exists, destroy the remaining ⟦0⟧Ceph metadata servers⟦1⟧ via the web interface at ⟦2⟧Ceph → CephFS⟦3⟧ or by running:

u9d7d74c31fe93380f45d.text: Finally, remove the now empty Ceph bucket (Proxmox VE node to be removed) from the CRUSH hierarchy.

u2d285948273d9a6bf86c.text: Proxmox VE use a quorum-based technique to provide a consistent state among all cluster nodes.

u0c53cff118429e9bd885.text: A quorum is the minimum number of votes that a distributed transaction has to obtain in order to be allowed to perform an operation in a distributed system.

u0ec0f0af58ccaa97ef0e.text: In case of network partitioning, state changes requires that a majority of nodes are online. The cluster switches to read-only mode if it loses quorum.

u7f5da9057b0dea225ab8.text: Proxmox VE assigns a single vote to each node by default.

u17e417399e6ce83e7be7.text: The cluster network is the core of a cluster. All messages sent over it have to be delivered reliably to all nodes in their respective order. In Proxmox VE this part is done by corosync, an implementation of a high performance, low overhead, high availability development toolkit. It serves our decentralized configuration file system (⟦0⟧).

u0c5d5276ebf9859bdb86.text: The Proxmox VE cluster stack requires a reliable network with latencies under 5 milliseconds (LAN performance) between all nodes to operate stably. While on setups with a small node count a network with higher latencies ⟦0⟧may⟦1⟧ work, this is not guaranteed and gets rather unlikely with more than three nodes and latencies above around 10 ms.

u1820ae347ea58d7ecd00.text: The network should not be used heavily by other members, as while corosync does not use much bandwidth, it is sensitive to latency jitters; ideally corosync runs on its own physically separated network. Especially do not use a shared network for corosync and storage (except as a potential low-priority fallback in a ⟦0⟧redundant⟦1⟧ configuration).

u99a522c6085cac189e1c.text: Before setting up a cluster, it is good practice to check if the network is fit for that purpose. To ensure that the nodes can connect to each other on the cluster network, you can test the connectivity between them with the ⟦0⟧ tool.

ua0108d6b6ff9684fc30d.text: If the Proxmox VE firewall is enabled, ACCEPT rules for corosync will automatically be generated - no manual action is required.

u3dbec6bd2015742df5aa.text: Corosync used Multicast before version 3.0 (introduced in Proxmox VE 6.0). Modern versions rely on ⟦0⟧Kronosnet⟦1⟧ for cluster communication, which, for now, only supports regular UDP unicast.

u9ee3d45466f18e8f56cd.text: You can still enable Multicast or legacy unicast by setting your transport to ⟦0⟧ or ⟦1⟧ in your ⟦2⟧⟦3⟧⟦4⟧, but keep in mind that this will disable all cryptography and redundancy support. This is therefore not recommended.

u3e772bb9f8bd68deb444.text: We recommend at least one dedicated physical NIC for the primary Corosync link, see ⟦0⟧Requirements⟦1⟧. ⟦2⟧Bonds⟦3⟧ may be used as additional links for increased redundancy. The following caveats apply ⟦4⟧whenever a bond is used for Corosync traffic⟦5⟧:

ub0e922daa37e4a7a1ca1.text: Bond mode ⟦0⟧active-backup⟦1⟧ may not provide the expected redundancy in certain failure scenarios, see below for details.

ua10d19f9c5b63d2b0d7e.text: We ⟦0⟧advise against⟦1⟧ using bond modes ⟦2⟧balance-rr⟦3⟧, ⟦4⟧balance-xor⟦5⟧, ⟦6⟧balance-tlb⟦7⟧, or ⟦8⟧balance-alb⟦9⟧ for Corosync traffic. They are known to be problematic in certain failure scenarios, see below for details.

ud9f98d66ff799088f2e2.text: ⟦0⟧IEEE 802.3ad (LACP)⟦1⟧: If LACP bonds are used for corosync traffic, we strongly recommend setting ⟦2⟧ on the ⟦3⟧Proxmox VE⟦4⟧ node and the ⟦5⟧switch⟦6⟧! With the default setting ⟦7⟧, this mode is known to be problematic in certain failure scenarios, see below for details.

u6523b957e78f3df0e845.text: Using a ⟦0⟧bond⟦1⟧ as a Corosync link can be problematic in certain failure scenarios. Consider the failure scenario where one of the bonded interfaces fails and stops transmitting packets, but its link state stays up, and there are no other Corosync links available. In this scenario, some bond modes may cause a state of asymmetric connectivity where cluster nodes can only communicate with different subsets of other nodes. Affected are bond modes that provide load balancing, as these modes may still try to send out a subset of packets via the failed interface. In case of asymmetric connectivity, Corosync may not be able to form a stable quorum in the cluster. If this state persists and HA is enabled, even nodes whose bond does not have any issues may fence themselves. In the worst case, the whole cluster may fence itself.

u24dc608399388198448c.text: The bond mode ⟦0⟧active-backup⟦1⟧ will ⟦2⟧not⟦3⟧ cause asymmetric connectivity in the failure scenario described above. However, the bond with the interface failure may not switch over to the backup link. The node may lose connection to the cluster and, if HA is enabled, fence itself.

u99d5f875b6245e408637.text: Bond modes ⟦0⟧balance-rr⟦1⟧, ⟦2⟧balance-xor⟦3⟧, ⟦4⟧⟦5⟧⟦6⟧, or ⟦7⟧balance-alb⟦8⟧ may cause asymmetric connectivity in the failure scenario above, which can lead to unexpected fencing if HA is enabled.

ub3c4b2d61e2db1da3c89.text: Bond mode ⟦0⟧IEEE 802.3ad (LACP)⟦1⟧ can cause asymmetric connectivity in the failure scenario above, but it can recover from this state, as each side of the bond (Proxmox VE node and switch) can stop using a bonded interface if it has not received three LACPDUs in a row on it. However, with default settings, LACPDUs are only sent every 30 seconds, yielding a failover time of 90 seconds. This is too long, as nodes with HA resources will fence themselves already after roughly one minute without a stable quorum. If LACP bonds are used for corosync traffic, we recommend setting ⟦2⟧ on the ⟦3⟧Proxmox VE⟦4⟧ node and the ⟦5⟧switch⟦6⟧! Setting this option on one side requests the other side to send an LACPDU every second. Setting this option on both sides can reduce the failover time in the scenario above to 3 seconds and thus prevent fencing.

u4149aec58bbe9a1ec267.text: Links are used according to a priority setting. You can configure this priority by setting ⟦0⟧⟦1⟧⟦2⟧ in the corresponding interface section in ⟦3⟧, or, preferably, using the ⟦4⟧priority⟦5⟧ parameter when creating your cluster with ⟦6⟧:

u1d45cd07845c14bdc7a2.text: This would cause ⟦0⟧link1⟦1⟧ to be used first, since it has the higher priority.

u5968bb6627b0cc7c3705.text: If no priorities are configured manually (or two links have the same priority), links will be used in order of their number, with the lower number having higher priority.

u0502f4d7a13352dd0015.text: Even if all links are working, only the one with the highest priority will see corosync traffic. Link priorities cannot be mixed, meaning that links with different priorities will not be able to communicate with each other.

ub29d67fffb39e94fcef3.text: Since lower priority links will not see traffic unless all higher priorities have failed, it becomes a useful strategy to specify networks used for other tasks (VMs, storage, etc.) as low-priority links. If worst comes to worst, a higher latency or more congested connection might be better than no connection at all.

u7aff1fb464b666905e63.text: This section describes a way to deploy an external voter in a Proxmox VE cluster. When configured, the cluster can sustain more node failures without violating safety properties of the cluster communication.

u9007cefbfe9b90ff453e.text: For this to work, there are two services involved:

uf1a815e8dd0342320b86.text: A QDevice daemon which runs on each Proxmox VE node

ue7ea140e1fcce320e1af.text: An external vote daemon which runs on an independent server

u97a34daa968950660bf9.text: As a result, you can achieve higher availability, even in smaller setups (for example 2+1 nodes).

u1373467ccd93dc797a07.text: The Corosync Quorum Device (QDevice) is a daemon which runs on each cluster node. It provides a configured number of votes to the cluster’s quorum subsystem, based on an externally running third-party arbitrator’s decision. Its primary use is to allow a cluster to sustain more node failures than standard quorum rules allow. This can be done safely as the external device can see all nodes and thus choose only one set of nodes to give its vote. This will only be done if said set of nodes can have quorum (again) after receiving the third-party vote.

ub6cde1e74e75cb9d1cbf.text: Currently, only ⟦0⟧QDevice Net⟦1⟧ is supported as a third-party arbitrator. This is a daemon which provides a vote to a cluster partition, if it can reach the partition members over the network. It will only give votes to one partition of a cluster at any time. It’s designed to support multiple clusters and is almost configuration and state free. New clusters are handled dynamically and no configuration file is needed on the host running a QDevice.

u5e1deba355b1d6ad2aaf.text: The only requirements for the external host are that it needs network access to the cluster and to have a corosync-qnetd package available. We provide a package for Debian based hosts, and other Linux distributions should also have a package available through their respective package manager.

u44a06ba6ffff47f095f7.text: Unlike corosync itself, a QDevice connects to the cluster over TCP/IP. The daemon can also run outside the LAN of the cluster and isn’t limited to the low latencies requirements of corosync.

ua1229e65c23d90d0647a.text: We support QDevices for clusters with an even number of nodes and recommend it for 2 node clusters, if they should provide higher availability. For clusters with an odd node count, we currently discourage the use of QDevices. The reason for this is the difference in the votes which the QDevice provides for each cluster type. Even numbered clusters get a single additional vote, which only increases availability, because if the QDevice itself fails, you are in the same position as with no QDevice at all.

uf0a4c444c289958fc59b.text: On the other hand, with an odd numbered cluster size, the QDevice provides ⟦0⟧(N-1)⟦1⟧ votes — where ⟦2⟧N⟦3⟧ corresponds to the cluster node count. This alternative behavior makes sense; if it had only one additional vote, the cluster could get into a split-brain situation. This algorithm allows for all nodes but one (and naturally the QDevice itself) to fail. However, there are two drawbacks to this:

ue6acaa220b1d055def72.text: If the QNet daemon itself fails, no other node may fail or the cluster immediately loses quorum. For example, in a cluster with 15 nodes, 7 could fail before the cluster becomes inquorate. But, if a QDevice is configured here and it itself fails, ⟦0⟧no single node⟦1⟧ of the 15 may fail. The QDevice acts almost as a single point of failure in this case.

ufee6df2d00537ee19ed3.text: The fact that all but one node plus QDevice may fail sounds promising at first, but this may result in a mass recovery of HA services, which could overload the single remaining node. Furthermore, a Ceph server will stop providing services if only ⟦0⟧((N-1)⟦1⟧)⟦2⟧ nodes or less remain online.

u0370d8e77a5bd23453ee.text: If you understand the drawbacks and implications, you can decide yourself if you want to use this technology in an odd numbered cluster setup.

u024eefef6e4b6224dc73.text: We recommend running any daemon which provides votes to corosync-qdevice as an unprivileged user. Proxmox VE and Debian provide a package which is already configured to do so. The traffic between the daemon and the cluster must be encrypted to ensure a safe and secure integration of the QDevice in Proxmox VE.

u8265b83e7018bb9d9461.text: First, install the ⟦0⟧corosync-qnetd⟦1⟧ package on your external server

u4b7267e5bcad45138837.text: and the ⟦0⟧corosync-qdevice⟦1⟧ package on all cluster nodes

u23a866132310b2777af0.text: The token coefficient can be configured in the ⟦0⟧ section in ⟦1⟧. If the token coefficient is not explicitly set, it defaults to 650 milliseconds. Since Proxmox VE 9.2, new clusters are created with a lower token coefficient of 125 milliseconds explicitly set in ⟦2⟧. This reduces the time needed for reestablishing a new cluster membership after a node failure.

u90aa8b6925d1d2c17636.text: corosync uses the token coefficient to calculate several timeouts in relation to the cluster size ⟦0⟧⟦1⟧[⟦2⟧ in the corosync manual page ⟦3⟧⟦4⟧⟦5⟧]⟦6⟧⟦7⟧, most importantly the token timeout and consensus timeout. corosync implements a token-passing protocol. The token timeout specifies how long a node waits for the token until it declares the token to be lost ⟦8⟧⟦9⟧[⟦10⟧ in the corosync manual page ⟦11⟧⟦12⟧⟦13⟧]⟦14⟧⟦15⟧. The consensus timeout ⟦16⟧⟦17⟧[⟦18⟧ in the corosync manual page ⟦19⟧⟦20⟧⟦21⟧]⟦22⟧⟦23⟧ specifies the time nodes wait for a consensus on a new cluster membership. The sum of token and consensus timeouts defines the minimum time needed to reestablish a new cluster membership after a node goes offline.

u8ff04d771dc3f225df3f.text: Keeping the sum of token and consensus timeouts below 30 seconds reduces the time needed for reestablishing a new cluster membership after a node failure. When HA is enabled, it is especially important that this time stays below 45 seconds to ensure that a new cluster membership is formed before the ⟦0⟧watchdog timeout⟦1⟧ of 60 seconds expires, which would trigger a node fence. A safety margin below this 45 second limit is advisable so that transient timing variations do not push the cluster past the watchdog threshold. The recommended mechanism for lowering the token and consensus timeouts is lowering the token coefficient as explained below.

ubd049ada5c0163dadc27.text: Migrating virtual guests to other nodes is a useful feature in a cluster. There are settings to control the behavior of such migrations. This can be done via the configuration file ⟦0⟧ or for a specific migration via API or command-line parameters.

uf3697623cb72ed41c7bb.text: It makes a difference if a guest is online or offline, or if it has local resources (like a local disk).

u149c7cda089c626f5816.text: For details about virtual machine migration, see the ⟦0⟧QEMU/KVM Migration Chapter⟦1⟧.

u7ae53c2828c8065b38f7.text: For details about container migration, see the ⟦0⟧Container Migration Chapter⟦1⟧.

ucffe83a4261e82d7bd4f.text: The migration type defines if the migration data should be sent over an encrypted (⟦0⟧) channel or an unencrypted (⟦1⟧) one. Setting the migration type to ⟦2⟧ means that the RAM content of a virtual guest is also transferred unencrypted, which can lead to information disclosure of critical data from inside the guest (for example, passwords or encryption keys).

ub9e547e1c6ed82490586.text: Therefore, we strongly recommend using the secure channel if you do not have full control over the network and can not guarantee that no one is eavesdropping on it.

u2b303d4eac63faecd2b9.text: Storage migration does not follow this setting. Currently, it always sends the storage content over a secure channel.

u6c10222fba170ef6b10a.text: Encryption requires a lot of computing power, so this setting is often changed to ⟦0⟧ to achieve better performance. The impact on modern systems is lower because they implement AES encryption in hardware. The performance impact is particularly evident in fast networks, where you can transfer 10 Gbps or more.

ue9afb29ec2428be8d0f0.text: By default, Proxmox VE uses the network in which cluster communication takes place to send the migration traffic. This is not optimal both because sensitive cluster traffic can be disrupted and this network may not have the best bandwidth available on the node.

u0ef9f6c36a691b519fda.text: Setting the migration network parameter allows the use of a dedicated network for all migration traffic. In addition to the memory, this also affects the storage traffic for offline migrations.

uabc70711ea19f993db60.text: The migration network is set as a network using CIDR notation. This has the advantage that you don’t have to set individual IP addresses for each node. Proxmox VE can determine the real address on the destination node from the network specified in the CIDR form. To enable this, the network must be specified so that each node has exactly one IP in the respective network.

u22775f7a79b28af2e98b.text: The Proxmox VE storage model is very flexible. Virtual machine images can either be stored on one or several local storages, or on shared storage like NFS or iSCSI (NAS, SAN). There are no limits, and you may configure as many storage pools as you like. You can use all storage technologies available for Debian Linux.

u9782dae97e4444ab201d.text: One major benefit of storing VMs on shared storage is the ability to live-migrate running machines without any downtime, as all nodes in the cluster have direct access to VM disk images. There is no need to copy VM image data, so live migration is very fast in that case.

u93061777acd6b1b4725c.text: The storage library (package ⟦0⟧) uses a flexible plugin system to provide a common interface to all storage types. This can be easily adopted to include further storage types in the future.

ucdbe18ca052f567df0e1.text: There are basically two different classes of storage types:

u66b3b0591195ec46b7c7.text: File level based storage technologies allow access to a fully featured (POSIX) file system. They are in general more flexible than any Block level storage (see below), and allow you to store content of any type. ZFS is probably the most advanced system, and it has full support for snapshots and clones.

u709435d50a971092e5c7.text: Allows to store large ⟦0⟧raw⟦1⟧ images. It is usually not possible to store other files (ISO, backups, ..) on such storage types. Most modern block level storage implementations support snapshots and clones. Ceph RADOS is a distributed systems, replicating storage data to different nodes that can be accessed as RBD (RADOS Block Device).

u8b4ad8519181b34c41d7.text: ⟦0⟧: Disk images for VMs are stored in ZFS volume (zvol) datasets, which provide block device functionality.

u43273545caa105fa5d80.text: ⟦0⟧: On file based storages, snapshots are possible with the ⟦1⟧qcow2⟦2⟧ format, either using the internal snapshot function, or snapshots as volume chains⟦3⟧. Creating and deleting internal ⟦4⟧qcow2⟦5⟧ snapshots will block a running VM and is not an efficient operation. The performance is particularly bad with network storages like NFS. On some setups and for large disks (multiple hundred GiB or TiB sized), these operations may take several minutes, or in extreme cases, even hours. If your setup is affected, create and remove snapshots while the VM is shut down, expecting a long task duration.

u146056e23cdcd506ced2.text: ⟦0⟧: With iSCSI, FibreChannel (FC), or SAS block storage as shared storage in a cluster, LVM is used to split the LUN into virtual disks. The ⟦1⟧Multipath Guide⟦2⟧ explains how to configure it in a cluster, including multipathing which is usually a requirement in these scenarios.

u974b0fc127e80b422157.text: ⟦0⟧: Since Proxmox VE 9, snapshots as a volume chain have been available for VMs. These snapshots use separate volumes for the snapshot data and layer them. For more details, see the description for ⟦1⟧ in the ⟦2⟧LVM configuration⟦3⟧ section.

uc7bdb636908c45fd344c.text: ⟦0⟧ Fibre Channel (FC) and SAS block storage is handled directly by the host without a dedicated storage plugin.

ue92f0ca3d239915fad7d.text: A number of storages, and the QEMU image format ⟦0⟧, support ⟦1⟧thin provisioning⟦2⟧. With thin provisioning activated, only the blocks that the guest system actually use will be written to the storage.

ufab3159ac949d1db5ab3.text: Say for instance you create a VM with a 32GB hard disk, and after installing the guest system OS, the root file system of the VM contains 3 GB of data. In that case only 3GB are written to the storage, even if the guest VM sees a 32GB hard drive. In this way thin provisioning allows you to create disk images which are larger than the currently available storage blocks. You can create large disk images for your VMs, and when the need arises, add more disks to your storage without resizing the VMs' file systems.

uef4c261b6d09e3fa4a81.text: All storage types which have the “Snapshots” feature also support thin provisioning.

u6f9422987c9c187553a2.text: If a storage runs full, all guests using volumes on that storage receive IO errors. This can cause file system inconsistencies and may corrupt your data. So it is advisable to avoid over-provisioning of your storage resources, or carefully observe free space to avoid such conditions.

u4aada172ae78c985da11.text: All Proxmox VE related storage configuration is stored within a single text file at ⟦0⟧. As this file is within ⟦1⟧, it gets automatically distributed to all cluster nodes. So all nodes share the same storage configuration.

ub504dbaa49efab289da0.text: Sharing storage configuration makes perfect sense for shared storage, because the same “shared” storage is accessible from all nodes. But it is also useful for local storage types. In this case such local storage is available on all nodes, but it is physically different and can have totally different content.

u204a254a0ce0e5237635.text: Proxmox Backup Server only supports backups, they can be block-level or file-level based. Proxmox VE uses block-level for virtual machines and file-level for container.

ud9fff96587d7e3970da6.text: Optionally, you can configure client-side encryption with AES-256 in GCM mode. Encryption can be configured either via the web interface, or on the CLI with the ⟦0⟧ option (see above). The key will be saved in the file ⟦1⟧, which is only accessible by the root user.

u4f9e2362bef60f691220.text: Without their key, backups will be inaccessible. Thus, you should keep keys ordered and in a place that is separate from the contents being backed up. It can happen, for example, that you back up an entire system, using a key on that system. If the system then becomes inaccessible for any reason and needs to be restored, this will not be possible as the encryption key will be lost along with the broken system.

u160c632e172a9ca36a3c.text: It is recommended that you keep your key safe, but easily accessible, in order for quick disaster recovery. For this reason, the best place to store it is in your password manager, where it is immediately recoverable. As a backup to this, you should also save the key to a USB flash drive and store that in a secure place. This way, it is detached from any system, but is still easy to recover from, in case of emergency. Finally, in preparation for the worst case scenario, you should also consider keeping a paper copy of your key locked away in a safe place. The ⟦0⟧ subcommand can be used to create a QR encoded version of your key. The following command sends the output of the ⟦1⟧ command to a text file, for easy printing.

udcc04f0d02ea6f931235.text: Additionally, it is possible to use a single RSA master key pair for key recovery purposes: configure all clients doing encrypted backups to use a single public master key, and all subsequent encrypted backups will contain a RSA-encrypted copy of the used AES encryption key. The corresponding private master key allows recovering the AES key and decrypting the backup even if the client system is no longer available.

u125fb82f8e30ac3b3a5d.text: The same safe-keeping rules apply to the master key pair as to the regular encryption keys. Without a copy of the private key recovery is not possible! The ⟦0⟧ command supports generating paper copies of private master keys for storage in a safe, physical location.

u0f76641aba23c3f2b9fc.text: Because the encryption is managed on the client side, you can use the same datastore on the server for unencrypted backups and encrypted backups, even if they are encrypted with different keys. However, deduplication between backups with different keys is not possible, so it is often better to create separate datastores.

ubde9ab6ba069b0b0686d.text: Do not use encryption if there is no benefit from it, for example, when you are running the server locally in a trusted network. It is always easier to recover from unencrypted backups.

u03fc3062a7ffebd26fb4.text: LVM is a lightweight software layer that sits on top of hard disks and partitions. It can be used to divide available disk space into smaller logical volumes.

ucb32a03c2937ab79641b.text: Another use case is placing LVM on top of a large iSCSI LUN (Logical Unit Number) or a SAN (Storage Area Network) connected via Fibre Channel. This allows you to easily manage the space on the iSCSI LUN, which would otherwise be impossible because the iSCSI specification does not define a management interface for space allocation.

u60f566f037c25209b946.text: The LVM backend supports the common storage properties ⟦0⟧, ⟦1⟧, ⟦2⟧, and the following LVM specific properties:

u10ae0163fd2a761d9d21.text: Called "Wipe Removed Volumes" in the web UI. Zero-out data when removing LVs. When removing a volume, this makes sure that all data gets erased and cannot be accessed by other LVs created later (which happen to be assigned the same physical extents). This is a costly operation, but may be required as a security measure in certain environments.

u8708002014093ea27c46.text: Storage devices that support the "write zeroes" operation will use ⟦0⟧ to zero blocks. Otherwise, a fallback to ⟦1⟧ is performed.

u11bb8bebaa6abed59ff3.text: Wipe step size in MiB (⟦0⟧ parameter value), capped to the maximum step size supported by the underlying storage. Up to 32 MiB (maximum) by default.

u44896ded9fcd64e48dd6.text: Set this flag to enable snapshot support for virtual machines on LVM with a volume backing chain. With this setting, taking a snapshot persists the current state under the snapshot’s name and starts a new volume backed by the snapshot.

ub2e55fd28e65e7a56d7d.text: A volume based on a snapshot references its parent snapshot volume as its backing volume and records only the differences to that backing volume. Snapshot volumes are currently thick-provisioned LVM logical volumes.

u4bf539b7c561706c5288.text: This design avoids issues with native LVM snapshots, such as significant input/output (I/O) penalties and unexpected, dangerous behavior when running out of pre-allocated space.

u783ca5dfbc15dddf7d62.text: Snapshots as volume chains provide vendor-agnostic support for snapshots on any storage system that supports block storage. This includes iSCSI and Fibre Channel-attached SANs.

ue292f69c30ce385c1570.text: Note that, although this feature relies on qcow2, it only uses qcow2’s ability to layer multiple volumes in a backing chain, not qcow2’s snapshot functionality. The snapshot functionality is managed by the PVE storage system.

u074c1d878ae59e62ecf1.text: Enabling or disabling this flag only affects newly created virtual disk volumes.

uc26d736b7a4422db4ca3.text: For efficient support of ⟦0⟧, the backing storage must support thin-provisioning and discard. Each snapshot will appear to use the full volume size on the PVE side, but the actual space usage on the underlying storage will be smaller if those requirements are met.

u77193c0d85d318cfa1b0.text: Snapshots as volume chains are currently a ⟦0⟧technology preview⟦1⟧ in Proxmox VE.

u50f43f827c72f82d0f1b.text: The backend use basically the same naming conventions as the ZFS pool backend.

ucac08ff4964d75b9adfe.text: LVM is a typical block storage system. Unfortunately, regular LVM snapshots are inefficient because they interfere with all write operations within the entire volume group while the snapshot is active, which causes significant I/O degradation. This is why LVM does not support linked clones, and why Proxmox VE added support for snapshots as volume chains. This feature manages the snapshot volume through the storage plugin and uses qcow2 to layer separate volumes as a backing chain. This creates a single disk state that is exposed to the guest.

u7fe20a74c340cb13cce9.text: A benefit of LVM is that it can be used with shared storage. For example, an iSCSI LUN. The backend implements proper cluster-wide locking if the storage is marked as shared in the configuration.

u1a7843150f4a7e563d50.text: You can use the LVM-thin backend for non-shared local storage. It supports snapshots and linked clones.
