u492ad8e26cc41fb7470e.text: Proxmox VE unifies your compute and storage systems, that is, you can use the same physical nodes within a cluster for both computing (processing VMs and containers) and replicated storage. The traditional silos of compute and storage resources can be wrapped up into a single hyper-converged appliance. Separate storage networks (SANs) and connections via network attached storage (NAS) disappear. With the integration of Ceph, an open source software-defined storage platform, Proxmox VE has the ability to run and manage Ceph storage directly on the hypervisor nodes.

u3bd6e44a2aac4e410afb.text: Ceph is a distributed object store and file system designed to provide excellent performance, reliability and scalability.

u17c0cf3b9bfb9f1dd608.text: Some advantages of Ceph on Proxmox VE are:

u444f09804c450377b05a.text: Easy setup and management via CLI and GUI

u281f9b8788d23b52c715.text: Provides block, file system, and object storage

uf8ea1eb3ef09c1583d15.text: Setup pools with different performance and redundancy characteristics

u9027febf4ba8d8133206.text: Data is replicated, making it fault tolerant

ua05a8adc09201e86dff6.text: No need for hardware RAID controllers

u3b6ab2c07d9235b632be.text: For small to medium-sized deployments, it is possible to install a Ceph server for using RADOS Block Devices (RBD) or CephFS directly on your Proxmox VE cluster nodes (see ⟦0⟧Ceph RADOS Block Devices (RBD)⟦1⟧). Recent hardware has a lot of CPU power and RAM, so running storage services and virtual guests on the same node is possible.

u559baea239faf21d90f7.text: To simplify management, Proxmox VE provides you native integration to install and manage ⟦0⟧Ceph⟦1⟧ services on Proxmox VE nodes either via the built-in web interface, or using the ⟦2⟧pveceph⟦3⟧ command line tool.

u51cab46fa37913386406.text: ⟦0⟧8.3. Recommendations for a Healthy Ceph Cluster⟦1⟧

u99320417bde6207a9bf8.text: To build a hyper-converged Proxmox + Ceph Cluster, you must use at least three (preferably) identical servers for the setup.

uac7f5ec01dbb2ac45d62.text: Check also the recommendations from ⟦0⟧Ceph’s website⟦1⟧.

uee1c9a848d9224c3c0e2.text: The recommendations below should be seen as a rough guidance for choosing hardware. Therefore, it is still essential to adapt it to your specific needs. You should test your setup and monitor health and performance continuously.

ub1db1c09712f010d664c.text: Ceph services can be classified into two categories:

u7bfc9518d5b193298292.text: Intensive CPU usage, benefiting from high CPU base frequencies and multiple cores. Members of that category are:

uc560ff63a2c27456ade8.text: Meta Data Service (MDS) used for CephFS

u131d9dcdabe093ec3cb4.text: Moderate CPU usage, not needing multiple CPU cores. These are:

u85a0a39102cda9cc9834.text: As a simple rule of thumb, you should assign at least one CPU core (or thread) to each Ceph service to provide the minimum resources required for stable and durable Ceph performance.

u0b1df21463bca2f98b30.text: For example, if you plan to run a Ceph monitor, a Ceph manager and 6 Ceph OSDs services on a node you should reserve 8 CPU cores purely for Ceph when targeting basic and stable performance.

u11dbb3b23794c8e97777.text: Note that an OSD’s CPU usage depends mostly on the disk’s performance. The higher the possible IOPS (⟦0⟧IO⟦1⟧ ⟦2⟧O⟦3⟧perations per ⟦4⟧S⟦5⟧econd) of a disk, the more CPU can be utilized by an OSD service. For modern enterprise SSD disks, like NVMes that can permanently sustain a high IOPS load over 100’000 with sub millisecond latency, each OSD can use multiple CPU threads, e.g., four to six CPU threads utilized per NVMe backed OSD is likely for very high performance disks.

u39f6c9d9ba87bfa54b18.text: Especially in a hyper-converged setup, the memory consumption needs to be carefully planned out and monitored. In addition to the predicted memory usage of virtual machines and containers, you must also account for having enough memory available for Ceph to provide excellent and stable performance.

u761c8048d1ca868725ca.text: While usage may be less under normal conditions, it will consume more memory during critical operations, such as recovery, rebalancing, or backfilling. That means you should avoid maxing out your available memory already on regular operation, but rather leave some headroom to cope with outages.

ubebe767f73b6bbe82d0c.text: The current recommendation is to ⟦0⟧configure⟦1⟧ OSDs with at least ⟦2⟧8 GiB of memory⟦3⟧ for good performance. The OSD daemon requires 4 GiB by default.

u9d192de8a4393ae12d71.text: Total memory consumption is primarily determined by the number of OSD daemons. However, for critical operations, all Ceph services may require additional memory.

uc50e8aaf1d476aa216f0.text: We recommend a network bandwidth of at least 10 Gbps, or more, to be used exclusively for Ceph traffic. A meshed network setup ⟦0⟧⟦1⟧[Full Mesh Network for Ceph ⟦2⟧⟦3⟧⟦4⟧]⟦5⟧⟦6⟧ is also an option for three to five node clusters, if there are no 10+ Gbps switches available.

u512b8b758b23b84e9c50.text: The volume of traffic, especially during recovery, will interfere with other services on the same network, especially the latency sensitive Proxmox VE corosync cluster stack can be affected, resulting in possible loss of cluster quorum. Moving the Ceph traffic to dedicated and physical separated networks will avoid such interference, not only for corosync, but also for the networking services provided by any virtual guests.

u56f3d7e19cdbc6c7f6d2.text: For estimating your bandwidth needs, you need to take the performance of your disks into account.. While a single HDD might not saturate a 1 Gb link, multiple HDD OSDs per node can already saturate 10 Gbps too. If modern NVMe-attached SSDs are used, a single one can already saturate 10 Gbps of bandwidth, or more. For such high-performance setups we recommend at least a 25 Gpbs, while even 40 Gbps or 100+ Gbps might be required to utilize the full performance potential of the underlying disks.

u553254fadd77e010ba7f.text: If unsure, we recommend using three (physical) separate networks for high-performance setups:

u66e4520d3e29579a6caf.text: one very high bandwidth (25+ Gbps) network for Ceph (internal) cluster traffic.

u15ef7f7fa4e53cd3e2cf.text: one high bandwidth (10+ Gpbs) network for Ceph (public) traffic between the ceph server and ceph client storage traffic. Depending on your needs this can also be used to host the virtual guest traffic and the VM live-migration traffic.

u9e6902208a606cc59d45.text: one medium bandwidth (1 Gbps) exclusive for the latency sensitive corosync cluster communication.

udb4f32bf158858449b5e.text: If a firewall is enabled you will have to open the ports used by Ceph, the easiest way to do this is to use a firewall ⟦0⟧.

u066a2eff755bab0ee71b.text: When planning the size of your Ceph cluster, it is important to take the recovery time into consideration. Especially with small clusters, recovery might take long. It is recommended that you use SSDs instead of HDDs in small setups to reduce recovery time, minimizing the likelihood of a subsequent failure event during recovery.

u6d1963d5ce8f2b256350.text: In general, SSDs will provide more IOPS than spinning disks. With this in mind, in addition to the higher cost, it may make sense to implement a ⟦0⟧class based⟦1⟧ separation of pools. Another way to speed up OSDs is to use a faster disk as a journal or DB/⟦2⟧W⟦3⟧rite-⟦4⟧A⟦5⟧head-⟦6⟧L⟦7⟧og device, see ⟦8⟧creating Ceph OSDs⟦9⟧. If a faster disk is used for multiple OSDs, a proper balance between OSD and WAL / DB (or journal) disk must be selected, otherwise the faster disk becomes the bottleneck for all linked OSDs.

ufed06ecb5ef272594f3b.text: Aside from the disk type, Ceph performs best with an evenly sized, and an evenly distributed amount of disks per node. For example, 4 x 500 GB disks within each node is better than a mixed setup with a single 1 TB and three 250 GB disk.

u6ceb5cebe11cdce01819.text: You also need to balance OSD count and single OSD capacity. More capacity allows you to increase storage density, but it also means that a single OSD failure forces Ceph to recover more data at once.

u505306e9bf4615835616.text: As Ceph handles data object redundancy and multiple parallel writes to disks (OSDs) on its own, using a RAID controller normally doesn’t improve performance or availability. On the contrary, Ceph is designed to handle whole disks on its own, without any abstraction in between. RAID controllers are not designed for the Ceph workload and may complicate things and sometimes even reduce performance, as their write and caching algorithms may interfere with the ones from Ceph.

ub63038e3173aef03129b.text: Avoid RAID controllers. Use host bus adapter (HBA) instead.

u3bc53c62e302c2d30b09.text: With Proxmox VE you have the benefit of an easy to use installation wizard for Ceph. Click on one of your cluster nodes and navigate to the Ceph section in the menu tree. If Ceph is not already installed, you will see a prompt offering to do so.

ue530f12eaaa831469697.text: The wizard is divided into multiple sections, where each needs to finish successfully, in order to use Ceph.

u66130637ccdd293895a9.text: First you need to choose which Ceph version you want to install. Prefer the one from your other nodes, or the newest if this is the first node you install Ceph.

u97230a9045df8664fb9a.text: After starting the installation, the wizard will download and install all the required packages from Proxmox VE’s Ceph repository.

u14bbc13ca4c747955c3f.text: After finishing the installation step, you will need to create a configuration. This step is only needed once per cluster, as this configuration is distributed automatically to all remaining cluster members through Proxmox VE’s clustered ⟦0⟧configuration file system (pmxcfs)⟦1⟧.

u0d0bc2c67cad1b752cf2.text: The configuration step includes the following settings:

u5f7ae13a6e30fbdc5741.text: ⟦0⟧Public Network:⟦1⟧ This network will be used for public storage communication (e.g., for virtual machines using a Ceph RBD backed disk, or a CephFS mount), and communication between the different Ceph services. This setting is required. ⟦2⟧ Separating your Ceph traffic from the Proxmox VE cluster communication (corosync), and possibly the front-facing (public) networks of your virtual guests, is highly recommended. Otherwise, Ceph’s high-bandwidth IO-traffic could cause interference with other low-latency dependent services.

u4f5c953fa583d29a584e.text: ⟦0⟧Cluster Network:⟦1⟧ Specify to separate the ⟦2⟧OSD⟦3⟧ replication and heartbeat traffic as well. This setting is optional. ⟦4⟧ Using a physically separated network is recommended, as it will relieve the Ceph public and the virtual guests network, while also providing a significant Ceph performance improvements. ⟦5⟧ The Ceph cluster network can be configured and moved to another physically separated network at a later time.

u42ef66fc9a0d36aeed72.text: You have two more options which are considered advanced and therefore should only be changed if you know what you are doing.

u729cd2c60378c119e1ab.text: ⟦0⟧Number of replicas⟦1⟧: Defines how often an object is replicated.

uabf567bd501d57f61d92.text: ⟦0⟧Minimum replicas⟦1⟧: Defines the minimum number of required replicas for I/O to be marked as complete.

ub4eed94cd0ebd69ac82f.text: Additionally, you need to choose your first monitor node. This step is required.

u15ea5c15cddc14c6592f.text: That’s it. You should now see a success page as the last step, with further instructions on how to proceed. Your system is now ready to start using Ceph. To get started, you will need to create some additional ⟦0⟧monitors⟦1⟧, ⟦2⟧OSDs⟦3⟧ and at least one ⟦4⟧pool⟦5⟧.

uf76c5bb2ae875a11905b.text: A pool is a logical group for storing objects. It holds a collection of objects, known as ⟦0⟧P⟦1⟧lacement ⟦2⟧G⟦3⟧roups (⟦4⟧, ⟦5⟧).

u3e065d8b4edb4dbcc552.text: Erasure coding (EC) is a form of ‘forward error correction’ codes that allows to recover from a certain amount of data loss. Erasure coded pools can offer more usable space compared to replicated pools, but they do that for the price of performance.

u1af57081dc41d8a15108.text: For comparison: in classic, replicated pools, multiple replicas of the data are stored (⟦0⟧) while in erasure coded pool, data is split into ⟦1⟧ data chunks with additional ⟦2⟧ coding (checking) chunks. Those coding chunks can be used to recreate data should data chunks be missing.

ua64baeb6ae6981f55886.text: The number of coding chunks, ⟦0⟧, defines how many OSDs can be lost without losing any data. The total amount of objects stored is ⟦1⟧.

u54bd976d5fa262f4c6ee.text: Erasure coded (EC) pools can be created with the ⟦0⟧ CLI tooling. Planning an EC pool needs to account for the fact, that they work differently than replicated pools.

u4f0eda370eff18fdabc0.text: The default ⟦0⟧ of an EC pool depends on the ⟦1⟧ parameter. If ⟦2⟧, the ⟦3⟧ of the EC pool will be ⟦4⟧. The ⟦5⟧ will be ⟦6⟧ if ⟦7⟧. The Ceph documentation recommends a conservative ⟦8⟧ of ⟦9⟧ ⟦10⟧⟦11⟧[Ceph Erasure Coded Pool Recovery ⟦12⟧⟦13⟧⟦14⟧]⟦15⟧⟦16⟧.

u1dd58f1344306e946409.text: If there are less than ⟦0⟧ OSDs available, any IO to the pool will be blocked until there are enough OSDs available again.

uaea99d1d0072a2e61c2e.text: When planning an erasure coded pool, keep an eye on the ⟦0⟧ as it defines how many OSDs need to be available. Otherwise, IO will be blocked.

ue44e5db861a39267de45.text: For example, an EC pool with ⟦0⟧ and ⟦1⟧ will have ⟦2⟧, ⟦3⟧ and will stay operational if one OSD fails. If the pool is configured with ⟦4⟧, ⟦5⟧, it will have a ⟦6⟧ and ⟦7⟧ and stay operational if one OSD is lost.

u0f9706b015952b806c27.text: Ceph Tentacle introduces a new erasure coding I/O path called FastEC, enabled per pool via the ⟦0⟧ flag. FastEC adds partial reads and partial writes on EC pools, substantially improving small random I/O performance — the dominant access pattern of virtual machine disk I/O. Upstream recommends it for RBD and CephFS backed storage ⟦1⟧⟦2⟧[Ceph Erasure Code ⟦3⟧⟦4⟧⟦5⟧]⟦6⟧⟦7⟧.

u7daef8eb7fd88ade80f8.text: FastEC has four requirements that the Ceph monitor enforces:

u790cae3e8f84653222fb.text: the pool must be erasure coded;

uef8c40e3d3e0e7aa6ded.text: If any precondition is not met, ⟦0⟧ fails with a descriptive error — no silent degradation.

ub07319fefcc5c077bea7.text: ⟦0⟧ does not set the plugin or technique explicitly when creating an EC profile — both are seeded from the monitor’s ⟦1⟧ option (⟦2⟧ by default on both Squid and Tentacle). The technique requirement is therefore satisfied out of the box unless the operator has overridden this setting. Verify with:

u00ee229111ebad61ef57.text: When the flag is set on a populated pool, be aware of the following:

u4ab4b239921af0af79ce.text: ⟦0⟧Primary re-election.⟦1⟧ FastEC marks data shards 1 through k-1 as non-primary, so PGs whose primary was on one of those shards will re-peer. This is a normal peering event and causes a brief I/O pause per affected PG.

ucabb9e83ccc157af0084.text: The PG autoscaler allows the cluster to consider the amount of (expected) data stored in each pool and to choose the appropriate ⟦0⟧ values automatically. It is available since Ceph Nautilus.

u53a186527ca463b0b783.text: You may need to activate the PG autoscaler module before adjustments can take effect.

uead186d73265792aec45.text: The autoscaler is configured on a per pool basis and has the following modes:

u017c6110557e499ca5c7.text: A health warning is issued if the suggested ⟦0⟧ value differs too much from the current value.

uae81b6938b99238ca3f3.text: The ⟦0⟧ is adjusted automatically with no need for any manual interaction.

ua98f9d3ad4fc300b9705.text: No automatic ⟦0⟧ adjustments are made, and no warning will be issued if the PG count is not optimal.

uf2bdc6db89741a942fae.text: The scaling factor can be adjusted to facilitate future data storage with the ⟦0⟧, ⟦1⟧ and the ⟦2⟧ options.

u1a100eb9fe78971afee3.text: By default, the autoscaler considers tuning the PG count of a pool if it is off by a factor of 3. This will lead to a considerable shift in data placement and might introduce a high load on the cluster.

u3ba27e72f852e9313875.text: You can find a more in-depth introduction to the PG autoscaler on Ceph’s Blog - ⟦0⟧New in Nautilus: PG merging and autotuning⟦1⟧.

uc7765a60a5b313e3dd0e.text: The ⟦0⟧⟦1⟧[⟦2⟧⟦3⟧⟦4⟧]⟦5⟧⟦6⟧ (⟦7⟧C⟦8⟧ontrolled ⟦9⟧R⟦10⟧eplication ⟦11⟧U⟦12⟧nder ⟦13⟧S⟦14⟧calable ⟦15⟧H⟦16⟧ashing) algorithm is at the foundation of Ceph.

u4f37118b017ebc1de237.text: CRUSH calculates where to store and retrieve data from. This has the advantage that no central indexing service is needed. CRUSH works using a map of OSDs, buckets (device locations) and rulesets (data replication) for pools.

u5e51a4e2d46a84e36384.text: Further information can be found in the Ceph documentation, under the section CRUSH map ⟦0⟧⟦1⟧[CRUSH map ⟦2⟧⟦3⟧⟦4⟧]⟦5⟧⟦6⟧.

u07376a0ab7a93730cc36.text: This map can be altered to reflect different replication hierarchies. The object replicas can be separated (e.g., failure domains), while maintaining the desired distribution.

u84137c1e02b7e86018d3.text: A common configuration is to use different classes of disks for different Ceph pools. For this reason, Ceph introduced device classes with luminous, to accommodate the need for easy ruleset generation.

uef6dd0df89f995c1d511.text: The device classes can be seen in the ⟦0⟧ceph osd tree⟦1⟧ output. These classes represent their own root bucket, which can be seen with the below command.

ub231c801326045b9e8d8.text: name of the rule, to connect with a pool (seen in GUI & CLI)

uf9ee36e7283f4c7854ee.text: which crush root it should belong to (default Ceph root "default")

u026cbbd112939a433f25.text: Once the rule is in the CRUSH map, you can tell a pool to use the ruleset.

u92c526e59c99dd8e3b52.text: If the pool already contains objects, these must be moved accordingly. Depending on your setup, this may introduce a big performance impact on your cluster. As an alternative, you can create a new pool and move disks separately.

u7a21409d921464349a5f.text: When using the PG autoscaler, all pools in the cluster are required to use CRUSH rules of the same kind, either all specifying a device class, or none. Otherwise the autoscaler will skip the affected pools and their ⟦0⟧ will not be adjusted.

u51e405f6a5b0fd6545c6.text: Cephx ⟦0⟧⟦1⟧[Cephx authorization and authentication protocol ⟦2⟧⟦3⟧⟦4⟧]⟦5⟧⟦6⟧ protects access to a Ceph cluster.

ua6c2b4b80f1178077a04.text: Every Ceph service and client, including storage consumers and tools, authenticates to a monitor as a Ceph user, such as ⟦0⟧ or ⟦1⟧, with that user’s long-term secret key. The monitor then issues temporary credentials called tickets:

u21a782f0d05e978a128f.text: Long-term secret used by a client or Ceph service to authenticate to a monitor.

u5b5d1a1454b50cb24b5c.text: Lets an authenticated Ceph user request tickets for Ceph services.

ub7dd4da4e8f09b024c85.text: Grants temporary access to an OSD, manager, or metadata server.

u812eceacb1e6454590be.text: Lets Ceph services validate service tickets. Monitors replace these keys automatically.

ucda1f8f3db4d8430fd51.text: A running client usually reads its user key only when it starts. Updating a saved key or keyring file does not update that process. Existing tickets and connections can also remain usable for some time. A key rotation must therefore account for running and temporarily disconnected clients.

u02b2c0bce03080545b32.text: The authoritative ⟦0⟧ keyring in a Proxmox VE Ceph cluster is ⟦1⟧, not the copy in ⟦2⟧. The ⟦3⟧Proxmox cluster file system (pmxcfs)⟦4⟧ synchronizes it to every node. Credentials for managed Ceph storages are below ⟦5⟧.

u09aa06fe34968007c7e6.text: Keyrings below ⟦0⟧ belong to one Ceph service and are local to its node. ⟦1⟧ contains both the shared ⟦2⟧ key and ⟦3⟧. Always merge updates into this file instead of overwriting it. ⟦4⟧ uses its ⟦5⟧ entry when it initializes a monitor.

u58b18d79e5f7ad75c760.text: Each encrypted OSD uses a dedicated Ceph user named ⟦0⟧. Its authentication key is called the lockbox key. It is not the disk-encryption key itself: it lets the OSD retrieve that key from Ceph and unlock its storage when it starts. Ceph and the OSD’s block device must contain matching copies of the lockbox key.

u00b14bfe610712cf6ce7.text: Never rotate a lockbox key with ⟦0⟧ alone. Use the migration helper, which verifies the OSD identity and updates both copies together.

u176b9cd8c9bc248753cd.text: Add an ⟦0⟧RBD storage⟦1⟧ in the web interface to use a Ceph pool for virtual machine and container disks. For an external cluster, follow the ⟦2⟧authentication instructions⟦3⟧ to configure a dedicated Ceph user and its keyring.

u6e5c2ee49fe4b7757e44.text: Ceph also provides a filesystem, which runs on top of the same object storage as RADOS block devices do. A ⟦0⟧M⟦1⟧eta⟦2⟧d⟦3⟧ata ⟦4⟧S⟦5⟧erver (⟦6⟧) is used to map the RADOS backed objects to files and directories, allowing Ceph to provide a POSIX-compliant, replicated filesystem. This allows you to easily configure a clustered, highly available, shared filesystem. Ceph’s Metadata Servers guarantee that files are evenly distributed over the entire Ceph cluster. As a result, even cases of high load will not overwhelm a single host, which can be an issue with traditional shared filesystem approaches, for example ⟦7⟧.

If an MDS or its node becomes unresponsive (or crashes), another ⟦0⟧ MDS will get promoted to ⟦1⟧. You can speed up the handover between the active and standby MDS by using the ⟦2⟧hotstandby⟦3⟧ parameter option on creation, or if you have already created it you may set/add:

Changing it to a different network is not as simple as changing the Ceph Cluster network. uc1aaf4a7c8aabecb1145.text: The ⟦0⟧ command-line tool manages the Proxmox VE storage replication framework. Storage replication brings redundancy for guests using local storage and reduces migration time.

u57fb2a7b97632807fe67.text: It replicates guest volumes to another node so that all data is available without using shared storage. Replication uses snapshots to minimize traffic sent over the network. Therefore, new data is sent only incrementally after the initial full sync. In the case of a node failure, your guest data is still available on the replicated node.

ue3426bf4b3def1e7566e.text: The replication is done automatically in configurable intervals. The minimum replication interval is one minute, and the maximal interval once a week. The format used to specify those intervals is a subset of ⟦0⟧ calendar events, see ⟦1⟧Schedule Format⟦2⟧ section:

u5e3f4d8eb482f00f13c1.text: It is possible to replicate a guest to multiple target nodes, but not twice to the same target node.

u388cf5a635b8331f3c25.text: Each replications bandwidth can be limited, to avoid overloading a storage or server.

ua13b2f27f4e3efe1d22a.text: Only changes since the last replication (so-called ⟦0⟧) need to be transferred if the guest is migrated to a node to which it already is replicated. This reduces the time needed significantly. The replication direction automatically switches if you migrate a guest to the replication target node.

u2b4ec4ba92d4fe041033.text: For example: VM100 is currently on ⟦0⟧ and gets replicated to ⟦1⟧. You migrate it to ⟦2⟧, so now it gets automatically replicated back from ⟦3⟧ to ⟦4⟧.

uddf8a85a16aedeb15f1f.text: If you migrate to a node where the guest is not replicated, the whole disk data must send over. After the migration, the replication job continues to replicate this guest to the configured nodes.

u976d51d6f00bcfb7453f.text: High-Availability is allowed in combination with storage replication, but there may be some data loss between the last synced time and the time a node failed.

u49a7a4f1ad477c21e185.text: Replication uses ⟦0⟧calendar events⟦1⟧ for configuring the schedule.

uf53b027d5c0218dd0891.text: If a replication job encounters problems, it is placed in an error state. In this state, the configured replication intervals get suspended temporarily. The failed replication is repeatedly tried again in a 30 minute interval. Once this succeeds, the original schedule gets activated again.

ub5efc3c700512b7fa88b.text: Some of the most common issues are in the following list. Depending on your setup there may be another cause.

u63f48642ba9c6397639c.text: No free space left on the replication target storage.

u537ead84692afe8723e9.text: Storage with the same storage ID is not available on the target node.

u3782ee5b56f55b7f350d.text: You can always use the replication log to find out what is causing the problem.

udb48d8ff9ad31123d1dc.text: QEMU (short form for Quick Emulator) is an open source hypervisor that emulates a physical computer. From the perspective of the host system where QEMU is running, QEMU is a user program which has access to a number of local resources like partitions, files, network cards which are then passed to an emulated computer which sees them as if they were real devices.

u1962997d3313e687c29f.text: A guest operating system running in the emulated computer accesses these devices, and runs as if it were running on real hardware. For instance, you can pass an ISO image as a parameter to QEMU, and the OS running in the emulated computer will see a real CD-ROM inserted into a CD drive.

ua0261e456bea032a5569.text: QEMU can emulate a great variety of hardware, from ARM to Sparc. On x86 hosts, Proxmox VE is concerned with 32-bit and 64-bit PC clone emulation, since it represents the overwhelming majority of server hardware. On arm64 hosts, Proxmox VE emulates 64-bit ARM (aarch64) machines instead. Emulating the same architecture as the host is also one of the fastest options, due to the availability of processor extensions which greatly speed up QEMU when the emulated architecture matches the host architecture.

uf464e6a32d7229da4131.text: You may sometimes encounter the term ⟦0⟧KVM⟦1⟧ (Kernel-based Virtual Machine). It means that QEMU is running with the support of the virtualization processor extensions, via the Linux KVM module. In the context of Proxmox VE ⟦2⟧QEMU⟦3⟧ and ⟦4⟧KVM⟦5⟧ can be used interchangeably, as QEMU in Proxmox VE will always try to load the KVM module.

uf526169b7bc956d68341.text: QEMU inside Proxmox VE runs as a root process, since this is required to access block and PCI devices.

ue29d270e7684362b13a5.text: The PC hardware emulated by QEMU includes a motherboard, network controllers, SCSI, IDE and SATA controllers, serial ports (the complete list can be seen in the ⟦0⟧ man page) all of them emulated in software. All these devices are the exact software equivalent of existing hardware devices, and if the OS running in the guest has the proper drivers it will use the devices as if it were running on real hardware. This allows QEMU to run ⟦1⟧unmodified⟦2⟧ operating systems.

u6e4e5f73cb55673e751a.text: This however has a performance cost, as running in software what was meant to run in hardware involves a lot of extra work for the host CPU. To mitigate this, QEMU can present to the guest operating system ⟦0⟧paravirtualized devices⟦1⟧, where the guest OS recognizes it is running inside QEMU and cooperates with the hypervisor.

ua028d7936ed5110f875f.text: QEMU relies on the virtio virtualization standard, and is thus able to present paravirtualized virtio devices, which includes a paravirtualized generic disk controller, a paravirtualized network card, a paravirtualized serial port, a paravirtualized SCSI controller, etc …

u8407a22cbeb098e4cf9b.text: It is ⟦0⟧highly recommended⟦1⟧ to use the virtio devices whenever you can, as they provide a big performance improvement and are generally better maintained. Using the virtio generic disk controller versus an emulated IDE controller will double the sequential write throughput, as measured with ⟦2⟧. Using the virtio network interface can deliver up to three times the throughput of an emulated Intel E1000 network card, as measured with ⟦3⟧. ⟦4⟧⟦5⟧[See this benchmark on the KVM wiki ⟦6⟧⟦7⟧⟦8⟧]⟦9⟧⟦10⟧

u45e7f256a52c75c8e309.text: Generally speaking Proxmox VE tries to choose sane defaults for virtual machines (VM). Make sure you understand the meaning of the settings you change, as it could incur a performance slowdown, or putting your data at risk.

u2eadea7fba2c4d8d7c69.text: General settings of a VM include

uf4905e6f7bf8f3681ba3.text: the ⟦0⟧Node⟦1⟧ : the physical server on which the VM will run

ua784101c03e39d2c73be.text: the ⟦0⟧VM ID⟦1⟧: a unique number in this Proxmox VE installation used to identify your VM

u1d7dbf172f5d766036ea.text: ⟦0⟧Name⟦1⟧: a free form text string you can use to describe the VM

udef1fe660ad88ecc8142.text: ⟦0⟧Resource Pool⟦1⟧: a logical group of VMs

ufff6051bfb87b39dd920.text: When creating a virtual machine (VM), setting the proper Operating System(OS) allows Proxmox VE to optimize some low level parameters. For instance Windows OS expect the BIOS clock to use the local time, while Unix based OS expect the BIOS clock to have the UTC time.

u4eda4b8def97ee87b3ef.text: On VM creation you can change some basic system components of the new VM. You can specify which ⟦0⟧display type⟦1⟧ you want to use.

u06adcb76778d0d1868e0.text: Additionally, the ⟦0⟧SCSI controller⟦1⟧ can be changed. If you plan to install the QEMU Guest Agent, or if your selected ISO image already ships and installs it automatically, you may want to tick the ⟦2⟧QEMU Agent⟦3⟧ box, which lets Proxmox VE know that it can use its features to show some more information, and complete some actions (for example, shutdown or snapshots) more intelligently.

u2e31bafe52537cf4f6a7.text: Proxmox VE allows to boot VMs with different firmware and machine types, namely ⟦0⟧SeaBIOS and OVMF⟦1⟧. In most cases you want to switch from the default SeaBIOS to OVMF only if you plan to use ⟦2⟧PCIe passthrough⟦3⟧. On arm64 hosts OVMF is the default and only option, as SeaBIOS is x86-only.

u0d81d82303dcb5d419de.text: A VM’s ⟦0⟧Machine Type⟦1⟧ defines the hardware layout of the VM’s virtual motherboard. You can choose between the default ⟦2⟧Intel 440FX⟦3⟧ or the ⟦4⟧Q35⟦5⟧ chipset, which also provides a virtual PCIe bus, and thus may be desired if you want to pass through PCIe hardware. Additionally, you can select a ⟦6⟧vIOMMU⟦7⟧ implementation.

u26b074a836a042de2b8a.text: The Intel 440FX and Q35 chipsets are specific to x86 guests. On arm64 hosts, virtual machines use the ⟦0⟧ machine type, which models a generic, UEFI-based ARM machine.

u7d714636f02bb96ec5b7.text: Each machine type is versioned in QEMU and a given QEMU binary supports many machine versions. New versions might bring support for new features, fixes or general improvements. However, they also change properties of the virtual hardware. To avoid sudden changes from the guest’s perspective and ensure compatibility of the VM state, live-migration and snapshots with RAM will keep using the same machine version in the new QEMU instance.

u5e330d9cde85dc29d5b6.text: For Windows guests, the machine version is pinned during creation, because Windows is sensitive to changes in the virtual hardware - even between cold boots. For example, the enumeration of network devices might be different with different machine versions. Other OSes like Linux can usually deal with such changes just fine. For those, the ⟦0⟧Latest⟦1⟧ machine version is used by default. This means that after a fresh start, the newest machine version supported by the QEMU binary is used (e.g. the newest machine version QEMU 8.1 supports is version 8.1 for each machine type).

ueb8c33230bba29b088e0.text: The machine version is also used as a safeguard when implementing new features or fixes that would change the hardware layout to ensure backward compatibility. For operations on a running VM, such as live migrations, the running machine version is saved to ensure that the VM can be recovered exactly as it was, not only from a QEMU virtualization perspective, but also in terms of how Proxmox VE will create the QEMU virtual machine instance.

u707b16077b7b6a2cdb60.text: Sometimes Proxmox VE needs to make changes to the hardware layout or modify options without waiting for a new QEMU release. For this, Proxmox VE has added an extra downstream revision in the form of ⟦0⟧. In these revisions, ⟦1⟧ is 0 for each new QEMU machine version and is omitted in this case, e.g. machine version ⟦2⟧ would be the same as machine version ⟦3⟧.

u1cfc3df4884cfeb79a0f.text: If Proxmox VE wants to change the hardware layout or a default option, the revision is incremented and used for newly created guests or on reboot for VMs that always use the latest machine version.

uee8137ddb9a2bde93f53.text: Starting with QEMU 10.1, machine versions are removed from upstream QEMU after 6 years. In Proxmox VE, major releases happen approximately every 2 years, so a major Proxmox VE release will support machine versions from approximately two previous major Proxmox VE releases.

u118992f122ed32dedd45.text: Before upgrading to a new major Proxmox VE release, you should update VM configurations to avoid all machine versions that will be dropped during the next major Proxmox VE release. This ensures that the guests can still be used throughout that release. See the section ⟦0⟧Update to a Newer Machine Version⟦1⟧.

u92f33c5d9063f8e3d417.text: The removal policy is not yet in effect for Proxmox VE 8, so the baseline for supported machine versions is 2.4. The last QEMU binary version released for Proxmox VE 9 is expected to be QEMU 11.2. This QEMU binary will remove support for machine versions older than 6.0, so 6.0 is the baseline for the Proxmox VE 9 release life cycle. The baseline is expected to increase by 2 major versions for each major Proxmox VE release, for example 8.0 for Proxmox VE 10.

u1fcefe356e62b9b8cfc7.text: Update to a Newer Machine Version

uc4c0b9f23923aee4c80a.text: If you see a deprecation warning, you should change the machine version to a newer one. Be sure to have a working backup first and be prepared for changes to how the guest sees hardware. In some scenarios, re-installing certain drivers might be required. You should also check for snapshots with RAM that were taken with these machine versions (i.e. the ⟦0⟧ configuration entry). Unfortunately, there is no way to change the machine version of a snapshot, so you’d need to load the snapshot to salvage any data from it.

u8d033574af2577a91cac.text: QEMU can emulate a number of storage controllers:

u471e20e9953f7a647225.text: It is highly recommended to use the ⟦0⟧VirtIO SCSI⟦1⟧ or ⟦2⟧VirtIO Block⟦3⟧ controller for performance reasons and because they are better maintained.

u3b0fd4b19195ef949732.text: the ⟦0⟧IDE⟦1⟧ controller, has a design which goes back to the 1984 PC/AT disk controller. Even if this controller has been superseded by recent designs, each and every OS you can think of has support for it, making it a great choice if you want to run an OS released before 2003. You can connect up to 4 devices on this controller.

u94460b55add8ab7e8ecf.text: the ⟦0⟧SATA⟦1⟧ (Serial ATA) controller, dating from 2003, has a more modern design, allowing higher throughput and a greater number of devices to be connected. You can connect up to 6 devices on this controller.

u5edae72535b5e602bc77.text: the ⟦0⟧SCSI⟦1⟧ controller, designed in 1985, is commonly found on server grade hardware, and can connect up to 14 storage devices. Proxmox VE emulates by default a LSI 53C895A controller.

u0f12022ad4b7bb840bec.text: A SCSI controller of type ⟦0⟧VirtIO SCSI single⟦1⟧ and enabling the ⟦2⟧IO Thread⟦3⟧ setting for the attached disks is recommended if you aim for performance. This is the default for newly created Linux VMs since Proxmox VE 7.3. Each disk will have its own ⟦4⟧VirtIO SCSI⟦5⟧ controller, and QEMU will handle the disks IO in a dedicated thread. Linux distributions have support for this controller since 2012, and FreeBSD since 2014. For Windows OSes, you need to provide an extra ISO containing the drivers during the installation.

uf9db90db51b8148f5738.text: The ⟦0⟧VirtIO Block⟦1⟧ controller, often just called VirtIO or virtio-blk, is an older type of paravirtualized controller. It has been superseded by the VirtIO SCSI Controller, in terms of features.

u743b8566d20d10ec21e6.text: On each controller you attach a number of emulated hard disks, which are backed by a file or a block device residing in the configured storage. The choice of a storage type will determine the format of the hard disk image. Storages which present block devices (LVM, ZFS, Ceph) will require the ⟦0⟧raw disk image format⟦1⟧, whereas files based storages (like Ext4, XFS, NFS, or CIFS) will let you to choose either the ⟦2⟧raw disk image format⟦3⟧ or the ⟦4⟧QEMU image format⟦5⟧.

ue41f522940a64973e746.text: the ⟦0⟧QEMU image format⟦1⟧ is a copy on write format which allows snapshots, and thin provisioning of the disk image.

u7f58da275880c876317e.text: the ⟦0⟧raw disk image⟦1⟧ is a bit-to-bit image of a hard disk, similar to what you would get when executing the ⟦2⟧ command on a block device in Linux. This format does not support thin provisioning or snapshots by itself, requiring cooperation from the storage layer for these tasks. It may, however, be up to 10% faster than the ⟦3⟧QEMU image format⟦4⟧. ⟦5⟧⟦6⟧[See this benchmark for details ⟦7⟧⟦8⟧⟦9⟧]⟦10⟧⟦11⟧

u24c644ba5597ba047dcf.text: the ⟦0⟧VMware image format⟦1⟧ only makes sense if you intend to import/export the disk image to other hypervisors.

u49c8944a03eb5055b2ec.text: Setting the ⟦0⟧Cache⟦1⟧ mode of the hard drive will impact how the host system will notify the guest systems of block write completions. The ⟦2⟧No cache⟦3⟧ default means that the guest system will be notified that a write is complete when each block reaches the physical storage write queue, ignoring the host page cache. This provides a good balance between safety and speed.

u1ea177e2e2802b684507.text: If you want the Proxmox VE backup manager to skip a disk when doing a backup of a VM, you can set the ⟦0⟧No backup⟦1⟧ option on that disk.

u4158eac83c96999132a6.text: If you want the Proxmox VE storage replication mechanism to skip a disk when starting a replication job, you can set the ⟦0⟧Skip replication⟦1⟧ option on that disk. As of Proxmox VE 5.0, replication requires the disk images to be on a storage of type ⟦2⟧, so adding a disk image to other storages when the VM has replication configured requires to skip replication for this disk image.

u2a1dbdf0c544f7d1b486.text: If your storage supports ⟦0⟧thin provisioning⟦1⟧ (see the storage chapter in the Proxmox VE guide), you can activate the ⟦2⟧Discard⟦3⟧ option on a drive. With ⟦4⟧Discard⟦5⟧ set and a ⟦6⟧TRIM⟦7⟧-enabled guest OS ⟦8⟧⟦9⟧[TRIM, UNMAP, and discard ⟦10⟧⟦11⟧⟦12⟧]⟦13⟧⟦14⟧, when the VM’s filesystem marks blocks as unused after deleting files, the controller will relay this information to the storage, which will then shrink the disk image accordingly. For the guest to be able to issue ⟦15⟧TRIM⟦16⟧ commands, you must enable the ⟦17⟧Discard⟦18⟧ option on the drive. Some guest operating systems may also require the ⟦19⟧SSD Emulation⟦20⟧ flag to be set. Note that ⟦21⟧Discard⟦22⟧ on ⟦23⟧VirtIO Block⟦24⟧ drives is only supported on guests using Linux Kernel 5.0 or higher.

u6250c79a2b52dfc573a8.text: If you would like a drive to be presented to the guest as a solid-state drive rather than a rotational hard disk, you can set the ⟦0⟧SSD emulation⟦1⟧ option on that drive. There is no requirement that the underlying storage actually be backed by SSDs; this feature can be used with physical media of any type. Note that ⟦2⟧SSD emulation⟦3⟧ is not supported on ⟦4⟧VirtIO Block⟦5⟧ drives.

u67767636fda2a30d9380.text: The ⟦0⟧IO thread⟦1⟧ option can only be used when using a disk with one of the following bus/device controllers:

u8af4ca3068df7758541f.text: ⟦0⟧SCSI⟦1⟧, if the emulated SCSI controller type is ⟦2⟧VirtIO SCSI single⟦3⟧, or

u2fb1b76a2dfaa4a14e83.text: With ⟦0⟧IO thread⟦1⟧ enabled, QEMU creates one I/O thread per storage controller rather than handling all I/O in the main event loop or vCPU threads. One benefit is better work distribution and utilization of the underlying storage. Another benefit is reduced latency (hangs) in the guest for very I/O-intensive host workloads, since neither the main thread nor a vCPU thread can be blocked by disk I/O.

u037dbc2efd83945243da.text: A ⟦0⟧CPU socket⟦1⟧ is a physical slot on a PC motherboard where you can plug a CPU. This CPU can then contain one or many ⟦2⟧cores⟦3⟧, which are independent processing units. Whether you have a single CPU socket with 4 cores, or two CPU sockets with two cores is mostly irrelevant from a performance point of view. However some software licenses depend on the number of sockets a machine has, in that case it makes sense to set the number of sockets to what the license allows you.

u7241b962203362c70043.text: Increasing the number of virtual CPUs (cores and sockets) will usually provide a performance improvement though that is heavily dependent on the use of the VM. Multi-threaded applications will of course benefit from a large number of virtual CPUs, as for each virtual cpu you add, QEMU will create a new thread of execution on the host system. If you’re not sure about the workload of your VM, it is usually a safe bet to set the number of ⟦0⟧Total cores⟦1⟧ to 2.

u3a68f012c09b56c4c179.text: It is perfectly safe if the ⟦0⟧overall⟦1⟧ number of cores of all your VMs is greater than the number of cores on the server (for example, 4 VMs each with 4 cores (= total 16) on a machine with only 8 cores). In that case the host system will balance the QEMU execution threads between your server cores, just like if you were running a standard multi-threaded application. However, Proxmox VE will prevent you from starting VMs with more virtual CPU cores than physically available, as this will only bring the performance down due to the cost of context switches.

u9ac628fcbf053822387f.text: In addition to the number of virtual cores, the total available “Host CPU Time” for the VM can be set with the ⟦0⟧cpulimit⟦1⟧ option. It is a floating point value representing CPU time in percent, so ⟦2⟧ is equal to ⟦3⟧, ⟦4⟧ to ⟦5⟧ and so on. If a single process would fully use one single core it would have ⟦6⟧ CPU Time usage. If a VM with four cores utilizes all its cores fully it would theoretically use ⟦7⟧. In reality the usage may be even a bit higher as QEMU can have additional threads for VM peripherals besides the vCPU core ones.

u76ec2c948365486e079c.text: This setting can be useful when a VM should have multiple vCPUs because it is running some processes in parallel, but the VM as a whole should not be able to run all vCPUs at 100% at the same time.

ucae9a435cca90d2c7bbb.text: For example, suppose you have a virtual machine that would benefit from having 8 virtual CPUs, but you don’t want the VM to be able to max out all 8 cores running at full load - because that would overload the server and leave other virtual machines and containers with too little CPU time. To solve this, you could set ⟦0⟧cpulimit⟦1⟧ to ⟦2⟧ (=400%). This means that if the VM fully utilizes all 8 virtual CPUs by running 8 processes simultaneously, each vCPU will receive a maximum of 50% CPU time from the physical cores. However, if the VM workload only fully utilizes 4 virtual CPUs, it could still receive up to 100% CPU time from a physical core, for a total of 400%.

u3dd6d4920128dcc85608.text: VMs can, depending on their configuration, use additional threads, such as for networking or IO operations but also live migration. Thus a VM can show up to use more CPU time than just its virtual CPUs could use. To ensure that a VM never uses more CPU time than vCPUs assigned, set the ⟦0⟧cpulimit⟦1⟧ to the same value as the total core count.

u9e6eba8eac0d2385cdbe.text: With the ⟦0⟧cpuunits⟦1⟧ option, nowadays often called CPU shares or CPU weight, you can control how much CPU time a VM gets compared to other running VMs. It is a relative weight which defaults to ⟦2⟧ (or ⟦3⟧ if the host uses legacy cgroup v1). If you increase this for a VM it will be prioritized by the scheduler in comparison to other VMs with lower weight.

u817bbc0a359985fcbe59.text: For example, if VM 100 has set the default ⟦0⟧ and VM 200 was changed to ⟦1⟧, the latter VM 200 would receive twice the CPU bandwidth than the first VM 100.

u16e142b3b2cad2d668bb.text: For more information see ⟦0⟧, here ⟦1⟧ corresponds to ⟦2⟧ and ⟦3⟧ to our ⟦4⟧ setting. Visit its Notes section for references and implementation details.

u03a01a4c42bd94e823e4.text: With the ⟦0⟧affinity⟦1⟧ option, you can specify the physical CPU cores that are used to run the VM’s vCPUs. Peripheral VM processes, such as those for I/O, are not affected by this setting. Note that the ⟦2⟧CPU affinity is not a security feature⟦3⟧.

u41e308027cff272e34ba.text: Forcing a CPU ⟦0⟧affinity⟦1⟧ can make sense in certain cases but is accompanied by an increase in complexity and maintenance effort. For example, if you want to add more VMs later or migrate VMs to nodes with fewer CPU cores. It can also easily lead to asynchronous and therefore limited system performance if some CPUs are fully utilized while others are almost idle.

u2fd8729a48942acb3b37.text: The ⟦0⟧affinity⟦1⟧ is set through the ⟦2⟧ CLI tool. It accepts the host CPU numbers (see ⟦3⟧) in the ⟦4⟧ from ⟦5⟧. This ASCII decimal list can contain numbers but also number ranges. For example, the ⟦6⟧affinity⟦7⟧ ⟦8⟧ (expanded ⟦9⟧) would allow the VM to run on only these six specific host cores.

ucb1f9382cca5a5f23404.text: QEMU can emulate a number different of ⟦0⟧CPU types⟦1⟧ from 486 to the latest Xeon processors. Each new processor generation adds new features, like hardware assisted 3d rendering, random number generation, memory protection, etc. Also, a current generation can be upgraded through ⟦2⟧microcode update⟦3⟧ with bug or security fixes.

u39a8b6828fcb1c53fbb2.text: Usually you should select for your VM a processor type which closely matches the CPU of the host system, as it means that the host CPU features (also called ⟦0⟧CPU flags⟦1⟧ ) will be available in your VMs. If you want an exact match, you can set the CPU type to ⟦2⟧host⟦3⟧ in which case the VM will have exactly the same CPU flags as your host system.

u46da5dd509b52b6cfd93.text: This has a downside though. If you want to do a live migration of VMs between different hosts, your VM might end up on a new system with a different CPU type or a different microcode version. If the CPU flags passed to the guest are missing, the QEMU process will stop. To remedy this QEMU has also its own virtual CPU types, that Proxmox VE uses by default.

u7a591dc0d65e6b4330c5.text: You can also optionally emulate a ⟦0⟧NUMA⟦1⟧ ⟦2⟧⟦3⟧[⟦4⟧⟦5⟧⟦6⟧]⟦7⟧⟦8⟧ architecture in your VMs. The basics of the NUMA architecture mean that instead of having a global memory pool available to all your cores, the memory is spread into local banks close to each socket. u7b3571c7c4ff599b0a4f.text: When multiple VMs use the autoallocate facility, it is possible to set a ⟦0⟧Shares⟦1⟧ coefficient which indicates the relative amount of the free host memory that each VM should take. Suppose for instance you have four VMs, three of them running an HTTP server and the last one is a database server. The host is configured to target 80% RAM usage. To cache more database blocks in the database server RAM, you would like to prioritize the database VM when spare RAM is available. For this you assign a Shares property of 3000 to the database VM, leaving the other VMs to the Shares default setting of 1000. The host server has 32GB of RAM, and is currently using 16GB, leaving 32 * 80/100 - 16 = 9GB RAM to be allocated to the VMs on top of their configured minimum memory amount. The database VM will benefit from 9 * 3000 / (3000 + 1000 + 1000 + 1000) = 4.5 GB extra RAM and each HTTP server from 1.5 GB.

u9e2e6d023eef958cf3e3.text: Each VM can have many ⟦0⟧Network interface controllers⟦1⟧ (NIC), of four different types:

ude481427c333c5c4aaf6.text: ⟦0⟧Intel E1000⟦1⟧ is the default, and emulates an Intel Gigabit network card.

uddf48ee76fc01c81b534.text: the ⟦0⟧VirtIO⟦1⟧ paravirtualized NIC should be used if you aim for maximum performance. Like all VirtIO devices, the guest OS should have the proper driver installed.

u827668a516db60e15ad6.text: the ⟦0⟧Realtek 8139⟦1⟧ emulates an older 100 MB/s network card, and should only be used when emulating older operating systems ( released before 2002 )

u46dc7f67fa1f65c4fd22.text: the ⟦0⟧vmxnet3⟦1⟧ is another paravirtualized device, which should only be used when importing a VM from another hypervisor.

u06ae213c12bad8892f82.text: Proxmox VE will generate for each NIC a random ⟦0⟧MAC address⟦1⟧, so that your VM is addressable on Ethernet networks.

u1262934663347bdea505.text: The NIC you added to the VM can follow one of two different models:

u79b46f6ba8f78a859b79.text: in the default ⟦0⟧Bridged mode⟦1⟧ each virtual NIC is backed on the host by a ⟦2⟧tap device⟦3⟧, ( a software loopback device simulating an Ethernet NIC ). This tap device is added to a bridge, by default vmbr0 in Proxmox VE. In this mode, VMs have direct access to the Ethernet LAN on which the host is located.

ufdaee0fbd107631eb23b.text: in the alternative ⟦0⟧NAT mode⟦1⟧, each virtual NIC will only communicate with the QEMU user networking stack, where a built-in router and DHCP server can provide network access. This built-in DHCP will serve addresses in the private 10.0.2.0/24 range. The NAT mode is much slower than the bridged mode, and should only be used for testing. This mode is only available via CLI or the API, but not via the web UI.

u46a8a9d1bde638615bb6.text: You can also skip adding a network device when creating a VM by selecting ⟦0⟧No network device⟦1⟧.

u5c0bac47ccd07e5f93d5.text: You can overwrite the ⟦0⟧MTU⟦1⟧ setting for each VM network device manually. Leaving the field empty or setting ⟦2⟧ will inherit the MTU from the underlying bridge. This option is only available for ⟦3⟧VirtIO⟦4⟧ network devices.

uf21aa89df1fc9db6244b.text: If you are using the VirtIO driver, you can optionally activate the ⟦0⟧Multiqueue⟦1⟧ option. This option allows the guest OS to process networking packets using multiple virtual CPUs, providing an increase in the total number of packets transferred.

u15ce41916da0b934d086.text: When using the VirtIO driver with Proxmox VE, each NIC network queue is passed to the host kernel, where the queue will be processed by a kernel thread spawned by the vhost driver. With this option activated, it is possible to pass ⟦0⟧multiple⟦1⟧ network queues to the host kernel for each NIC.

u9ce62c700fb95d748ba2.text: When using Multiqueue, it is recommended to set it to a value equal to the number of vCPUs of your guest. Remember that the number of vCPUs is the number of sockets times the number of cores configured for the VM. You also need to set the number of multi-purpose channels on each VirtIO NIC in the VM with this ethtool command:

ue6a3a24e4391ceed4752.text: where X is the number of the number of vCPUs of the VM.

u51e4652685a4511d2683.text: To configure a Windows guest for Multiqueue install the ⟦0⟧Redhat VirtIO Ethernet Adapter drivers⟦1⟧, then adapt the NIC’s configuration as follows. Open the device manager, right click the NIC under "Network adapters", and select "Properties". Then open the "Advanced" tab and select "Receive Side Scaling" from the list on the left. Make sure it is set to "Enabled". Next, navigate to "Maximum number of RSS Queues" in the list and set it to the number of vCPUs of your VM. Once you verified that the settings are correct, click "OK" to confirm them.

ub16965caf6356044ded3.text: You should note that setting the Multiqueue parameter to a value greater than one will increase the CPU load on the host and guest systems as the traffic increases. We recommend to set this option only when the VM has to process a great number of incoming connections, such as when the VM is running as a router, reverse proxy or a busy HTTP server doing long polling.

u7e5b11e7a3a0d6301bb2.text: There are two different types of USB passthrough devices:

u18b713fec5bddb1bb1b6.text: Host USB passthrough works by giving a VM a USB device of the host. This can either be done via the vendor- and product-id, or via the host bus and port.

u54bd3691fbb9786cf5ad.text: The vendor/product-id looks like this: ⟦0⟧0123:abcd⟦1⟧, where ⟦2⟧0123⟦3⟧ is the id of the vendor, and ⟦4⟧abcd⟦5⟧ is the id of the product, meaning two pieces of the same usb device have the same id.

u6f741c346467a29363d0.text: The bus/port looks like this: ⟦0⟧1-2.3.4⟦1⟧, where ⟦2⟧1⟦3⟧ is the bus and ⟦4⟧2.3.4⟦5⟧ is the port path. This represents the physical ports of your host (depending of the internal order of the usb controllers).

u2de785379af8851ae3d1.text: If a device is present in a VM configuration when the VM starts up, but the device is not present in the host, the VM can boot without problems. As soon as the device/port is available in the host, it gets passed through.

ub6850b1b71b49e50d54a.text: Using this kind of USB passthrough means that you cannot move a VM online to another host, since the hardware is only available on the host the VM is currently residing.

u98c05c97aea6206b0249.text: The second type of passthrough is SPICE USB passthrough. If you add one or more SPICE USB ports to your VM, you can dynamically pass a local USB device from your SPICE client through to the VM. This can be useful to redirect an input device or hardware dongle temporarily.

ue5ba6680671858d78e58.text: It is also possible to map devices on a cluster level, so that they can be properly used with HA and hardware changes are detected and non root users can configure them. See ⟦0⟧Resource Mapping⟦1⟧ for details on that.

u7bb1db0eed57ee53d525.text: In order to properly emulate a computer, QEMU needs to use a firmware. Which, on common PCs often known as BIOS or (U)EFI, is executed as one of the first steps when booting a VM. It is responsible for doing basic hardware initialization and for providing an interface to the firmware and hardware for the operating system. By default QEMU uses ⟦0⟧SeaBIOS⟦1⟧ for this, which is an open-source, x86 BIOS implementation. SeaBIOS is a good choice for most standard setups.

u2c00573b7aba0fa583ce.text: SeaBIOS, and thus ⟦0⟧, is available for x86 guests only. On arm64 hosts, virtual machines always boot through UEFI, using the ARM build of OVMF (AAVMF), so ⟦1⟧ is the only supported setting there.

ufa1f3cb9f7ad0f85a55a.text: Some operating systems (such as Windows 11) may require use of an UEFI compatible implementation. In such cases, you must use ⟦0⟧OVMF⟦1⟧ instead, which is an open-source UEFI implementation. ⟦2⟧⟦3⟧[See the OVMF Project ⟦4⟧⟦5⟧⟦6⟧]⟦7⟧⟦8⟧

uea24ce7a5b29196af874.text: Virtiofs is a shared filesystem designed for virtual environments. It allows to share a directory tree available on the host by mounting it within VMs. It does not use the network stack and aims to offer similar performance and semantics as the source filesystem.

u858307d837d19de6b4bf.text: Linux VMs with kernel >=5.4 support virtiofs by default (⟦0⟧virtiofs kernel module⟦1⟧), but some features require a newer kernel.

uc3027dc53d43314ae1e9.text: If virtiofsd crashes, its mount point will hang in the VM until the VM is completely stopped.

ub55013b685d548673280.text: virtiofsd not responding may result in a hanging mount in the VM, similar to an unreachable NFS.

u70a75a1a67acd9e4d84f.text: Memory hotplug does not work in combination with virtiofs (also results in hanging access).

uc2e49e1f81f918fcc0f8.text: 10.2.18. Automatic Start and Shutdown of Virtual Machines

u4cddfa67e11c4481cf59.text: After creating your VMs, you probably want them to start automatically when the host system boots. For this you need to select the option ⟦0⟧Start at boot⟦1⟧ from the ⟦2⟧Options⟦3⟧ Tab of your VM in the web interface, or set it with the following command:

u3efc87a9ca1d37c83915.text: In some case you want to be able to fine tune the boot order of your VMs, for instance if one of your VM is providing firewalling or DHCP to other guest systems. For this you can use the following parameters:

ucc422d3aa2be0aa45a37.text: ⟦0⟧Start/Shutdown order⟦1⟧: Defines the start order priority. For example, set it to 1 if you want the VM to be the first to be started. (We use the reverse startup order for shutdown, so a machine with a start order of 1 would be the last to be shut down). If multiple VMs have the same order defined on a host, they will additionally be ordered by ⟦2⟧VMID⟦3⟧ in ascending order.

u203063061d75889068fe.text: ⟦0⟧Startup delay⟦1⟧: Defines the interval between this VM start and subsequent VMs starts. For example, set it to 240 if you want to wait 240 seconds before starting other VMs.

u3e9f45c25a2c0a6a05cd.text: ⟦0⟧Shutdown timeout⟦1⟧: Defines the duration in seconds Proxmox VE should wait for the VM to be offline after issuing a shutdown command. By default this value is set to 180, which means that Proxmox VE will issue a shutdown request and wait 180 seconds for the machine to be offline. If the machine is still online after the timeout it will be stopped forcefully.

u25f7cf546d5147f4ebf4.text: VMs managed by the HA stack do not follow the ⟦0⟧start on boot⟦1⟧ and ⟦2⟧boot order⟦3⟧ options currently. Those VMs will be skipped by the startup and shutdown algorithm as the HA manager itself ensures that VMs get started and stopped.

uaa4037f9407353ab097b.text: The QEMU Guest Agent is a service which runs inside the VM, providing a communication channel between the host and the guest. It is used to exchange information and allows the host to issue commands to the guest.

uced30689cb8a01ba00b2.text: For example, the IP addresses in the VM summary panel are fetched via the guest agent.

u10dd90dd198b94110fbc.text: Or when starting a backup, the guest is told via the guest agent to sync outstanding writes via the ⟦0⟧ and ⟦1⟧ commands.

u05fd86e92f5a25a53d2b.text: For the guest agent to work properly the following steps must be taken:

u4e630e594f10f187a2dd.text: install the agent in the guest and make sure it is running

ubab3a549c41213e9a300.text: enable the communication via the agent in Proxmox VE

u71395c6c6cd8ac3b37ce.text: For most Linux distributions, the guest agent is available. The package is usually named ⟦0⟧.

u97f42ea10bd14f7a2626.text: For Windows, see our ⟦0⟧Windows VirtIO Drivers⟦1⟧ article for more information on how to acquire and install the drivers.

u7eb6242cbd86108ff6aa.text: Communication from Proxmox VE with the guest agent can be enabled in the VM’s ⟦0⟧Options⟦1⟧ panel. A fresh start of the VM is necessary for the changes to take effect.

uada8f90b895163781ab7.text: It is possible to enable the ⟦0⟧Run guest-trim⟦1⟧ option. With this enabled, Proxmox VE will issue a trim command to the guest after the following operations that have the potential to write out zeros to the storage:

u5a37a3ee25542463d985.text: moving a disk to another storage

u359f5597a40481973693.text: On a thin provisioned storage, this can help to free up unused space.

u0d72206f1096b54a4eed.text: There is a caveat with ext4 on Linux, because it uses an in-memory optimization to avoid issuing duplicate TRIM requests. Since the guest doesn’t know about the change in the underlying storage, only the first guest-trim will run as expected. Subsequent ones, until the next reboot, will only consider parts of the filesystem that changed since then.

u191880fac6ff19567a41.text: By default, if the QEMU Guest Agent is enabled in the guest’s config and if the agent is available inside of the guest, then the virtual machine’s filesystems are synced via the ⟦0⟧ QEMU Guest Agent command when certain operations are performed. This is done to provide data consistency.

u1754ab53f30aef012754.text: See the ⟦0⟧QEMU Guest Agent Protocol Reference⟦1⟧ for more details.

u495a239644ea3f9d3da9.text: A freeze will be issued for any of the following operations on a VM:

ue6f720b68d0c0713165f.text: Performing a backup in snapshot mode

ue0618c039ec5c48eee0d.text: Creating a clone of a VM while it is running

uc3b9f31f3fa6c58fe7c4.text: Importing a disk image from a running guest will issue a freeze for that running guest

u3cafb941b03077f8997d.text: On Windows guests, some applications might handle consistent backups themselves by hooking into the Windows VSS (Volume Shadow Copy Service) layer, a freeze then might interfere with that. For example, it has been observed that calling ⟦0⟧ with some SQL Servers triggers VSS to call the SQL Writer VSS module in a mode that breaks the SQL Server backup chain for differential backups.

u53768c4e33a41c7ee3f4.text: There are two options on how to handle such a situation.

ua6dd5e249112ab145a25.text: Configure the QEMU Guest Agent to use a different VSS variant that does not interfere with other VSS users. The ⟦0⟧Proxmox VE wiki⟦1⟧ has more details.

u449d6d905de08859632d.text: Alternatively, you can configure Proxmox VE to not issue a freeze-and-thaw cycle by disabling the ⟦0⟧ guest agent option. This can also be done in the GUI: open the ⟦1⟧Options⟦2⟧ panel of the virtual machine, then the ⟦3⟧QEMU Guest Agent⟦4⟧ dialog, and disable the ⟦5⟧Freeze/thaw guest filesystems during certain operations for consistency⟦6⟧ option.

u01085387fe034344ae3f.text: Disabling this option can potentially lead to backups with inconsistent filesystems. Therefore, adapting the QEMU Guest Agent configuration in the guest is the preferred option.

u5cfc56b54696857c498b.text: Make sure the guest agent is installed and running.

ub9bd467d3baff5e59951.text: Once the guest agent is enabled, Proxmox VE will send power commands like ⟦0⟧shutdown⟦1⟧ via the guest agent. If the guest agent is not running, commands cannot get executed properly and the shutdown command will run into a timeout.

u3b6181ea4f7ad691aaed.text: If you have a cluster, you can migrate your VM to another host with

ue2caee4e8784c21099b0.text: There are generally two mechanisms for this

u010c65677dfbb7f2d651.text: If your VM is running and no locally bound resources are configured (such as devices that are passed through), you can initiate a live migration with the ⟦0⟧ flag in the ⟦1⟧ command evocation. The web interface defaults to live migration when the VM is running.

u81ba8e3c2126c31f4b53.text: Live migration is only possible between hosts of the same CPU architecture. A running guest’s CPU state cannot be transferred between an x86 and an arm64 host.

u29143734c955d496e509.text: Online migration first starts a new QEMU process on the target host with the ⟦0⟧incoming⟦1⟧ flag, which performs only basic initialization with the guest vCPUs still paused and then waits for the guest memory and device state data streams of the source Virtual Machine. All other resources, such as disks, are either shared or got already sent before runtime state migration of the VMs begins; so only the memory content and device state remain to be transferred.

u5ebed38fd9898f541cdc.text: Once this connection is established, the source begins asynchronously sending the memory content to the target. If the guest memory on the source changes, those sections are marked dirty and another pass is made to send the guest memory data. This loop is repeated until the data difference between running source VM and incoming target VM is small enough to be sent in a few milliseconds, because then the source VM can be paused completely, without a user or program noticing the pause, so that the remaining data can be sent to the target, and then unpause the targets VM’s CPU to make it the new running VM in well under a second.

u89fbf115247f632d0bcf.text: For Live Migration to work, there are some things required:

ufb20e6c8d6f97626301a.text: The VM has no local resources that cannot be migrated. For example, PCI or USB devices that are passed through currently block live-migration. Local Disks, on the other hand, can be migrated by sending them to the target just fine.

u58ba0a63def976fedca2.text: The hosts are located in the same Proxmox VE cluster.

uf428b33c308f3660d0e5.text: The hosts have a working (and reliable) network connection between them.

ua6ac828b6a79d52f8634.text: The target host must have the same, or higher versions of the Proxmox VE packages. Although it can sometimes work the other way around, this cannot be guaranteed.

uab91c3b63e304f430e62.text: The hosts have CPUs from the same vendor with similar capabilities. Different vendor ⟦0⟧might⟦1⟧ work depending on the actual models and VMs CPU type configured, but it cannot be guaranteed - so please test before deploying such a setup in production.

u14b6a616fb9da1188e00.text: Conntrack state migration is considered best-effort only and might not work, as it heavily depends on the network setup. For example, setups using ⟦0⟧source address masquerading (SNAT)⟦1⟧ on the host will most likely ⟦2⟧not⟦3⟧ work.

ucf32b132bb2539ddd9ad.text: Conntrack is a Linux kernel mechanism to enable a stateful firewall by tracking individual connection. When live migrating running VMs, active in- and/or outbound connections ⟦0⟧might⟦1⟧ get interrupted as soon as the VM starts running on the target host, as the new host node does not have the same conntrack entries and thus the firewall can drop packets.

ucb77d16565bc7d388580.text: Conntrack state migration copies all conntrack entries on the host for the live-migrated VM to the target node and afterwards flushes the migrated entries from the conntrack table on the source node.

uf69fed3ee4869e8d09a5.text: If you have local resources, you can still migrate your VMs offline as long as all disk are on storage defined on both hosts. Migration then copies the disks to the target host over the network, as with online migration. Note that any hardware passthrough configuration may need to be adapted to the device location on the target host.

u94159392f09b65e9eeb8.text: VM installation is usually done using an installation media (CD-ROM) from the operating system vendor. Depending on the OS, this can be a time consuming task one might want to avoid.

uf7577876b39f3c49cca6.text: An easy way to deploy many VMs of the same type is to copy an existing VM. We use the term ⟦0⟧clone⟦1⟧ for such copies, and distinguish between ⟦2⟧linked⟦3⟧ and ⟦4⟧full⟦5⟧ clones.

uef0e0ccd71389f6a7054.text: The result of such copy is an independent VM. The new VM does not share any storage resources with the original.

u75aec88ddb7e11e5c08d.text: It is possible to select a ⟦0⟧Target Storage⟦1⟧, so one can use this to migrate a VM to a totally different storage. You can also change the disk image ⟦2⟧Format⟦3⟧ if the storage driver supports several formats.

u15c8e1f94f76ea904916.text: A full clone needs to read and copy all VM image data. This is usually much slower than creating a linked clone.

u6d0afc5d020049600a16.text: Some storage types allows to copy a specific ⟦0⟧Snapshot⟦1⟧, which defaults to the ⟦2⟧current⟦3⟧ VM data. This also means that the final copy never includes any additional snapshots from the original VM.

uf258bc936fd84e1b081a.text: Modern storage drivers support a way to generate fast linked clones. Such a clone is a writable copy whose initial contents are the same as the original data. Creating a linked clone is nearly instantaneous, and initially consumes no additional space.

ub8cf62606d6a39a120dd.text: They are called ⟦0⟧linked⟦1⟧ because the new image still refers to the original. Unmodified data blocks are read from the original image, but modification are written (and afterwards read) from a new location. This technique is called ⟦2⟧Copy-on-write⟦3⟧.

u5e68cb4fdf5d4deaf8bb.text: This requires that the original volume is read-only. With Proxmox VE one can convert any VM into a read-only ⟦0⟧Template⟦1⟧). Such templates can later be used to create linked clones efficiently.

u9a2ac12884ec1b300190.text: You cannot delete an original template while linked clones exist.

ub25c023a055363b30fbd.text: It is not possible to change the ⟦0⟧Target storage⟦1⟧ for linked clones, because this is a storage internal feature.

u568ab5caec7132c44322.text: The ⟦0⟧Target node⟦1⟧ option allows you to create the new VM on a different node. The only restriction is that the VM is on shared storage, and that storage is also available on the target node.

u531ab2040756d5dfa9f2.text: To avoid resource conflicts, all network interface MAC addresses get randomized, and we generate a new ⟦0⟧UUID⟦1⟧ for the VM BIOS (smbios1) setting.

uead4399cdc4092c34188.text: One can convert a VM into a Template. Such templates are read-only, and you can use them to create linked clones.

ub0c2e33163fcddeeb8c1.text: It is not possible to start templates, because this would modify the disk images. If you want to change the template, create a linked clone and modify that.

ua3a26ae316b4b2f16699.text: Proxmox VE supports Virtual Machine Generation ID (⟦0⟧vmgenid⟦1⟧) ⟦2⟧⟦3⟧[Official ⟦4⟧vmgenid⟦5⟧ Specification ⟦6⟧⟦7⟧⟦8⟧]⟦9⟧⟦10⟧ for virtual machines. This can be used by the guest operating system to detect any event resulting in a time shift event, for example, restoring a backup or a snapshot rollback.

u579b1c1571c8c24bf7bc.text: When creating new VMs, a ⟦0⟧vmgenid⟦1⟧ will be automatically generated and saved in its configuration file.

u48b3416b8fddbe0ef253.text: The initial addition of a ⟦0⟧vmgenid⟦1⟧ device to an existing VM, may result in the same effects as a change on snapshot rollback, backup restore, etc., has as the VM can interpret this as generation change.

u068a7434e40b4e33d49f.text: In the rare case the ⟦0⟧vmgenid⟦1⟧ mechanism is not wanted one can pass ‘0’ for its value on VM creation, or retroactively delete the property in the configuration with:

u138ae5c33f71bc34ce97.text: The most prominent use case for ⟦0⟧vmgenid⟦1⟧ are newer Microsoft Windows operating systems, which use it to avoid problems in time sensitive or replicate services (such as databases or domain controller ⟦2⟧⟦3⟧[⟦4⟧⟦5⟧⟦6⟧]⟦7⟧⟦8⟧) on snapshot rollback, backup restore or a whole VM clone operation.

u8d72fb6b048f73735064.text: Importing existing virtual machines from foreign hypervisors or other Proxmox VE clusters can be achieved through various methods, the most common ones are:

u95f5ed7027949e018b2a.text: Using the native import wizard, which utilizes the ⟦0⟧import⟦1⟧ content type, such as provided by the ESXi special storage.

uad7b8a67cfae72f4c19e.text: Performing a backup on the source and then restoring on the target. This method works best when migrating from another Proxmox VE instance.

u7667bf8a2126ad707d51.text: using the OVF-specific import command of the ⟦0⟧ command-line tool.

u6f8aa2f0f419a0352163.text: If you import VMs to Proxmox VE from other hypervisors, it’s recommended to familiarize yourself with the ⟦0⟧concepts of Proxmox VE⟦1⟧.

ufb0336734c1c8d1578b4.text: Proxmox VE provides an integrated VM importer using the storage plugin system for native integration into the API and web-based user interface. You can use this to import the VM as a whole, with most of its config mapped to Proxmox VE’s config model and reduced downtime.

u1c813f809ad31ad37046.text: The import wizard was added during the Proxmox VE 8.2 development cycle and is in tech preview state. While it’s already promising and working stable, it’s still under active development.

uc36a39617e94fe7171f2.text: To use the import wizard you have to first set up a new storage for an import source, you can do so on the web-interface under ⟦0⟧Datacenter → Storage → Add⟦1⟧.

u75264f3e98e24b6c7ead.text: Then you can select the new storage in the resource tree and use the ⟦0⟧Virtual Guests⟦1⟧ content tab to see all available guests that can be imported.

ua0e7dad19dab0aabd60c.text: Select one and use the ⟦0⟧Import⟦1⟧ button (or double-click) to open the import wizard. You can modify a subset of the available options here and then start the import. Please note that you can do more advanced modifications after the import finished.

ubfc265c8dd9f29ff6ebd.text: The ESXi import wizard has been tested with ESXi versions 6.5 through 8.0. Note that guests using vSAN storage cannot be directly imported directly; their disks must first be moved to another storage. While it is possible to use a vCenter as the import source, performance is dramatically degraded (5 to 10 times slower).

u6d656290d695cf00c7bc.text: For a step-by-step guide and tips for how to adapt the virtual guest to the new hyper-visor see our ⟦0⟧migrate to Proxmox VE wiki article⟦1⟧.

u89c4880322d76b1db82e.text: To import OVA/OVF files, you first need a File-based storage with the ⟦0⟧import⟦1⟧ content type. On this storage, there will be an ⟦2⟧import⟦3⟧ folder where you can put OVA files or OVF files with the corresponding images in a flat structure. Alternatively you can use the web UI to upload or download OVA files directly. You can then use the web UI to select those and use the import wizard to import the guests.

uf25b5bfd04950828b83a.text: For OVA files, there is additional space needed to temporarily extract the image. This needs a file-based storage that has the ⟦0⟧images⟦1⟧ content type configured. By default the source storage is selected for this, but you can specify a ⟦2⟧Import Working Storage⟦3⟧ on which the images will be extracted before importing to the actual target storage.

udf0ef05c47722d0642eb.text: Since OVA/OVF file structure and content are not always well maintained or defined, it might be necessary to adapt some guest settings manually. For example the SCSI controller type is almost never defined in OVA/OVF files, but the default is unbootable with OVMF (UEFI), so you should select ⟦0⟧Virtio SCSI⟦1⟧ or ⟦2⟧VMware PVSCSI⟦3⟧ for these cases.

u09097f5e4f0837663003.text: A VM export from a foreign hypervisor takes usually the form of one or more disk images, with a configuration file describing the settings of the VM (RAM, number of cores).⟦0⟧ The disk images can be in the vmdk format, if the disks come from VMware or VirtualBox, or qcow2 if the disks come from a KVM hypervisor. The most popular configuration format for VM exports is the OVF standard, but in practice interoperation is limited because many settings are not implemented in the standard itself, and hypervisors export the supplementary information in non-standard extensions.

ub81d2f292267ae4e61e7.text: Besides the problem of format, importing disk images from other hypervisors may fail if the emulated hardware changes too much from one hypervisor to another. Windows VMs are particularly concerned by this, as the OS is very picky about any changes of hardware. This problem may be solved by installing the MergeIDE.zip utility available from the Internet before exporting and choosing a hard disk type of ⟦0⟧IDE⟦1⟧ before booting the imported Windows VM.

ucecae64bbfa70ac38886.text: Finally there is the question of paravirtualized drivers, which improve the speed of the emulated system and are specific to the hypervisor. u11cbe0a3c1a500392e57.text: ⟦0⟧Cloud-Init⟦1⟧ is the de facto multi-distribution package that handles early initialization of a virtual machine instance. u9e6d06b34f8882d6065d.text: PCI(e) passthrough is a mechanism to give a virtual machine control over a PCI device from the host. This can have some advantages over using virtualized hardware, for example lower latency, higher performance, or more features (e.g., offloading).

uc26965fb52d2232a9d13.text: But, if you pass through a device to a virtual machine, you cannot use that device anymore on the host or in any other VM.

u982abe51b6305f320d1a.text: Note that, while PCI passthrough is available for i440fx and q35 machines, PCIe passthrough is only available on q35 machines. This does not mean that PCIe-capable devices that are passed through as PCI devices will only run at PCI speeds. Passing through devices as PCIe just sets a flag for the guest to tell it that the device is a PCIe device instead of a "really fast legacy PCI device". Some guest applications benefit from this.

u6e1edac76e43e9a2a2b4.text: Since passthrough is performed on real hardware, it needs to fulfill some requirements. A brief overview of these requirements is given below, for more information on specific devices, see ⟦0⟧PCI Passthrough Examples⟦1⟧.

ub3ad10608678ab67f587.text: The VM generation ID (vmgenid) device exposes a 128-bit integer value identifier to the guest OS. u74187eef51d9ff7f4801.text: The ⟦0⟧S⟦1⟧oftware-⟦2⟧D⟦3⟧efined ⟦4⟧N⟦5⟧etwork (SDN) feature in Proxmox VE enables the creation of virtual zones and networks (VNets). This functionality simplifies advanced networking configurations and multitenancy setup.

ua98c81ab9ba3c699a34b.text: The Proxmox VE SDN allows for separation and fine-grained control of virtual guest networks, using flexible, software-controlled configurations.

u77c875d20b89e09ac7ae.text: Separation is managed through ⟦0⟧zones⟦1⟧, virtual networks (⟦2⟧VNets⟦3⟧), and ⟦4⟧subnets⟦5⟧. A zone is its own virtually separated network area. A VNet is a virtual network that belongs to a zone. A subnet is an IP range inside a VNet.

ua99e4afa8eef243c5bfb.text: Depending on the type of the zone, the network behaves differently and offers specific features, advantages, and limitations.

uf55579aa5a4a216f424c.text: Use cases for SDN range from an isolated private network on each individual node to complex overlay networks across multiple PVE clusters on different locations.

u0e128ee736854b2c6e55.text: After configuring an VNet in the cluster-wide datacenter SDN administration interface, it is available as a common Linux bridge, locally on each node, to be assigned to VMs and Containers.

u061549490d63602b7dee.text: The Proxmox VE SDN stack has been available as an experimental feature since 2019 and has been continuously improved and tested by many developers and users. With its integration into the web interface in Proxmox VE 6.2, a significant milestone towards broader integration was achieved. During the Proxmox VE 7 release cycle, numerous improvements and features were added. Based on user feedback, it became apparent that the fundamental design choices and their implementation were quite sound and stable. Consequently, labeling it as ‘experimental’ did not do justice to the state of the SDN stack. For Proxmox VE 8, a decision was made to lay the groundwork for full integration of the SDN feature by elevating the management of networks and interfaces to a core component in the Proxmox VE access control stack. In Proxmox VE 8.1, two major milestones were achieved: firstly, DHCP integration was added to the IP address management (IPAM) feature, and secondly, the SDN integration is now installed by default.
