u4f2d0fbadc9306941888.text: Most configuration files in Proxmox VE reside on the ⟦0⟧shared cluster file system⟦1⟧ mounted at ⟦2⟧. There are exceptions, like the node-specific configuration file for backups in ⟦3⟧.

u0bac381dfdaff534df3e.text: Usually, the properties in a configuration file are derived from the JSON Schema that is also used for the associated API endpoints.

u226c794756a609e3a41f.text: Historically, longer properties (and sub-properties) often used ⟦0⟧, or were written as one word. This can likely be attributed to the Proxmox VE stack being developed mostly in the programming language Perl, where access to properties using ⟦1⟧ requires additional quotes, as well as less style enforcement during early development, so different developers used different conventions.

u6fc1a2a97f1b6a516477.text: For new properties, ⟦0⟧ is the preferred way and it is planned to introduce aliases for existing ⟦1⟧ properties, and in the long term, switch over to ⟦2⟧ for the API, CLI and in-use configuration files while maintaining backwards-compatibility when restoring a configuration.

u7f286832a47bc4f9f6da.text: Proxmox VE has a very flexible scheduling configuration. It is based on the systemd time calendar event format.⟦0⟧⟦1⟧[see ⟦2⟧ for more information]⟦3⟧⟦4⟧ Calendar events may be used to refer to one or more points in time in a single expression.

uc16f2e6c5e6ec59b50ca.text: Such a calendar event uses the following format:

ud7e9df89854d185b1228.text: This format allows you to configure a set of days on which the job should run. You can also set one or more start times. It tells the replication scheduler the moments in time when a job should start. With this information we, can create a job which runs every workday at 10 PM: ⟦0⟧ which could be abbreviated to: ⟦1⟧, most reasonable schedules can be written quite intuitive this way.

ub59d2139d6680e1b2e7c.text: To allow a convenient and shorter configuration, one or more repeat times per guest can be set. They indicate that replications are done on the start-time(s) itself and the start-time(s) plus all multiples of the repetition value. If you want to start replication at 8 AM and repeat it every 15 minutes until 9 AM you would use: ⟦0⟧

ue132cf4db35b6f1d3ed0.text: Here you see that if no hour separation (⟦0⟧), is used the value gets interpreted as minute. If such a separation is used, the value on the left denotes the hour(s), and the value on the right denotes the minute(s). Further, you can use ⟦1⟧ to match all possible values.

u75fbcfde0e56f082f9c7.text: To get additional ideas look at ⟦0⟧more Examples below⟦1⟧.

u09426c2449028c634146.text: Days are specified with an abbreviated English version: ⟦0⟧. You may use multiple days as a comma-separated list. A range of days can also be set by specifying the start and end day separated by “..”, for example ⟦1⟧. These formats can be mixed. If omitted ⟦2⟧ is assumed.
fragments: sun, mon, tue, wed, thu, fri and sat

u1ed9ac70229c89ac1249.text: A time format consists of hours and minutes interval lists. Hours and minutes are separated by ⟦0⟧. Both hour and minute can be list and ranges of values, using the same format as days. First are hours, then minutes. Hours can be omitted if not needed. In this case ⟦1⟧ is assumed for the value of hours. The valid range for values is ⟦2⟧ for hours and ⟦3⟧ for minutes.

u41d03ed2277d25b075ee.text: You can use ⟦0⟧ to see whether a given calendar event specification is valid and when it would be triggered next. By passing the ⟦1⟧ flag you can also let it output the next ⟦2⟧ times the calendar event would trigger (you need to replace ⟦3⟧ with a valid integer).

u7b09e7003f4aab1991f0.text: For small to medium-sized deployments, it is possible to install a Ceph server for using RADOS Block Devices (RBD) or CephFS directly on your Proxmox VE cluster nodes (see ⟦0⟧Ceph RADOS Block Devices (RBD)⟦1⟧). Recent hardware has a lot of CPU power and RAM, so running storage services and virtual guests on the same node is possible.

uf045f00724613d6b2e5b.text: Recommendations for a Healthy Ceph Cluster

u7595e830c57ea7999ca5.text: The current recommendation is to ⟦0⟧configure⟦1⟧ OSDs with at least ⟦2⟧8 GiB of memory⟦3⟧ for good performance. The OSD daemon requires 4 GiB by default.

u99b45d41de9fbc7ae6d4.text: In general, SSDs will provide more IOPS than spinning disks. With this in mind, in addition to the higher cost, it may make sense to implement a ⟦0⟧class based⟦1⟧ separation of pools. Another way to speed up OSDs is to use a faster disk as a journal or DB/⟦2⟧W⟦3⟧rite-⟦4⟧A⟦5⟧head-⟦6⟧L⟦7⟧og device, see ⟦8⟧creating Ceph OSDs⟦9⟧. If a faster disk is used for multiple OSDs, a proper balance between OSD and WAL / DB (or journal) disk must be selected, otherwise the faster disk becomes the bottleneck for all linked OSDs.

u3f12f00886d324e8cd06.text: After finishing the installation step, you will need to create a configuration. This step is only needed once per cluster, as this configuration is distributed automatically to all remaining cluster members through Proxmox VE’s clustered ⟦0⟧configuration file system (pmxcfs)⟦1⟧.

u0a10ae953761e01c18e7.text: Using a bond as a Corosync link can be problematic in certain failure scenarios. Consider the failure scenario where one of the bonded interfaces fails and stops transmitting packets, but its link state stays up, and there are no other Corosync links available. In this scenario, some bond modes may cause a state of asymmetric connectivity where cluster nodes can only communicate with different subsets of other nodes. Affected are bond modes that provide load balancing, as these modes may still try to send out a subset of packets via the failed interface. In case of asymmetric connectivity, Corosync may not be able to form a stable quorum in the cluster. If this state persists and HA is enabled, even nodes whose bond does not have any issues may fence themselves. In the worst case, the whole cluster may fence itself.

u4d34de7d7c77d8084d0f.text: Cluster-wide rolling restart of all Ceph daemons of the given type. For MON/MGR/MDS each daemon is restarted only after Ceph reports the previous one is back up and the next one is safe to stop. For OSDs the cluster path orchestrates the per-node endpoint at ⟦0⟧ on each node in turn, inheriting that endpoint's per-OSD 'noout' handling and resume support. The 'noout' flag itself is not exposed by this endpoint as it is OSD-specific (and for OSDs handled by the per-node sub-tasks).

Checks that ceph reports as muted, and checks known to be harmless for a rolling restart, never block and are named in the task log. The cluster-wide OSD map flags are only ever evaluated for an OSD restart, since they govern nothing a mon, mgr or mds restart touches. The operator is responsible for confirming the cluster is stable enough to absorb a rolling restart.

u3b75518e43429fbd248d.text: The policy for HA services on node shutdown. 'freeze' disables auto-recovery, 'failover' ensures recovery, 'conditional' recovers on poweroff and freezes on reboot. 'migrate' will migrate running services to other nodes, if possible. With 'freeze' or 'failover', HA Services will always get stopped first on shutdown.

uf730bfcdb7a09ede84e1.text: Describes the policy for handling HA services on poweroff or reboot of a node. Freeze will always freeze services which are still located on the node on shutdown, those services won't be recovered by the HA manager. Failover will not mark the services as frozen and thus the services will get recovered to other nodes, if the shutdown node does not come up again quickly (< 1min). 'conditional' chooses automatically depending on the type of shutdown, i.e., on a reboot the service will be frozen but on a poweroff the service will stay as is, and thus get recovered after about 2 minutes. Migrate will try to move all running services to another node when a reboot or shutdown was triggered. The poweroff process will only continue once no running services are located on the node anymore. If the node comes up again, the service will be moved back to the previously powered-off node, at least if no other migration, reloaction or recovery took place.

Accepts a semicolon-separated list of ⟦1⟧ entries.⟦2⟧⟦3⟧⟦4⟧ is ⟦5⟧ for UID or ⟦6⟧ for GID.⟦7⟧⟦8⟧⟦9⟧ is the first ID as seen inside the container.⟦10⟧⟦11⟧⟦12⟧ is the first corresponding ID on the underlying filesystem.⟦13⟧⟦14⟧⟦15⟧ is the number of consecutive IDs to map.⟦16⟧⟦17⟧Unmapped IDs fall back to the container's ⟦18⟧.⟦19⟧⟦20⟧Example 1: ⟦21⟧ maps UID 123 in the container to UID 456 on the disk. Files owned by UID 456 on the disk will appear as UID 123 inside the container.⟦22⟧⟦23⟧Example 2: ⟦24⟧ maps 5 consecutive GIDs, such that GIDs 100-104 in the container are mapped to GIDs 50-54 on the disk.⟦25⟧⟦26⟧Example 3: ⟦27⟧ identity-maps all UIDs and GIDs, meaning IDs inside the container will match the IDs on the disk.

u770ca19399de7da39d69.text: Rolling restart of all Ceph OSDs on this node. Each OSD is restarted only after Ceph reports the previous one is back up and the next one is safe to stop. For non-OSD Ceph daemons, use the cluster-wide endpoint at ⟦0⟧ The 'noout' flag is applied only to the OSDs targeted by this run, so unrelated OSDs on other nodes that fail during the restart window still get out-marked normally. Aborting the resulting task (for example via 'pvesh task stop') triggers a SIGTERM handler that unsets the per-OSD 'noout' if this endpoint set it. Per-daemon progress is checkpointed in Ceph's config-key store ('pve/ceph-bulk-restart/node/<node>'), so an aborted run can be resumed by re-issuing this endpoint with 'resume=1'.
